final_text:
The one that matters most is **#4 — "Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish"** (Stuart-Smith et al., 2026, Conservation Science and Practice).

Why it stands out for the early warning project:

- **It's the proof of concept you're building toward.** The whole point of an early warning system is that a forecast changes what people do. #4 is a documented case where a forecast of marine heatwaves ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño triggered an emergency rescue of a critically endangered species — 25 fish removed from the wild in January 2024, held through 80 days of record heat, and 18 returned after the event subsided. That's the "so what?" of your project made concrete.
- **It shows the full chain: forecast → expert assessment → action.** The paper describes how an expert workshop weighed the forecast risk (>20°C or +~3°C) and decided to act. That decision-making step is exactly where an early warning system has to earn its keep, and it's a useful template for how your lab's outputs could be operationalized with managers.
- **It's recent and current (2026), and it's the only item in the slate that connects MHW forecasting to a real-world management response.** The others are more about the forecasting machinery itself.

The runner-up is **#5 — "Evaluation of 1–14-Day Machine-Learning Forecasts of Marine Heatwaves in the Northern Bay of Bengal Against Persistence Benchmarks"** (Mojumder, 2026). It's the closest methodological match to your project — ML-based MHW forecasting evaluated against persistence baselines — and it's a small, recent study (a B.S. thesis from the University of Dhaka, with code and data on Zenodo), so it's a good quick read on how to benchmark short-range ML MHW forecasts. But it's a single-region evaluation rather than a demonstration of impact.

Worth a look next: **#3** (the seasonal Northeast Pacific ocean forecast system, now in routine real-time operation from October 2026) is relevant if you're thinking about how your early warning outputs could feed into existing seasonal forecasting infrastructure, and **#10** (the DIVAnd-based temperature climatology for Northern Chilean Patagonia) is a useful reference for building the baseline climatology your anomaly detection would sit on.

One caveat: I don't have the project's confirmed state (goals, blockers, milestones) loaded in this conversation, so I'm ranking by fit to the project's stated purpose rather than against specific open blockers. If you'd like, I can pull the full project record and tie the slate items to whatever blockers are currently open.

#4 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

#3 [paper] Comment on egusphere-2026-5844
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2026-5844-rc2
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Providing seasonal ocean forecasts for the Northeast Pacific to support marine resource management and ecosystem variability assessment.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A seasonal ocean forecasting system based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model, forced by GFDL-SPEAR global climate forecasts, with a ~10 km horizontal re…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Northeast Pacific region extending from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea; evaluation uses a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months, assessed against ocean reanalyses and in situ observations.
Abstract:
Abstract. Seasonal ocean forecasts offer critical insights for marine resource management, particularly in regions like the Northeast Pacific where ecosystem variability can have profound impacts on marine life, fisheries, and coastal communities. Under NOAA’s Changing Ecosystems and Fisheries Initiative, we developed a seasonal ocean forecasting system for the Northeast Pacific based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) ocean model coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) sea ice model and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model. The model domain extends from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea with ~10 km horizontal resolution. To evaluate forecast skill, we produced a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months. Forcing for the forecasts was derived from the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory's Seamless System for Prediction and Earth System Research (GFDL-SPEAR) global climate forecast system. Forecasts were assessed using ocean reanalyses and in situ observations, focusing on three ecologically- and societally-relevant variables: sea surface temperature, bottom temperature, and bottom oxygen concentration. Forecast skill varies by region, variable, and season, but generally remains high (anomaly correlation coefficient; ACC>0.5) for lead times of at least several months across all variables and regions. The downscaled forecasts reduce errors relative to the SPEAR global forecasts and in some cases increase ACC, while also enabling predictions of biogeochemical variables. These new forecasts compare favorably to previous downscaled ocean forecasts off the U.S. west coast, with increased ACC and small forecast errors that may be reduced further by future methodological changes. Routine real-time forecasts, available starting in October 2026, will support proactive decision making by managers, industry, and coastal communities.

#10 [paper] Climatology of the sea temperature from long-term in situ observations: Northern Chilean Patagonia
Authors: Cécile Pujol, Alexander Barth, Iván Pérez‐Santos, Pamela Linford, Aïda Alvera Azcarate
Venue: Earth system science data
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-18-8167-2026
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The need for a high-resolution, four-dimensional temperature climatology for Northern Chilean Patagonia to provide reference conditions for detecting anomalies, assessing ecosystem functioning, and identifying long-term trends in a region with complex fjords and channels where satellite observation…
Method (Mycelium's reading): Reconstruction of temperature fields using the Data Interpolating Variational Analysis (DIVAnd) tool from approximately three million in situ observations collected over 75 years, producing monthly fields from the surface to 400 m depth with a horizontal resolution of about 900 m and over 32 vertic…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Northern Chilean Patagonia, including specific features such as Reloncaví Sound, Comau and Puyuhuapi Fjords, Corcovado Gulf, and Ancud Gulf, based on in situ data collected over the past 75 years.
Abstract:
Abstract. Ocean climatologies are essential for understanding the mean state and variability of marine systems, providing reference conditions for detecting anomalies, assessing ecosystem functioning and identifying long-term trends. In this study, we present the first high-resolution, four-dimensional temperature climatology for Northern Chilean Patagonia, a region characterised by the presence of a complex network of fjords and channels. The climatology was generated from approximately three million in situ observations collected over the past 75 years from multiple datasets. Using the Data Interpolating Variational Analysis (DIVAnd) tool, temperature fields were reconstructed with a horizontal resolution of about 900 m and over 32 vertical levels, producing monthly fields from the surface to 400 m depth. The resulting climatology accurately reproduces the main spatial and seasonal temperature patterns reported in previous studies. Surface temperatures show strong summer gradients between the open Pacific and Northern Patagonia, while enclosed regions such as Reloncaví Sound, Comau and Puyuhuapi Fjords exhibit pronounced seasonal amplitude compared with the more stable Corcovado Gulf. Below surface, temperature gradients become smoother and the thermocline deepens in summer, typically ranging between 10 and 50 m. At 100 m depth, temperatures are relatively constant throughout the year, but spatial variations are still observed, with Ancud Gulf and Reloncaví Sound being slightly warmer. This climatology provides a refined and physically consistent representation of the oceanographic structure of Northern Patagonia, offering an essential baseline for future modelling, monitoring and climate-change assessments in a region where satellite observations are limited by persistent cloud cover and complex topography. All climatologies generated in this study are freely available online.

final_text:
The clearest fit is **#4 — "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter: development and application to field records from Uido, Republic of Korea"** (Lim & Hong, 2026, Zenodo).

Why it matters most for Plastic pathways:

- **It is the only item on the slate that is directly about marine litter.** The rest touch the project at best indirectly — #12 (loggerhead turtle habitat use) and #5 (a regional ocean forecast system) are oceanographic context, while #3, #9 (phytoplankton/NPP), #7 (internal waves), #8 (multi-object tracking), #10 (human-rights satellite imagery) and #11 (a lake's hydroclimatic trend) sit in other parts of your feed's interests.
- **It is a methods resource, not just a paper.** The deposit contains the actual code: a three-phase beaching kernel plus six other particle kernels for OceanParcels 3.1.4, the experiment scripts, and the aggregated result files behind every number in the manuscript. That means you can read the approach, verify it, and potentially reuse or adapt the kernel for your own particle-tracking work.
- **It is validated against field records.** The kernel was developed and tested against beaching observations at Uido, South Korea, using ROMS flow fields and particle trajectories — a concrete, reproducible setup rather than a purely theoretical one.
- **It is fresh and open.** It entered the slate on 2026-11-10 and is still current, so the code and results are recent and available.

One caveat: I could not read the project's confirmed state (goals, method, open blockers) for Plastic pathways in this conversation — the project record only showed its members (Jonah Whitcombe, Priya Raman, and you). So this ranking is based on topical fit to the project's subject. If the team has a specific open blocker — say, a need for a validated beaching/deposition model — #4 is almost certainly the item to pull first; if the blocker is elsewhere (e.g., transport modeling at sea), #5's forecast-system analyses might deserve a look too.

Suggested next step: have Jonah or Priya skim #4's README and kernel code to judge whether the OceanParcels setup maps onto your own particle-tracking pipeline. If you want, I can also pull the full text of #4 or any other slate item to go deeper.

Here's the comparison.

## The two grants at a glance

| | #1 – Stronger GOOS | #2 – Antarctica & Southern Ocean |
|---|---|---|
| **Amount** | €50 M | €5–11 M |
| **Deadline** | 16 Feb 2027 | 23 Sep 2027 |
| **Core focus** | Strengthening the *global observing infrastructure* — deploying equipment, running observing-system experiments, network optimisation, technology roadmaps with industry | *Scientific understanding and projections* of the Antarctic/Southern Ocean — ocean–ice–atmosphere interactions, tipping points, ecosystem vulnerability, improving Earth System Models |
| **Geographic scope** | Global, with attention to polar regions, deep sea, areas beyond national jurisdiction | Specifically the Antarctic and Southern Ocean, continental shelves, bottom-water formation regions |

## Which fits Marine heatwave early warning better?

**#1 (GOOS) is the stronger fit**, for a few reasons:

1. **Observation infrastructure is the backbone of an early-warning system.** The project's whole purpose is to detect and forecast marine heatwaves. #1 is explicitly about deploying observation equipment, running observing-system experiments (OSEs/OSSEs), and optimising sensor networks — exactly the kind of work that makes heatwave detection and forecasting more reliable. The project's data-assimilation and ML methods sit naturally inside that infrastructure story.

2. **Geographic scope is broader.** #1 covers the global ocean, including polar regions, so the project's coastal and mid-latitude heatwave work fits without needing to justify a polar focus. #2 is tightly scoped to Antarctica and the Southern Ocean; unless the project has a specific Southern Ocean component, most of its work would fall outside the call's geographic remit.

3. **Expected outcomes align.** #1 asks for strengthened observing capacities, data delivery "fit for purpose," and operational services (it names Copernicus Marine Service explicitly). An early-warning system is precisely a fit-for-purpose service built on observations. #2's expected outcomes are more about long-term projections, tipping-point science, and ecosystem vulnerability — valuable, but a different kind of contribution.

**Where #2 could still make sense:** if the project has a specific interest in how Southern Ocean dynamics (e.g. changes in overturning circulation or bottom-water formation) feed into regional heatwave patterns, #2's emphasis on improving regional coupled models and understanding extreme events in the Southern Ocean could be a relevant angle. But that would be a narrower, more specialised framing.

**One practical note:** #1 is €50 M with a February 2027 deadline, so it's a much bigger, earlier commitment. #2 is smaller and gives you until September 2027. If the project is still in an early stage, #2's longer runway might be easier to work with, even though the thematic fit is looser.

# Judging a call's fit

1. Read the call with `corpus_item` (deadlines, eligibility, amount, whether it is
   still open). If it is closed, say so first.
2. Read who it is for: `projects_get` for a project, `org_lab` for a lab,
   `me_profile` / `me_interests` for the person.
3. Compare concretely: the call's aims against the project's problem and
   method; its eligibility rules (career stage, citizenship, institution type)
   against what you know; its deadline against the project's milestones.
4. Say what fits, what does not, and what you could not check (eligibility you
   cannot see, a budget you do not know). Never guess eligibility.
5. If the question is who should apply, read the `who-should-apply` skill.

Honesty rules, as in Mylo's reports: no scores or percentages, no hype, no
"perfect fit". One plain sentence on the strongest reason and one on the
biggest doubt. Cite the call and the project by #n.

2. Present people by the slots they cover, strongest evidence first. Say the

4. Do not rank people with numbers, and do not judge anyone's eligibility you

#11 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

Setting (Mycelium's reading): Terrestrial, freshwater, and marine ecosystems in EU Member States and Associated Countries, specifically focusing on ecosystems under pressure or restoration priorities within the EU ecosystem typology.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- advancing robust, policy-relevant ecosystem assessment, nature protection and restoration planning activities, and biodiversity trend prediction based on fit for purpose data, thus supporting EU biodiversity and climate objectives;

- strengthened capacity of researchers, practitioners and decision-makers to improve biodiversity monitoring practices and address knowledge gaps via the integration of data and observations across sensors and platforms, ranging from omics-based data (genomic, transcriptomic, metabolomic), various in-situ to satellite-based Earth observation data;

- enhanced usability of in-situ datasets as training and validation resources for statistical, machine learning and advanced AI-based approaches, in support of applications such as habitat classification, ecosystem mapping and biodiversity trend prediction.

Scope:

Achieving the goals of the EU biodiversity strategy for 2030, the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, and assessing progress towards their defined targets, requires coherent, integrated and long-term monitoring approaches, underpinned by FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Re-usable) data systems. Many existing in-situ data collections (i.e. genomic assessments, ground sampling, drone and airborne observations) were not designed with Satellite Remote Sensing integration in mind (i.e. for validation and calibration, integrated data products, or statistical scaling of information) and lack the structure, interface and metadata required to support advanced analytics, including AI. FAIR data on species and ecosystems will also help to ensure that biodiversity preservation is a mainstream feature of other sectors, such as agriculture, transport, energy or the bioeconomy. Demonstration cases should be relevant to EO applications, such as AI-assisted ecosystem and habitat mapping, ensuring interoperability with European and global frameworks such as the Global Ecosystem Typology as well as EUNIS, and aligned with reporting requirements under the Habitats Directive, Birds Directive, Marine Strategy Framewor

Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

In line with the EU Common Fisheries Policy and the revised EU Fisheries Control Regulation, the European Ocean Pact, the Vision for Fisheries and Aquaculture with a 2040 perspective, the strategic guidelines for sustainable and competitive aquaculture, the EU algae initiative, Farm to Fork Strategy, the EU biodiversity strategy for 2030 and the Food 2030 policy framework, project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- economic prosperity is fostered in coastal, rural and urban communities through improved business models, value chain integration and market access for small scale producers that can contribute offering attractive jobs;

- consumers benefit from the availability of locally produced, nutritious, and safe aquatic food following high environmental and social standards;

- more resilient and empowered communities at local and regional levels by fostering innovation in aquatic food value chain and addressing challenges such as climate change, biodiversity loss, and resource management;

- a more competitive and sustainable aquatic food sector by advancing ecosystem-based management practices, digitalization and technological innovation based on the latest scientific research.

Scope:

Small-scale aquatic food production includes small-scale fisheries, recreational fisheries and aquaculture farms that are classified as SMEs. In 2021, small-scale fisheries contributed to 49% of employment in EU fisheries. Together with other maritime activities, small-scale fisheries play a vital role in local economies, particularly in the Mediterranean, where over half of the sector is concentrated. Recreational fisheries are non-commercial fishing activities exploiting marine biological resources for recreation, tourism or sport. While the marketing or sale of catches from recreational fisheries is prohibited, if properly monitored and managed they can contribute to conservation efforts and support community development. According to the Scientific, Technical and Economic Committee for Fisheries, the aquaculture sector in the EU consists primarily of small and family-owned enterprises- especially in the case of mollusk farms. However, small-scale actors often face difficulties in developing and adopting innovative technologies.

Selected proposals should advance knowledge and develop tools, including Nature-based Solutions, for managing and further developing small-scale aquatic food production. They should include, where relevant, both aspects of natural science and technical know-how to improve small-scale aquatic food production as well as issues related to social sciences and humanities (SSH) disciplines, to produce meaningful and significant effects enhancing the societal impact of the related innovation activities. In the frame of SSH, cultural elements such as local traditions related to aquatic food production and consumption could be included. The scope of the topic includes fisheries and aquaculture activities taking place in fresh, brackish and marine waters, such as small-scale fisheries, small-scale mollusk, seaweed and fish farms, recreational fisheries, urban aquaculture and aquaponics.

This could, for example, include diverse data sources (e.g. citizen science, social media) and advance data processing, validation, and interoperability solutions using for example AI, machine learning, and big data analytics to provide actionable insights.

These innovative solutions still need to be tested, operationalised and piloted in the context of the concrete implementation of the EU legislation.

Here's where **Plastic pathways** (#2) stands, plus what's new on its slate and a funding angle.

## Where the project stands

I can see the project is a lab project with three members — Jonah Whitcombe, Priya Raman, and you. However, I could not see any confirmed state for it: no recorded problem, method, stage, milestones, or open blockers. That means either the state hasn't been filled in yet, or it hasn't been confirmed recently — so treat this as "no confirmed picture" rather than "nothing is happening." If the team has been working on it, the app is where the state gets recorded and updated.

## Three most relevant new papers

All three entered the project's slate this week (since 2026-11-10):

1. **#6 — "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter"** (Lim & Hong, 2026, Zenodo). The closest match to the project's core: a three-phase beaching kernel for OceanParcels 3.1.4, validated against field records from Uido, Korea, using ROMS flow fields and particle trajectories. The deposit includes the kernel code, experiment scripts, and aggregated results — directly reusable for a debris-pathways particle-tracking setup.
2. **#10 — "A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery"** (Rong et al., 2026, Remote Sensing). Relevant as a method template: a YOLO11-based detection-and-segmentation framework for low-contrast, curved ocean features in MODIS imagery, with a decade of satellite data applied. The same pattern (automated extraction of a hard-to-see feature from satellite imagery) transfers to detecting and tracking floating debris from space.
3. **#11 — "Basin-scale changes in net primary production from the biogeochemical-Argo array"** (entered 2026-11-13). Less directly about plastic, but it's the strongest example on the slate of the in-situ-to-basin-scale integration approach — the kind of multi-scale observational backbone a debris-pathways project would want to mirror when connecting local field data to regional-scale conclusions.

The other new items (#4, #5, #7, #9) are further afield — Arctic phytoplankton, a forecast-system analysis, a comment, and a multi-agent tracking paper — and I'd rank them below the three above for this project.

## One funding opportunity

**#3 — "A stronger Global Ocean Observing System to enhance Europe's strategic autonomy, climate resilience and biodiversity conservation"** (Horizon Europe, €50,000,000, deadline 2027-02-16, still open).

- **Why it fits:** the call asks for proposals that strengthen global ocean observing networks, close structural gaps, and connect observation to biodiversity and ecosystem knowledge. Plastic pathways sits in the lab's declared "Debris pathways: marine litter tracking" cluster, and the lab's statement is built on combining ocean models, satellite observations and ML to track where floating debris ends up — that is exactly the kind of observation-to-knowledge chain this topic funds. The #6 beaching-kernel work (particle tracking against field records) is a concrete, fundable component: it is a new observational capability for a structurally under-observed problem.
- **The biggest doubt:** the call is heavily oriented toward the GOOS framework, areas beyond national jurisdiction, and biodiversity EOVs. A plastic-pathways proposal would need to be framed as contributing to the observing system (e.g., a debris-observation network or a new EOV-style data stream) rather than as a standalone modelling study. Also, at €50M this is almost certainly a consortium call — the lab would need partners, and I can't see eligibility rules (EU member/associated country requirements, SME participation) in what I've read, so those would need checking in the full call text.
- **Timing:** the deadline is 2027-02-16, giving roughly three months — enough to draft, but not to start from zero.

If the team wants, I can dig into the full text of #3 or #6 next, or look at the other two grants on the slate (#8, #12) to compare fit.

#10 [paper] A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery over the Northern South China Sea
Authors: Guocai Rong, Huanhe Dong, Yuan Kong, Ze Liu, Yong Hui Fang
Venue: Remote Sensing
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18213843
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Automated extraction of internal solitary waves (ISWs) from satellite imagery is challenging due to their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast.
Method (Mycelium's reading): YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, incorporating Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) for curved structures and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for low-contrast features.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea; the framework was also applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020.
Abstract:
Internal solitary waves (ISWs) play an important role in ocean energy transport and mixing, yet their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast make automated extraction from satellite imagery challenging. To address these challenges, this study proposes YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint ISW detection and pixel-level segmentation. Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea was constructed for model training and evaluation. YOLO11-ISW achieved detection Precision, Recall, and F1-score values of 92.01%, 80.73%, and 86.00%, respectively, and segmentation values of 93.14%, 82.60%, and 87.55%, respectively. The model achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the evaluated methods. The segmentation results were further georeferenced to extract ISW crest-line locations, and the framework was applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020 to investigate satellite-observed ISW spatiotemporal variability. The detected ISWs exhibited pronounced spatial clustering, strong spring–summer seasonality, and clear lunar-cycle modulation, consistent with previous observations in the northern South China Sea. These results demonstrate the potential of YOLO11-ISW for automated, long-term, and large-scale monitoring of ISWs using satellite remote sensing imagery.

# Judging a call's fit

1. Read the call with `corpus_item` (deadlines, eligibility, amount, whether it is
   still open). If it is closed, say so first.
2. Read who it is for: `projects_get` for a project, `org_lab` for a lab,
   `me_profile` / `me_interests` for the person.
3. Compare concretely: the call's aims against the project's problem and
   method; its eligibility rules (career stage, citizenship, institution type)
   against what you know; its deadline against the project's milestones.
4. Say what fits, what does not, and what you could not check (eligibility you
   cannot see, a budget you do not know). Never guess eligibility.
5. If the question is who should apply, read the `who-should-apply` skill.

Honesty rules, as in Mylo's reports: no scores or percentages, no hype, no
"perfect fit". One plain sentence on the strongest reason and one on the
biggest doubt. Cite the call and the project by #n.

final_text:
The clearest fit is **#4** — *Code and aggregated results for "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter: development and application to field records from Uido, Republic of Korea"* (Lim & Hong, 2026).

Why it matters most for Plastic pathways:

- **It's the only item on the slate that is squarely about marine litter transport.** The others touch the ocean (phytoplankton, ocean forecasting, internal waves, turtles) but not debris pathways.
- **It's a methods paper with reusable code.** It ships a three-phase beaching kernel plus six other particle kernels for OceanParcels 3.1.4, the experiment scripts, and the aggregated results behind the manuscript — so it's directly adoptable for your own particle-tracking work.
- **It's validated against field records.** The kernel was developed and tested against beaching observations at Uido, Korea, using ROMS flow fields — a concrete, checkable setup rather than a purely theoretical one.
- **It's recent and open.** Entered the slate 2026-11-10, still current, and the deposit includes a reproduction manifest so the numbers are verifiable.

One caveat: the full particle trajectories (~32 GB) and ROMS flow fields (~37 GB) are only available on request, so if you want to run their exact experiments you'd need to ask the authors.

If you'd like, I can pull the full text of #4 to dig into how their beaching kernel works, or check whether any of the other slate items connect to a specific blocker on the project.

final_text:
Here's the comparison:

## #1 — Global Ocean Observing System (GOOS)
- **Amount:** €50M
- **Deadline:** 2027-02-16
- **Core focus:** Strengthening the *infrastructure* of global ocean observation — deploying equipment, running observing system experiments (OSEs/OSSEs), network optimization, technology roadmaps with industry, and closing structural gaps in under-observed regions (deep sea, polar). It's framed around EU strategic autonomy, Copernicus Marine Service, and biodiversity monitoring.
- **What it wants:** A consortium that builds and operates observation capacity at global scale, with a strong governance and policy component.

## #2 — Antarctica & Southern Ocean "Safe Operating Space"
- **Amount:** €5M–€11M
- **Deadline:** 2027-09-23
- **Core focus:** Resolving uncertainties and improving *projections* of the Antarctic/Southern Ocean system — ocean–atmosphere–sea-ice–ice-sheet interactions, tipping points, extreme events, ecosystem vulnerability, and monitoring indicators. It explicitly calls for improving Earth System Models and regional coupled models, and for understanding extreme events and mid-latitude weather.
- **What it wants:** A multidisciplinary research project that advances understanding and predictive capability for a specific region, with policy and assessment outputs (IPCC, IPBES, WOA).

## Which fits Marine heatwave early warning better?

**#2 is the stronger fit.** Here's why:

1. **Method alignment.** Your project is about *forecasting* marine heatwaves — building and evaluating predictive models (your slate includes ML forecast evaluation #8, a regional ocean forecast system analysis #13, and an AI-based ESM #12). #2 explicitly asks for improving ESMs, regional coupled models, and understanding extreme events. That's the same kind of work.

2. **Scope alignment.** #2 is a research grant about understanding and projecting ocean change. Your project sits squarely in that space. #1 is an infrastructure and governance grant — it's about deploying hardware, running OSEs, and coordinating international observation networks. That's a different kind of project, even though it touches the same ocean.

3. **Scale and role.** At €50M, #1 is a flagship infrastructure call where a forecasting project would likely be a sub-component, not the lead. At €5–11M, #2 is a more typical research grant size where a marine heatwave forecasting team could be the core of the proposal.

**One caveat:** #2 is regionally scoped to Antarctica and the Southern Ocean. If your project's focus is on other regions (e.g., the Bay of Bengal, as in #8), you'd need to frame the proposal around Southern Ocean heatwaves specifically, or position your methods as transferable. #1 is globally scoped, so it has no regional constraint — but the infrastructure focus is a harder mismatch.

**Bottom line:** If you can anchor the proposal in the Southern Ocean, #2 is the better home for this project. If your work is firmly in other regions, neither is a perfect fit, but #2's emphasis on extreme events and model improvement still makes it the closer match.

Here's what I found.

## Best-fitting open grant: #5

**"Advancing understanding, modelling and prediction of extreme events in a changing climate"** — still open, deadline **2027-03-04**, €3M–€15M.

Why it fits #1:
- The call explicitly welcomes **AI-based approaches** to predict and project extreme events, and asks for **seamless prediction from short-term weather to sub-seasonal scales** — that's exactly what a marine heatwave early warning system is.
- It names **improved early warning systems** as an expected outcome, and covers phenomena from continental to local scale, which matches the project's coastal focus.
- It encourages integration with **Copernicus and Destination Earth**, and international cooperation with low- to middle-income countries — both natural for an ocean forecasting project.

The other open grant on the project's slate, #20 (NSF OTIC), is about **instrumentation development** — a weaker match for a forecasting/data-assimilation project unless you have a hardware component. #10 (Global Ocean Observing System) is about observing infrastructure and biodiversity, not prediction.

Biggest doubt: the call is broad and competitive (up to €15M), and it expects a **hierarchy of models including high-resolution Earth system models** — the project's ML/data-assimilation core fits, but you'd want to show how it plugs into that hierarchy, not just stand alone.

## Who should lead

From the lab's declared profiles:
- **Tomás Ferreira-Lind (#18)** is the strongest lead: he declares **circulation and turbulence** and **physics-informed ML**, and the nightly ranking flagged his fast, physics-informed surrogates for ocean models as directly relevant to the call's "seamless prediction and projection" requirement.
- **You (#14)** are the natural co-lead/PI: you declare **ocean extremes** and **data assimilation with ML**, and the ranking noted the lab's marine heatwave forecasting focus as directly addressing the call.

Gaps no one in the lab covers: **digital twins**, **Copernicus**, and **Destination Earth** — the call mentions all three, so you'd want a partner who can speak to at least one.

## Partners outside the lab

I can't suggest specific people here: **collaborator search is turned off on this instance**, so I have no view of who outside the lab has consented to be suggested. What I can say is what the call itself points to:

- **JRC (European Commission's Joint Research Centre)** — the call says selected proposals may involve them for scientific advice and technical support via the Copernicus Emergency Management Service.
- **Copernicus / Destination Earth** communities — integration or interoperability is explicitly encouraged.
- **ESA FutureEO** — successful consortia are asked to coordinate with ESA's FutureEO projects for satellite data access, which would suit Priya's satellite oceanography background.
- **Low- to middle-income country partners** — encouraged for capacity building, and automatically eligible for Horizon Europe funding.

If you'd like, I can pull the full details of any of the papers on the project's slate (#21, #22, #26, #27) to help build the scientific case for the application.

results.name: read_skill
results.content:
# Judging a call's fit

1. Read the call with `corpus_item` (deadlines, eligibility, amount, whether it is
   still open). If it is closed, say so first.
2. Read who it is for: `projects_get` for a project, `org_lab` for a lab,
   `me_profile` / `me_interests` for the person.
3. Compare concretely: the call's aims against the project's problem and
   method; its eligibility rules (career stage, citizenship, institution type)
   against what you know; its deadline against the project's milestones.
4. Say what fits, what does not, and what you could not check (eligibility you
   cannot see, a budget you do not know). Never guess eligibility.
5. If the question is who should apply, read the `who-should-apply` skill.

Honesty rules, as in Mylo's reports: no scores or percentages, no hype, no
"perfect fit". One plain sentence on the strongest reason and one on the
biggest doubt. Cite the call and the project by #n.

# Who should apply

1. Read the call (`corpus_item`). Then `knowledge_people_for_call`, which
   returns, per person, the requirement slots they cover and the evidence tier
   of each: **declared** (they said so in their profile), **demonstrated**
   (their own papers), **confirmed in conversation** (they told Mylo and said
   yes when asked).
2. Present people by the slots they cover, strongest evidence first. Say the
   tier in plain words for each claim ("from her papers", "she told Mylo in
   October").
3. Name gaps: slots no one covers. Outside-the-lab suggestions only appear when
   collaborator search is on and people consented; never speculate beyond them.
4. Do not rank people with numbers, and do not judge anyone's eligibility you
   cannot see.

Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- Improved understanding of past and present extreme events in the context of climate change in Europe and globally, as well as the interaction between different hazards, their cumulative and/or cascading effects.

- Enhanced seamless prediction and projection modelling and attribution capabilities for extreme events and their likelihood to support preparedness, response and resilience to climate change by EU and national and regional actors. The EU Union Preparedness Strategy, the EU Adaptation Strategy and the European Climate Adaptation Plan can act as a guidance in these efforts.

- Up-to-date contributions towards latest climate science, risk assessments, adaptation strategies and policies and improved early warning systems for single and multi-hazard events.

Scope:

Climate change is intensifying the frequency and severity of extreme events. Understanding and predicting extreme events and the interaction between different types of hazards is critical for building resilience and safeguarding communities.

Actions are expected to draw upon multiple lines of evidence from a hierarchy of models (including high resolution Earth system models and digital twins) and data of past and recent climate to further our understanding of processes, pre-conditioning and causality driving extreme events under climate change conditions, including anthropogenic factors and internal variability. Other innovative and efficient modelling and analysis methods, including AI-based approaches, to better predict, emulate and reveal climate change related extreme and unprecedented high impact events, and to capture their likelihood are particularly welcome.

Extreme events should be addressed in their broadest sense and types, encompassing isolated, compound or cascading events affecting lives, livelihoods, ecosystems, socio-economic sectors and infrastructures, from large-scale continental to local-scale phenomena.

Actions should encompass quantitative intercomparisons, retrospective analyses, lessons learned and case studies of recent emblematic and diverse extreme events, and demonstrate the corresponding progress offered by the project in terms of improved understanding, comprehensive integration of multiple lines of evidence, and seamless (e.g. from short-term weather to sub-seasonal and multi-decadal scales) prediction and projection capabilities and skills.

The work is expected to support the future European Climate Risk Assessment (EUCRA)[1], for example through storylines on extremes or other approaches. Project outcomes should demonstrate clear benefits for the prediction and attribution of extreme events and contribute to the activities of the EU Mission on Adaptation to Climate Change.

Cooperation with global, EU, national and regional actors in the field of Disaster Risk Reduction and climate adaptation, including through integration into or interoperability with Copernicus, Destination Earth and other relevant initiatives is encouraged. In addition, international cooperation with low- to middle-income countries automatically eligible for Horizon Europe funding[2] is encouraged in support of climate resilience efforts, especially for capacity building.

Selected proposals may consider the involvement of the European Commission's Joint Research Centre (JRC) whose contribution could consist of scientific advice and technical support in the context of the Copernicus Emergency Management Service and transfer of relevant research outcomes to operations.

## Three most relevant new papers

All three entered the project's slate this week (since 2026-11-10):

1. **#6 — "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter"** (Lim & Hong, 2026, Zenodo). The closest match to the project: a three-phase beaching kernel plus particle-tracking scripts for OceanParcels, validated against field records from Uido, Korea, using ROMS flow fields. If Plastic pathways involves particle tracking of debris, this is the one to read first — the code and aggregated results are all there.
2. **#10 — "A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery"** (Rong et al., 2026, *Remote Sensing*). Not about plastic, but a useful template: a YOLO11-based detector that handles low-contrast, curved features in satellite imagery. If any part of the project involves spotting debris or plumes from space, the detection-and-segmentation approach is directly transferable.
3. **#5 — "Daily Analyses of the Pacific Regional Ocean Forecast System model"** (in slate since 2026-11-10). Relevant as the operational forecasting context: daily analyses of a regional ocean forecast system, the kind of model output a debris-pathways project would typically be coupled to.

**#3 — "A stronger Global Ocean Observing System to enhance Europe's strategic autonomy, climate resilience and biodiversity conservation"** (Horizon Europe, €50,000,000, deadline 2027-02-16, still open).

The strongest application would frame the debris work as filling a gap in the observing system (e.g., in-situ beaching records plus satellite data feeding a shared, interoperable data product).

#10 [paper] A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery over the Northern South China Sea
Authors: Guocai Rong, Huanhe Dong, Yuan Kong, Ze Liu, Yong Hui Fang
Venue: Remote Sensing
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18213843
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Automated extraction of internal solitary waves (ISWs) from satellite imagery is challenging due to their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast.
Method (Mycelium's reading): YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, incorporating Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) for curved structures and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for low-contrast features.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea; the framework was also applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020.
Abstract:
Internal solitary waves (ISWs) play an important role in ocean energy transport and mixing, yet their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast make automated extraction from satellite imagery challenging. To address these challenges, this study proposes YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint ISW detection and pixel-level segmentation. Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea was constructed for model training and evaluation. YOLO11-ISW achieved detection Precision, Recall, and F1-score values of 92.01%, 80.73%, and 86.00%, respectively, and segmentation values of 93.14%, 82.60%, and 87.55%, respectively. The model achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the evaluated methods. The segmentation results were further georeferenced to extract ISW crest-line locations, and the framework was applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020 to investigate satellite-observed ISW spatiotemporal variability. The detected ISWs exhibited pronounced spatial clustering, strong spring–summer seasonality, and clear lunar-cycle modulation, consistent with previous observations in the northern South China Sea. These results demonstrate the potential of YOLO11-ISW for automated, long-term, and large-scale monitoring of ISWs using satellite remote sensing imagery.

**1. #6 — 14th International Conference on Machine Intelligence Theory and Applications**

**Paper to strengthen the application:**
- **#32** (Toedtli et al., 2026) — *Ensemble Covariance Propagation with Machine Learning Weather Prediction Models in a Realistic Data Assimilation System*. This is a proof-of-concept for integrating MLWP models (GraphCast) into a classical DA cycling system, which is exactly the methodological bridge your heatwave project needs. Citing it would show the manuscript is grounded in the current state of ML-DA integration.
- Alternatively, **#29** (Ali & Schulz-Stellenfleth, 2026) — *Toward real-time wave forecasting via data-driven reduced-order modeling with data assimilation* — is a strong fit if the manuscript leans on reduced-order + DA for operational coastal forecasting.

**Deadline: 2026-11-15 (in 2 days)** — manuscript

**Who fits:**

**Paper to strengthen the application:**

This review covers data integration across observing platforms, remote sensing, and management-focused applications — all of which are central to the Plastic pathways project. It would anchor the manuscript in the broader computing-for-ocean-science context.
- Alternatively, **#36** (Durand et al., 2026) — *Learning-Based Methods and the Future of Numerical Ocean and Sea-Ice Modeling* — if the manuscript emphasizes the computational methods side (hybrid modeling, emulators) rather than the data/communication side.

---

**Caveats:**
- I could not open the project records directly (the system denied access to #1 and #2 as project references), so I inferred project-to-deadline fit from the lab's feed and declared interests. If either project has a specific milestone tied to one of these deadlines, that would sharpen the match.

#29 [paper] Toward real-time wave forecasting via data-driven reduced-order modeling with data assimilation
Authors: Naseem Ali, Johannes Schulz‐Stellenfleth
Venue: Applied Ocean Research
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apor.2026.105282
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): real-time wave forecasting
Method (Mycelium's reading): data-driven reduced-order modeling with data assimilation
Abstract:
Reliable wave forecasts are a cornerstone of coastal risk management and offshore operations, yet operational products remain expensive to generate at high resolution and can be insufficiently calibrated for decision-making under uncertainty. We present a hybrid forecasting framework that couples data-driven reduced-order modeling with sequential data assimilation to produce flow-dependent, spatially coherent ensembles of significant wave height over the North Sea. The approach learns a nonlinear manifold of sea-state variability with a convolutional autoencoder trained on WAM wave model, then advances the system in a delay-embedded latent space using a control-aware linear dynamical model driven by low-dimensional controls extracted from wind forecasts. Uncertainty is propagated with an ensemble formulation, and buoy observations are assimilated using a deterministic ensemble square-root filter with innovation-based adaptive inflation to maintain reliability during energetic events. The proposed system reproduces the timing and magnitude of storm growth–peak–decay across the buoy network, while preserving physically consistent basin-scale storm footprints in reconstructed fields. Errors are spatially organized and regime dependent, concentrating near storm maxima where wind–wave misalignment, swell influence, and representativeness effects are strongest, but the assimilation layer mitigates drift and reduces persistent offsets without introducing spatial artifacts. Beyond forecasting, we introduce an observability metric derived from the posterior latent covariance and the decoder sensitivity, yielding time-varying maps that identify where additional in-situ measurements would most reduce forecast uncertainty. The introduced method provides a computationally efficient, uncertainty-aware alternative that bridges physics-based spectral modeling and purely data-driven prediction for operational decision support.

The field of operational oceanography is undergoing a significant evolution with the increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) methods, which are complementing and, in some cases, redefining traditional numerical modeling approaches. This review explores how AI methods—particularly model-based autoregressive emulators, hybrid modeling, and end-to-end model-free approaches—are reshaping the representation of ocean and sea-ice dynamics in operational systems. Problem (Mycelium's reading): To examine the current landscape of AI and machine learning applications in ocean sciences, identifying key uses, emerging trends, and challenges.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Literature-synthesis workflow supported by Schlitsummarizer and full-text extraction methods.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Ocean sciences research literature covering physical oceanography, coastal hazards, marine biogeochemistry, ecology, remote sensing, acoustics, marine geology, and applied ocean engineering.
Abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are increasingly used in ocean sciences to analyze large, complex, and unevenly sampled datasets from satellites, autonomous platforms, sensors, vessels, and genomic tools. This review examines how AI and ML are being applied across major areas of ocean research, including physical oceanography, coastal hazards, marine biogeochemistry, ecology, remote sensing, acoustics, marine geology, and applied ocean engineering. Using a literature-synthesis workflow supported by Schlitsummarizer and full-text extraction methods, this paper identifies key applications, emerging trends, research gaps, and limitations in ocean-based ML. The review shows that ML is particularly useful for predicting surface currents, reconstructing subsurface ocean conditions, forecasting waves, estimating biogeochemical variables, classifying marine organisms and habitats, improving remote-sensing products, and supporting autonomous observing systems. Emerging trends include the growth of deep learning, physics-informed machine learning, explainable AI, data integration across observing platforms, and management-focused applications related to climate adaptation, coastal planning, fisheries, and environmental monitoring. However, major challenges remain, including sparse and biased ocean observations, limited data from deep-ocean and polar regions, validation bias, poor model transferability, class imbalance in ecological datasets, black-box model behavior, and uncertainty under changing climate conditions. Overall, this review argues that AI and ML are valuable tools for expanding ocean observation and prediction, but they must be used alongside oceanographic knowledge, careful validation, and transparent interpretation to ensure reliable scientific and management outcomes.

final_text:
The paper that matters most for the Marine heatwave early warning project is **#5 — "Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish"** (Stuart-Smith et al., 2026, Conservation Science and Practice).

**Why it stands out:**

- **It's the clearest real-world example of an early warning system actually working end-to-end.** Forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño flagged a high risk of marine heatwaves; an expert workshop assessed the forecasted extremes (>20°C or +~3°C) as a severe threat; and that assessment triggered a pre-emptive rescue of 25 red handfish before the heatwave hit. The in-situ temperatures then exceeded records — 80 days more than 2°C above the long-term mean summer temperature — confirming the warning was warranted.

- **It directly models the "forecast → decision → action" loop** that an early warning project is built around. The paper documents how a forecast was translated into a concrete management decision, with approvals, timing, and post-release survival confirmation (18 of 25 fish returned and surviving after 2 months).

- **It's the most recent and most directly on-topic item in the slate.** It entered the slate on 2026-11-10 and is marked as new.

**The other strong candidates:**

- **#6** (Mojumder, 2026) is a direct evaluation of 1–14-day ML forecasts of marine heatwaves against persistence benchmarks — very relevant to the forecasting methodology side, but it's a B.S. thesis dataset (Zenodo) rather than a full published study, so it's more of a methodological reference than a strategic one.

- **#3** (Comment on egusphere-2026-5844) describes a seasonal ocean forecasting system for the Northeast Pacific with high skill (ACC > 0.5) at multi-month lead times, now producing routine real-time forecasts from October 2026. It's relevant as a forecasting-systems benchmark, but it's broader than MHWs specifically.

So if you want one paper to anchor the project's rationale — *why* early warning matters and *how* a forecast can drive a timely, effective response — **#5** is the one.

#5 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Providing seasonal ocean forecasts for the Northeast Pacific to support marine resource management and ecosystem variability assessment.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A seasonal ocean forecasting system based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model, forced by GFDL-SPEAR global climate forecasts, with a ~10 km horizontal re…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Northeast Pacific region extending from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea; evaluation uses a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months, assessed against ocean reanalyses and in situ observations.
Abstract:
Abstract. Seasonal ocean forecasts offer critical insights for marine resource management, particularly in regions like the Northeast Pacific where ecosystem variability can have profound impacts on marine life, fisheries, and coastal communities. Under NOAA’s Changing Ecosystems and Fisheries Initiative, we developed a seasonal ocean forecasting system for the Northeast Pacific based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) ocean model coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) sea ice model and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model. The model domain extends from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea with ~10 km horizontal resolution. To evaluate forecast skill, we produced a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months. Forcing for the forecasts was derived from the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory's Seamless System for Prediction and Earth System Research (GFDL-SPEAR) global climate forecast system. Forecasts were assessed using ocean reanalyses and in situ observations, focusing on three ecologically- and societally-relevant variables: sea surface temperature, bottom temperature, and bottom oxygen concentration. Forecast skill varies by region, variable, and season, but generally remains high (anomaly correlation coefficient; ACC>0.5) for lead times of at least several months across all variables and regions. The downscaled forecasts reduce errors relative to the SPEAR global forecasts and in some cases increase ACC, while also enabling predictions of biogeochemical variables. These new forecasts compare favorably to previous downscaled ocean forecasts off the U.S. west coast, with increased ACC and small forecast errors that may be reduced further by future methodological changes. Routine real-time forecasts, available starting in October 2026, will support proactive decision making by managers, industry, and coastal communities.

# Judging a call's fit

2. Read who it is for: `projects_get` for a project, `org_lab` for a lab,
   `me_profile` / `me_interests` for the person.
3. Compare concretely: the call's aims against the project's problem and
   method; its eligibility rules (career stage, citizenship, institution type)
   against what you know; its deadline against the project's milestones.
4. Say what fits, what does not, and what you could not check (eligibility you
   cannot see, a budget you do not know). Never guess eligibility.
5. If the question is who should apply, read the `who-should-apply` skill.

Honesty rules, as in Mylo's reports: no scores or percentages, no hype, no
"perfect fit". One plain sentence on the strongest reason and one on the

## Corrected answer

### 1. Best-fitting open grant

**#19 — Innovative Solutions for mitigating the environmental impact of waterborne transport in marine and aquatic Ecosystems (ZEWT Partnership)** is still the strongest fit, but I need to be more precise about *why*:

- #19 is about the environmental impact of **waterborne transport** (shipping, ports, inland waterways) on marine and aquatic ecosystems, with a specific focus on **renewable low- and zero-carbon fuels** and their pollution/spill risks. It asks for modelling of pollution sources, abatement/mitigation systems (TRL 5), and response scenarios.
- The Plastic pathways project (#4) is about **plastic transport and pathways** in the ocean (Lagrangian particle tracking, satellite-derived currents, ML nowcasting). The overlap is real but narrower than I first said: both deal with *how things move through water and impact ecosystems*, and both involve *modelling transport and pollution*. But #19's core is **fuel/transport pollution**, not plastic debris per se.

You're right — I rounded. Here's the corrected summary, using only what the items actually say.

## Where the project stands

Mylo's record for **Plastic pathways** (#2) is thin: three members — Jonah Whitcombe, Priya Raman, and you — but no confirmed goals, method, stage, milestones, or blockers on file. So I can't tell you how far along the work is; that record may be out of date or never filled in. Updating the project's state in the app would let me give a sharper review next time.

## Three most relevant new papers

1. **#7 — "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter: development and application to field records from Uido, Republic of Korea"** (Lim & Hong, 2026, Zenodo). The most directly on-point item: a three-phase beaching kernel plus six other particle kernels for OceanParcels 3.1.4, with scripts and aggregated results, validated against field records using ROMS flow fields. If Plastic pathways involves particle tracking of debris to shore, this is the one to read first — the code and results are deposited and reproducible.
2. **#12 — "A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery over the Northern South China Sea"** (Rong et al., 2026, Remote Sensing). A methodological template rather than a plastic study: YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11 framework for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, using Dynamic Snake Convolution for curved crest lines and CBAM for low-contrast features. #12 [paper] A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery over the Northern South China Sea
Authors: Guocai Rong, Huanhe Dong, Yuan Kong, Ze Liu, Yong Hui Fang
Venue: Remote Sensing
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18213843
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Automated extraction of internal solitary waves (ISWs) from satellite imagery is challenging due to their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast.
Method (Mycelium's reading): YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, incorporating Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) for curved structures and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for low-contrast features.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea; the framework was also applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020.
Abstract:
Internal solitary waves (ISWs) play an important role in ocean energy transport and mixing, yet their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast make automated extraction from satellite imagery challenging. To address these challenges, this study proposes YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint ISW detection and pixel-level segmentation. Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea was constructed for model training and evaluation. YOLO11-ISW achieved detection Precision, Recall, and F1-score values of 92.01%, 80.73%, and 86.00%, respectively, and segmentation values of 93.14%, 82.60%, and 87.55%, respectively. The model achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the evaluated methods. The segmentation results were further georeferenced to extract ISW crest-line locations, and the framework was applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020 to investigate satellite-observed ISW spatiotemporal variability. The detected ISWs exhibited pronounced spatial clustering, strong spring–summer seasonality, and clear lunar-cycle modulation, consistent with previous observations in the northern South China Sea. These results demonstrate the potential of YOLO11-ISW for automated, long-term, and large-scale monitoring of ISWs using satellite remote sensing imagery.

Here's the picture across both projects.

**The two most urgent deadlines**

1. **#14 — 10th International Conference on Geoinformatics and Data Analysis** — manuscript due **2026-11-20** (7 days). It's on the slate of *Marine heatwave early warning* (#1).
2. **#30 — 47th IEEE International Geoscience and Remote Sensing Symposium (IGARSS)** — abstract and manuscript due **2027-01-11** (about 2 months). It's on the slate of *Plastic pathways* (#3).

Everything else in the 60-day window is either a general feed item or a fellowship; these two are the only ones tied to your projects.

**Who fits each**

The ranking can only go on declared profiles for lab-mates, so treat these as starting points, not verdicts:

- **#14 (Geoinformatics & Data Analysis):** closest profile match is **Priya Raman** (#6, 59%), with you (#4, 58%) and **Jonah Whitcombe** (#5, 58%) close behind. Priya's declared satellite oceanography and coastal water quality sit naturally with a geoinformatics venue.
- **#30 (IGARSS):** again **Priya** leads (62%), then you (60%) and Jonah (59%). IGARSS is a remote-sensing venue, so Priya's satellite oceanography is the strongest declared fit; Jonah's Lagrangian analysis would pair well if the paper is about debris tracking from space.

**Which recent paper would strengthen each application**

- For **#14**, the strongest recent item on the heatwave slate is **#35** — *Evaluation of 1–14-Day Machine-Learning Forecasts of Marine Heatwaves in the Northern Bay of Bengal Against Persistence Benchmarks* (Mojumder, 2026). It's a direct ML-forecasting evaluation of marine heatwaves, which is exactly the project's core question, and it entered the slate on 2026-11-10.
- For **#30**, the best recent fit on the plastic pathways slate is **#36** — *A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter: development and application to field records from Uido, Republic of Korea* (Lim & Hong, 2026). It's a particle-tracking/beaching study with field validation, squarely in the debris-pathways space, and it's new on the slate (2026-11-10).

One caveat: the requirement slots for both calls haven't been read yet, so I can't confirm coverage of specific roles (e.g., who would lead the remote-sensing methods vs. the oceanography). If you'd like, I can dig into either call's full requirements and re-check who covers what.

final_text:
The paper that matters most for the Marine heatwave early warning project is **#5 — "Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish"** (Stuart-Smith et al., 2026, Conservation Science and Practice).

**Why it stands out:**

1. **It's the only paper in the slate that shows a marine heatwave forecast actually triggering a real-world action.** Ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño, forecasts indicated high MHW risk; an expert workshop used that forecast to trigger an emergency rescue of 25 red handfish in January 2024. That's the exact loop your project is building toward — forecast → decision → response — demonstrated end-to-end.

2. **It gives you a concrete template for the "early warning" part of your project.** The paper documents how the forecast was interpreted (extremes >20°C or +~3°C flagged as severe threat), how approvals were coordinated across commonwealth, state and institutional levels, and how the intervention was timed and released. That's a worked example of turning a forecast into a management protocol.

3. **It's directly on your declared interests** (marine heatwave prediction, SST forecasting) and on the project's core question of what makes an early warning actionable.

**The runner-up is #6** — the 1–14-day ML MHW forecast evaluation in the Northern Bay of Bengal — because it's the closest methodological match to your ML-for-data-assimilation interest, but it's a thesis code/data release with a thin abstract, so it's more of a methods reference than a strategic one.

The other papers in the slate are useful but further from the project's center: #3 is a seasonal (not extreme-event) Northeast Pacific forecast system, #10 is Arctic turbulence parameterization, #11 is an AI-coupled Earth system model, and #12 is a data release with no abstract visible to me.

#3 [paper] Comment on egusphere-2026-5844
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2026-5844-rc2
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Providing seasonal ocean forecasts for the Northeast Pacific to support marine resource management and ecosystem variability assessment.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A seasonal ocean forecasting system based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model, forced by GFDL-SPEAR global climate forecasts, with a ~10 km horizontal re…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Northeast Pacific region extending from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea; evaluation uses a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months, assessed against ocean reanalyses and in situ observations.
Abstract:
Abstract. Seasonal ocean forecasts offer critical insights for marine resource management, particularly in regions like the Northeast Pacific where ecosystem variability can have profound impacts on marine life, fisheries, and coastal communities. Under NOAA’s Changing Ecosystems and Fisheries Initiative, we developed a seasonal ocean forecasting system for the Northeast Pacific based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) ocean model coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) sea ice model and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model. The model domain extends from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea with ~10 km horizontal resolution. To evaluate forecast skill, we produced a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months. Forcing for the forecasts was derived from the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory's Seamless System for Prediction and Earth System Research (GFDL-SPEAR) global climate forecast system. Forecasts were assessed using ocean reanalyses and in situ observations, focusing on three ecologically- and societally-relevant variables: sea surface temperature, bottom temperature, and bottom oxygen concentration. Forecast skill varies by region, variable, and season, but generally remains high (anomaly correlation coefficient; ACC>0.5) for lead times of at least several months across all variables and regions. The downscaled forecasts reduce errors relative to the SPEAR global forecasts and in some cases increase ACC, while also enabling predictions of biogeochemical variables. These new forecasts compare favorably to previous downscaled ocean forecasts off the U.S. west coast, with increased ACC and small forecast errors that may be reduced further by future methodological changes. Routine real-time forecasts, available starting in October 2026, will support proactive decision making by managers, industry, and coastal communities.
