#5 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

#10 [paper] Data‐Driven Parameterization of Arctic Ocean Turbulent Mixing
Authors: Rafael Sebastian Reiss, Lisanne Blok, Nicholas Leonard, Kate Oglethorpe, Alberto C. Naveira Garabato, Colm-cille P. Caulfield, Ali Mashayek
Venue: Geophysical Research Letters
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1029/2026gl123721

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Arctic Ocean turbulent mixing is poorly characterized due to sparse observations, limitations of conventional parameterizations, and incomplete understanding, despite its importance for regional dynamics and global overturning.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Training gradient-boosted decision trees on global microstructure turbulence data to predict turbulent dissipation from hydrographic variables, using spatial block cross-validation for evaluation.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Global microstructure turbulence data (>5,000 profiles) for training; pan-Arctic hydrographic observations and high-resolution model output for application.
Abstract:
Abstract Turbulent mixing may become increasingly important in a changing Arctic Ocean, influencing regional dynamics and global overturning. Arctic turbulence remains poorly characterized due to sparse observations, limitations of conventional parameterizations, and incomplete understanding. We train gradient‐boosted decision trees on global microstructure turbulence data (>5,000 profiles; ∼ data points) to predict turbulent dissipation from more widely available hydrography. Global training is essential for skill across non‐Arctic and Arctic regions (, 75% within a factor of 2 of observations; = 0.47–0.55 under spatial block cross‐validation). Applied to pan‐Arctic hydrographic observations, predictions show enhanced dissipation along margins and shelves and weaker values in basin interiors, consistent with current understanding. Applied to high‐resolution model output, predictions reveal diffusivities and a basin‐integrated irreversible buoyancy flux consistent with observations, yet markedly different from the common K‐Profile Parameterization—with implications for simulated tracer transport. Our parameterization can help assess climate‐mixing feedbacks in projections while physics‐based parameterizations mature.

Abstract:
Earth system models underpin climate projections, but their cost limits how many scenarios, ensemble members and impact pathways can be explored. Machine-learning weather models forecast as skillfully as physics-based models at a fraction of the cost, yet coupled to an ocean they have produced weak El Nino variability or have learned it from climate-model output, and none carries the climate through rivers to the people exposed to it. Here we present Rescene-ESM, an Earth system model whose coupler, YAHO, yokes a frozen 20.8-million-parameter AI weather model to physically formulated ocean, sea-ice, land, river, carbon and energy components constrained by observations. Adding the couplings one at a time shows what each contributes: over a climatological ocean the AI atmosphere varies from year to year by a third of the observed amount over the oceans, and an interactive mixed layer, an equatorial wave ocean, the residual of the observed sea surface temperature (SST) equation as stochastic forcing and the land's moisture flux raise this step by step and bring El Nino and its teleconnections, leaving the mean climate almost unchanged. The full model simulates about 1,000 years per day on one graphics processing unit, holds the observed climate for a thousand years without drift, reproduces the observed 1979-2022 global warming, carries forced change with a physically based structure around the frozen network (transient climate response 1.60 K), routes runoff to 212 river gauges with a median seasonal-cycle correlation of 0.79 and, driven by emissions, separates the heatwave exposure of an SSP1 and an SSP3 world by a factor of 4.7 in 2081-2100, three-quarters of it through the warmer climate.

final_text:
Here's how the two stack up against the Marine heatwave early warning project:

**#1 — GOOS / OceanEye (€50M, deadline 2027-02-16)**
This one is about *observation infrastructure*: deploying equipment, running observing system experiments, network optimization, and closing structural gaps in under-observed regions. The project's core — ML-based MHW forecasting and data assimilation — is a *use* of observations, not an observation system itself. The fit is indirect: you could frame the early-warning system as a "fit-for-purpose data delivery" service that justifies new observing capacity, but the call's center of gravity is infrastructure and governance, not forecasting.

**#2 — Antarctica & Southern Ocean (€5–11M, deadline 2027-09-23)**
This one is about *understanding and projecting* the Southern Ocean: improving ESMs and regional coupled models, resolving uncertainties in near/mid/long-term changes, and explicitly calls out **extreme events** as in scope. That's much closer to what the project does — forecasting extremes, improving model-based projections, and connecting them to ecosystem vulnerability. The catch is geographic: the project's current work (Bay of Bengal ML forecasts, Pacific regional ocean forecast system, red handfish response in Australia) is not Southern Ocean. You'd need to anchor the proposal in Antarctic/Southern Ocean MHWs specifically.

**Bottom line:** #2 fits the project's *method and goals* better (extreme-event forecasting, model improvement, ecosystem impacts). #1 fits better only if you reframe the project around building new observing capacity for MHW detection. If the lab can credibly point at Southern Ocean heatwaves as a target region, #2 is the stronger match.

#7 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

Here's the picture across both projects.

## The two most urgent deadlines

**1. WHOI GFD Summer Graduate Research Fellowship — #36**
- Deadline: **2027-02-05** (application)
- In the slate of **both** projects (#26 Marine heatwave early warning and #27 Plastic pathways)
- Ten-week residential fellowship at Woods Hole for graduate students working on the nonlinear dynamics of rotating, stratified fluids — oceanography, geophysics, applied math, etc.
- **Who fits:** The nightly ranking names **Tomás Ferreira-Lind (#7)** first — his declared physics-informed ML for coastal circulation and turbulence maps directly onto the fellowship's fluid-dynamics focus. **You (#2)** are named second, on the strength of your data-assimilation and SST-forecasting work. Tomás is on the heatwave project; you're on both.
- **Paper to strengthen it:** **#38 "Data-Driven Parameterization of Arctic Ocean Turbulent Mixing"** (Reiss et al., 2026, GRL) — it's in the heatwave project's slate and is squarely about using ML to characterize turbulent mixing in a stratified, rotating fluid. It's the most on-point recent paper for a GFD fellowship application. Tomás's declared turbulence interests make it a natural anchor for his application.

**2. 47th IEEE International Geoscience and Remote Sensing Symposium (IGARSS) — #32**
- Deadline: **2027-01-11** (abstract and manuscript, same date)
- In the slate of **Plastic pathways (#27)** only
- **Who fits:** The ranking names **Priya Raman (#4)** as the closest profile match (satellite oceanography, coastal water quality), then you (#2), then Jonah (#3). Priya is on the plastic pathways project.
- **Paper to strengthen it:** **#34 "A LiDAR-based reconstruction reveals increasing Arctic phytoplankton production during low-light winter-shoulder period"** (Zhang et al., 2026, Science Advances) — it's in the plastic pathways slate and is a strong satellite-remote-sensing paper (spaceborne LiDAR, bio-optical retrieval, MODIS). It's open access (PMC13754007), so you can pull the full text in the app if you want to mine it for the proposal. For a plastic-pathways framing, you could also lean on **#37 "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter"** (Lim & Hong, 2026), which is also in the slate and directly about marine-litter particle tracking — but #34 is the stronger remote-sensing paper for an IGARSS submission.

## Caveats
- The fellowship and conference requirement slots haven't been read by Mycelium yet, so the "who fits" above is **profile fit only** (declared interests), not a confirmed slot-by-slot match.

#34 [paper] A LiDAR-based reconstruction reveals increasing Arctic phytoplankton production during low-light winter-shoulder period.
Authors: Zhenhua Zhang, Peng Chen, Siqi Zhang, Delu Pan
Venue: Science Advances
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aej4633
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Arctic marine productivity is traditionally considered concentrated in the sunlit season, yet low-light winter-shoulder periods remain poorly constrained because passive ocean color observations require sufficient solar illumination.
Method (Mycelium's reading): The authors used 2.39 million spaceborne LiDAR profiles from CALIOP (2006–2023) to reconstruct Arctic net primary production (NPP). A bio-optical retrieval model was trained using MODIS-constrained observations under illuminated conditions, and low-light estimates were generated as physically const…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Arctic region, specifically marginal seas and seasonal ice-edge regions, using spaceborne LiDAR data from 2006 to 2023.
Abstract:
Arctic marine productivity is traditionally considered concentrated in the sunlit season, yet low-light winter-shoulder periods remain poorly constrained because passive ocean color observations require sufficient solar illumination. Here, we use 2.39 million spaceborne LiDAR profiles from CALIOP (2006–2023) to reconstruct Arctic net primary production (NPP) and evaluate how active-sensor observations reduce this seasonal blind spot. The bio-optical retrieval model was trained using MODIS-constrained observations under illuminated conditions; accordingly, low-light estimates represent physically constrained extrapolations beyond the primary MODIS-observable training domain rather than direct NPP measurements. Within this framework, LiDAR increases winter half-year observational coverage from ∼20 to 30% to ∼70 to 75% and reveals widespread low-light winter-shoulder production across marginal seas and seasonal ice-edge regions. Pan-Arctic NPP integrated over this period increased at an estimated rate of 0.75 Tg C year −1 during 2007–2023, whereas the corresponding passive-sensor signal was negligible. Accounting for this component raises annual Arctic NPP estimates by ∼13.3% indicating that passive sensor-based assessments may underrepresent the magnitude and seasonal structure of Arctic productivity. Associations with declining sea ice and surface warming suggest this underrepresented production is consistent with ongoing seasonal reorganization of Arctic carbon fixation. Uncertainties from model parameterization, low-light extrapolation, and limited in situ validation are largest in the lowest-light and highest-latitude regimes. These findings do not imply photosynthesis during absolute polar night, but show that active LiDAR observations with explicit light constraints and transparent extrapolation limits can test how unresolved low-light winter-shoulder production may alter Arctic NPP seasonality under continuing sea-ice loss.

#38 [paper] Data‐Driven Parameterization of Arctic Ocean Turbulent Mixing
Authors: Rafael Sebastian Reiss, Lisanne Blok, Nicholas Leonard, Kate Oglethorpe, Alberto C. Naveira Garabato, Colm-cille P. Caulfield, Ali Mashayek
Venue: Geophysical Research Letters
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1029/2026gl123721
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Arctic Ocean turbulent mixing is poorly characterized due to sparse observations, limitations of conventional parameterizations, and incomplete understanding, despite its importance for regional dynamics and global overturning.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Training gradient-boosted decision trees on global microstructure turbulence data to predict turbulent dissipation from hydrographic variables, using spatial block cross-validation for evaluation.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Global microstructure turbulence data (>5,000 profiles) for training; pan-Arctic hydrographic observations and high-resolution model output for application.
Abstract:
Abstract Turbulent mixing may become increasingly important in a changing Arctic Ocean, influencing regional dynamics and global overturning. Arctic turbulence remains poorly characterized due to sparse observations, limitations of conventional parameterizations, and incomplete understanding. We train gradient‐boosted decision trees on global microstructure turbulence data (>5,000 profiles; ∼ data points) to predict turbulent dissipation from more widely available hydrography. Global training is essential for skill across non‐Arctic and Arctic regions (, 75% within a factor of 2 of observations; = 0.47–0.55 under spatial block cross‐validation). Applied to pan‐Arctic hydrographic observations, predictions show enhanced dissipation along margins and shelves and weaker values in basin interiors, consistent with current understanding. Applied to high‐resolution model output, predictions reveal diffusivities and a basin‐integrated irreversible buoyancy flux consistent with observations, yet markedly different from the common K‐Profile Parameterization—with implications for simulated tracer transport. Our parameterization can help assess climate‐mixing feedbacks in projections while physics‐based parameterizations mature.

#39 [paper] Rescene-ESM: an Earth system model built around a frozen AI weather model
Authors: Minjong Cheon, Kaoru Kakinuma
Year: 2026
Link: https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/e1c22d8441861158dd7f9e6021cb718096d3f29f
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The high computational cost of Earth system models limits the exploration of scenarios and ensemble members, while existing machine-learning weather models coupled to oceans have produced weak El Niño variability or relied on climate-model output, and none effectively routes climate impacts through…
Method (Mycelium's reading): Rescene-ESM, an Earth system model using a coupler named YAHO that links a frozen 20.8-million-parameter AI weather model to physically formulated ocean, sea-ice, land, river, carbon, and energy components constrained by observations; the model uses an interactive mixed layer, an equatorial wave oc…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Simulations of approximately 1,000 years on one graphics processing unit; evaluation against observed climate data from 1979-2022; routing of runoff to 212 river gauges; and future projections for SSP1 and SSP3 scenarios for the period 2081-2100.
Abstract:
Earth system models underpin climate projections, but their cost limits how many scenarios, ensemble members and impact pathways can be explored. Machine-learning weather models forecast as skillfully as physics-based models at a fraction of the cost, yet coupled to an ocean they have produced weak El Nino variability or have learned it from climate-model output, and none carries the climate through rivers to the people exposed to it. Here we present Rescene-ESM, an Earth system model whose coupler, YAHO, yokes a frozen 20.8-million-parameter AI weather model to physically formulated ocean, sea-ice, land, river, carbon and energy components constrained by observations. Adding the couplings one at a time shows what each contributes: over a climatological ocean the AI atmosphere varies from year to year by a third of the observed amount over the oceans, and an interactive mixed layer, an equatorial wave ocean, the residual of the observed sea surface temperature (SST) equation as stochastic forcing and the land's moisture flux raise this step by step and bring El Nino and its teleconnections, leaving the mean climate almost unchanged. The full model simulates about 1,000 years per day on one graphics processing unit, holds the observed climate for a thousand years without drift, reproduces the observed 1979-2022 global warming, carries forced change with a physically based structure around the frozen network (transient climate response 1.60 K), routes runoff to 212 river gauges with a median seasonal-cycle correlation of 0.79 and, driven by emissions, separates the heatwave exposure of an SSP1 and an SSP3 world by a factor of 4.7 in 2081-2100, three-quarters of it through the warmer climate.

#41 [paper] A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery over the Northern South China Sea
Authors: Guocai Rong, Huanhe Dong, Yuan Kong, Ze Liu, Yong Hui Fang
Venue: Remote Sensing
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18213843
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Automated extraction of internal solitary waves (ISWs) from satellite imagery is challenging due to their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast.
Method (Mycelium's reading): YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, incorporating Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) for curved structures and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for low-contrast features.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea; the framework was also applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020.
Abstract:
Internal solitary waves (ISWs) play an important role in ocean energy transport and mixing, yet their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast make automated extraction from satellite imagery challenging. To address these challenges, this study proposes YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint ISW detection and pixel-level segmentation. Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea was constructed for model training and evaluation. YOLO11-ISW achieved detection Precision, Recall, and F1-score values of 92.01%, 80.73%, and 86.00%, respectively, and segmentation values of 93.14%, 82.60%, and 87.55%, respectively. The model achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the evaluated methods. The segmentation results were further georeferenced to extract ISW crest-line locations, and the framework was applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020 to investigate satellite-observed ISW spatiotemporal variability. The detected ISWs exhibited pronounced spatial clustering, strong spring–summer seasonality, and clear lunar-cycle modulation, consistent with previous observations in the northern South China Sea. These results demonstrate the potential of YOLO11-ISW for automated, long-term, and large-scale monitoring of ISWs using satellite remote sensing imagery.

final_text:
The one that matters most is **#5 — "Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish"** (Stuart-Smith et al., 2026, *Conservation Science and Practice*).

Why it stands out for this project:

- **It is the clearest real-world example of a forecast actually triggering action.** Ahead of the 2023/24 El Niño, forecasts flagged a high risk of marine heatwaves; an expert workshop judged the predicted extremes (>20°C or ~+3°C) a severe threat, and that triggered an emergency rescue of 25 red handfish in January 2024. That is exactly the loop your project is building: forecast → risk assessment → early warning → response.
- **It quantifies the stakes of getting the warning right.** During the hold period, in situ temperatures exceeded records — 80 days more than 2°C above the long-term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C) — and three fish died in captivity. It shows what a missed or late warning costs.
- **It is a template for your warning protocol.** The paper's structure — forecast input, expert workshop assessment, pre-agreed trigger thresholds, approvals, and post-release verification (survival confirmed after 2 months) — is a ready-made blueprint for how your early warning system should be operationalized with managers and stakeholders.

The other two strong candidates are worth a look but sit a step removed:

- **#6** (Mojumder, 2026) evaluates 1–14-day ML MHW forecasts in the Northern Bay of Bengal against persistence benchmarks — directly relevant to your ML forecasting methods, but it is a short-term, single-region evaluation rather than an end-to-end early warning case.
- **#3** (the comment on the Northeast Pacific seasonal ocean forecast system) is a solid seasonal SST forecasting system with routine real-time forecasts starting October 2026, but it is a general seasonal forecasting paper, not heatwave-specific.

If you want, I can pull the full text of #5 and map its trigger-and-response workflow onto your project's current state.

#5 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Providing seasonal ocean forecasts for the Northeast Pacific to support marine resource management and ecosystem variability assessment.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A seasonal ocean forecasting system based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model, forced by GFDL-SPEAR global climate forecasts, with a ~10 km horizontal re…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Northeast Pacific region extending from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea; evaluation uses a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months, assessed against ocean reanalyses and in situ observations.
Abstract:
Abstract. Seasonal ocean forecasts offer critical insights for marine resource management, particularly in regions like the Northeast Pacific where ecosystem variability can have profound impacts on marine life, fisheries, and coastal communities. Under NOAA’s Changing Ecosystems and Fisheries Initiative, we developed a seasonal ocean forecasting system for the Northeast Pacific based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) ocean model coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) sea ice model and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model. The model domain extends from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea with ~10 km horizontal resolution. To evaluate forecast skill, we produced a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months. Forcing for the forecasts was derived from the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory's Seamless System for Prediction and Earth System Research (GFDL-SPEAR) global climate forecast system. Forecasts were assessed using ocean reanalyses and in situ observations, focusing on three ecologically- and societally-relevant variables: sea surface temperature, bottom temperature, and bottom oxygen concentration. Forecast skill varies by region, variable, and season, but generally remains high (anomaly correlation coefficient; ACC>0.5) for lead times of at least several months across all variables and regions. The downscaled forecasts reduce errors relative to the SPEAR global forecasts and in some cases increase ACC, while also enabling predictions of biogeochemical variables. These new forecasts compare favorably to previous downscaled ocean forecasts off the U.S. west coast, with increased ACC and small forecast errors that may be reduced further by future methodological changes. Routine real-time forecasts, available starting in October 2026, will support proactive decision making by managers, industry, and coastal communities.

The paper that matters most for Plastic pathways is **#7 — "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter: development and application to field records from Uido, Republic of Korea"** (Lim & Hong, 2026).

Why it stands out:

- **It's the only item in the slate that is directly about marine litter.** The others touch the project only indirectly — #6 is a data-assimilation product for a Pacific forecast system, #12 is about detecting internal solitary waves in satellite imagery, and #5 is Arctic phytoplankton. #7 is squarely on the project's subject.
- **It's a methods paper you can actually use.** It provides a three-phase beaching kernel plus six other particle kernels for OceanParcels 3.1.4, the scripts that ran the particle-tracking experiments, and the aggregated results behind every number in the manuscript. That's a ready-made component for modelling where plastic ends up on shore — the "pathways" part of your project.
- **It's validated against field records.** The kernel was developed and tested against beaching observations from Uido, Korea, using ROMS flow fields and particle trajectories, so it's not just a theoretical construction.
- **It's reproducible.** The deposit includes a reproduction manifest with a checker, and the full particle trajectories (~32 GB) and ROMS flow fields (~37 GB) are available on request — useful if you want to benchmark your own setup against theirs.

The practical takeaway: if Plastic pathways involves particle-tracking of debris to shore, #7 gives you a published, field-validated beaching kernel and the code to run it — a strong candidate to build on or compare against.

One caveat: Mycelium's reading of #7 is brief (problem, method, setting), and the abstract describes the code deposit rather than the full manuscript. If you want, I can check whether the underlying paper's full text is stored so we can dig into the kernel's design and validation in detail.

#12 [paper] A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery over the Northern South China Sea
Authors: Guocai Rong, Huanhe Dong, Yuan Kong, Ze Liu, Yong Hui Fang
Venue: Remote Sensing
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18213843
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Automated extraction of internal solitary waves (ISWs) from satellite imagery is challenging due to their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast.
Method (Mycelium's reading): YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, incorporating Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) for curved structures and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for low-contrast features.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea; the framework was also applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020.
Abstract:
Internal solitary waves (ISWs) play an important role in ocean energy transport and mixing, yet their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast make automated extraction from satellite imagery challenging. To address these challenges, this study proposes YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint ISW detection and pixel-level segmentation. Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea was constructed for model training and evaluation. YOLO11-ISW achieved detection Precision, Recall, and F1-score values of 92.01%, 80.73%, and 86.00%, respectively, and segmentation values of 93.14%, 82.60%, and 87.55%, respectively. The model achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the evaluated methods. The segmentation results were further georeferenced to extract ISW crest-line locations, and the framework was applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020 to investigate satellite-observed ISW spatiotemporal variability. The detected ISWs exhibited pronounced spatial clustering, strong spring–summer seasonality, and clear lunar-cycle modulation, consistent with previous observations in the northern South China Sea. These results demonstrate the potential of YOLO11-ISW for automated, long-term, and large-scale monitoring of ISWs using satellite remote sensing imagery.

final_text:
Here's the comparison.

**#1 — A stronger Global Ocean Observing System (€50M, deadline 2027-02-16)**
This grant is about *building and sustaining the observation infrastructure* — deploying equipment, running observing-system experiments, network optimization, and technology roadmaps with industry. The emphasis is on closing structural gaps in under-observed regions (polar, deep sea, areas beyond national jurisdiction) and keeping the GOOS/Copernicus pipeline resilient and open. It's a big, systems-level call: the deliverable is a stronger, more autonomous observing network, not a specific forecasting product.

**#2 — Unlocking a safe operating space for Antarctica and the Southern Ocean (€5–11M, deadline 2027-09-23)**
This one is about *understanding and projecting* the Southern Ocean and Antarctic cryosphere: ocean–atmosphere–sea-ice–ice dynamics, distinguishing human from natural change, improving Earth-system and regional coupled models, monitoring indicators, and ecosystem vulnerability. It explicitly calls for work on extreme events, tipping elements, and decadal-to-millennial projections.

**Which fits the Marine heatwave early warning project (#3) better?**

**#2 is the closer fit.** The project's slate is dominated by forecasting and prediction work — ML-based marine heatwave forecasts (#8), a forecast-triggered rapid-response strategy for a threatened species (#7), and ocean forecast-system analyses (#13). #2's scope — improving projections, reducing uncertainty in future ocean change, extreme events, and monitoring indicators — lines up directly with what the project is doing. The project could contribute a forecasting/prediction workstream (e.g., ML-based heatwave prediction or early-warning indicators) within a broader Southern Ocean proposal.

**#1 is a weaker fit** for this project specifically. It's an infrastructure and governance call: the core ask is deploying and sustaining observation hardware and networks, not developing forecasting methods. Your project's strength is in the prediction and data-assimilation side, not in building observing infrastructure. That said, #1 could be relevant if the project wanted to argue that better heatwave early warning *depends on* closing observation gaps — but that would be a supporting role, not the lead.

**Practical note:** #1 has a much earlier deadline (Feb 2027) and a much larger budget (€50M), which suggests it's likely a consortium-scale call. #2 (€5–11M, Sep 2027) is more typical of a research-project scale and gives you more time to shape a proposal around the project's forecasting work.

If you'd like, I can dig into either grant's full text or look at who in the lab might be best positioned to lead or contribute to a proposal.

Amount: €50,000,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-NATURE-2027-04-01
Still open/current: yes

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The global ocean observing system faces risks to continuity, openness, and resilience due to evolving geopolitical dynamics, reduced engagement by key international partners, and structural gaps in under-observed regions like the deep sea and polar regions, which threatens scientific sovereignty an…
Method (Mycelium's reading): Strengthening the Global Ocean Observing System (GOOS) through the deployment of observation equipment, performing observing system experiments (OSEs) and observing system simulation experiments (OSSEs), applying network optimization approaches, co-creating technology roadmaps with industry, and in…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Global ocean observing frameworks, specifically the Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission’s Global Ocean Observing System (GOOS), areas beyond national jurisdiction, and the Copernicus Marine Service.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Proposals are expected to contribute to all the following expected outcomes, in full alignment with the OceanEye initiative:

- scientists, public authorities and businesses benefit from strengthened and resilient global ocean observing capacities, coordinated under the Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission’s Global Ocean Observing System (GOOS),[1] through the deployment of ocean observation equipment, in particular for the provision of critical observations for marine biodiversity and ecosystem knowledge;

- public authorities prioritise investments on infrastructures and capacity building to advance ocean research, protect and restore ocean health and biodiversity and provide critical services through a global ocean observing system and data delivery that is fit-for purpose, cost efficient and designed across all its components;

- increased EU leadership and strategic autonomy in global ocean observation capabilities, in support of EU climate and biodiversity goals, strengthening the EU’s contribution to and influence within GOOS, and reducing the risk of critical dependencies, notably for key services (i.e. Copernicus Services);

- enhanced collaboration between observation communities, marine research infrastructures, European SMEs and technology providers, maritime industries, and service operators, actionably contributing to the validation, procurement readiness, uptake and large-scale deployment of innovative ocean observing technologies and approaches, in particular for biodiversity observations, while reinforcing the long-term sustainability of the global ocean observing system.

Scope:

Here's what I found, Mara.

## Best-fitting open grant: #21 — "Advancing understanding, modelling and prediction of extreme events in a changing climate"

**Why it fits the Marine heatwave early warning project (#7):**

- **Problem match:** The call explicitly asks for improved prediction, projection, and attribution of extreme events in a changing climate, with a specific emphasis on *early warning systems* for single and multi-hazard events. Marine heatwaves are exactly the kind of extreme event this topic targets.
- **Method match:** It welcomes AI-based approaches, a hierarchy of models (including digital twins), quantitative intercomparisons, and retrospective analyses — all of which align with the project's ML + data assimilation approach.
- **Scale and scope:** €3M–€15M, deadline **2027-03-04**, Europe and global scope with encouragement to integrate with Copernicus and Destination Earth.
- **Why not the others:**
  - #10 (NSF OTIC) is about *instrumentation development* — a different flavour of project.
  - #15 (GOOS) is about *observing system infrastructure and governance* — broader and more about the observation network than prediction.
  - #20 (Antarctica/Southern Ocean) is regionally specific and more about projections and cryosphere dynamics.
  - #24 (Decision support for disaster crises) is a possible secondary fit but is more about operational civil-protection systems than the science of prediction.
  - #19 (Wave/tidal energy) and #22 (ONR communications) are off-topic.

## Who in the lab should lead

The nightly ranking and the requirement-slot analysis point to two people:

- **Tomás Ferreira-Lind (#6)** — declared interests in *circulation and turbulence* and *physics-informed ML*. He's the one who covers the "Earth system models" slot (declared: regional ocean models). His work on fast, physics-informed surrogates for ocean models maps directly onto the call's ask for "seamless prediction and projection modelling capabilities." He's also a member of the Marine heatwave early warning project. **He's the strongest lead candidate.**

- **You (Mara Ellison, #2)** — declared interests in *data assimilation with ML* and *ocean extremes*. You're the PI and a project member. The call's emphasis on AI-based approaches and data assimilation is squarely in your declared territory. You could co-lead or take the lead if you prefer, especially given the project is yours.

**Gaps to fill with partners:** No one in the lab currently covers *digital twins*, *Copernicus integration*, or *Destination Earth*. These are named in the call and will need to come from outside.

## Who outside the lab could partner

I couldn't find introduction paths to specific external researchers in Mycelium's network (the people I checked aren't in the system), but based on the papers in the project's slate, here are natural partner candidates:

1. **Ruiqi Shu, Ruijian Gou, Yanfei Xiang, Xiaomeng Huang** — authors of #32 *Ocean-E2E: Hybrid Physics-Based and Data-Driven Global Forecasting of Marine Heatwaves with End-to-End Neural Assimilation*. Their work is almost a direct twin of your project's method (hybrid physics + ML, end-to-end assimilation, 40-day MHW forecasts). They'd be a strong scientific partner, especially for the "AI-based approaches" and "seamless prediction" components.

2. **Jemina Stuart-Smith, Tyson Bessell, Alistair Hobday, et al.** — authors of #11 *Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish*. They demonstrate the *impact and application* side: using MHW forecasts to trigger conservation action. They'd strengthen the "early warning → early action" narrative and the biodiversity/impact angle the call asks for.

3. **Simon Toedtli, D. Ahijevych, Wei Wang, C. Snyder** — authors of #30 *Ensemble Covariance Propagation with Machine Learning Weather Prediction Models in a Realistic Data Assimilation System*. They work on integrating ML models into operational DA cycling systems — directly relevant to the "data assimilation" and "operational prediction" components.

4. **For the Copernicus / Destination Earth / digital twin gaps:** You'd want to bring in a partner with experience in those EU frameworks. The call specifically mentions coordination with ESA's FutureEO programme and the European Commission's Joint Research Centre (JRC). A partner from a European institution with Copernicus Marine Service or Destination Earth experience would close that gap.

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

Scope:

Climate change is intensifying the frequency and severity of extreme events. Understanding and predicting extreme events and the interaction between different types of hazards is critical for building resilience and safeguarding communities.

Actions are expected to draw upon multiple lines of evidence from a hierarchy of models (including high resolution Earth system models and digital twins) and data of past and recent climate to further our understanding of processes, pre-conditioning and causality driving extreme events under climate change conditions, including anthropogenic factors and internal variability. Other innovative and efficient modelling and analysis methods, including AI-based approaches, to better predict, emulate and reveal climate change related extreme and unprecedented high impact events, and to capture their likelihood are particularly welcome.

Extreme events should be addressed in their broadest sense and types, encompassing isolated, compound or cascading events affecting lives, livelihoods, ecosystems, socio-economic sectors and infrastructures, from large-scale continental to local-scale phenomena.

#11 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

#32 [paper] Ocean-E2E: Hybrid Physics-Based and Data-Driven Global Forecasting of Marine Heatwaves with End-to-End Neural Assimilation
Authors: Ruiqi Shu, Ruijian Gou, Yanfei Xiang, Xiaomeng Huang
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1145/3770855.3818893
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This work focuses on the end-to-end forecast of global extreme marine heatwaves (MHWs), which are unusually warm sea surface temperature events with profound impacts on marine ecosystems. Accurate prediction of extreme MHWs has significant scientific and financial worth. However, existing methods still have certain limitations in forecasting general patterns and extreme events. In this study, to address these issues, based on the physical nature of MHWs, we created a novel hybrid data-driven and numerical MHWs forecast framework Ocean-E2E, which is capable of 40-day accurate MHW forecasting with end-to-end data assimilation. Our framework significantly improves the forecast ability of MHWs by explicitly modeling the effect of oceanic mesoscale advection and air-sea interaction based on a dynamic kernel. Furthermore, Ocean-E2E is capable of end-to-end MHWs forecast and regional high-resolution prediction, allowing our framework to operate completely independently of numerical models while outperforming the current state-of-the-art ocean numerical/AI forecasting-assimilation models. Experimental results show that the proposed framework performs excellently on global-to-regional scales and short-to-long-term forecasts, especially in those most extreme MHWs. Overall, our model provides a framework for forecasting and understanding MHWs and other climate extremes. The source code is available at https://github.com/ChiyodaMomo01/Ocean-E2E.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Integrating machine learning weather prediction (MLWP) models into classical data assimilation (DA) workflows requires that they accurately evolve ensemble covariances.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A two-way coupled DA system where an ensemble variational (EnVar) component evolves the mean and an ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF) evolves the covariances. The system uses the MLWP model GraphCast for the EnKF and the physics-based MPAS model for the EnVar, cycled over one month.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A realistic DA cycling system assimilating a wide range of real-world observations, including microwave radiances, over a one-month period.
Abstract:
Integrating machine learning weather prediction (MLWP) models into classical data assimilation (DA) workflows requires that they accurately evolve ensemble covariances. We evaluate this capability in a two-way coupled DA system, where an ensemble variational (EnVar) component evolves the mean and an ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF) evolves the covariances. The system is cycled over one month and assimilates a wide range of real-world observations, including microwave radiances. Using the MLWP model GraphCast for the EnKF and the physics-based MPAS model for the EnVar yields ensemble spread and covariances comparable to a reference configuration in which MPAS evolves both components. The resulting EnVar mean achieves consistently lower RMSE against GFS analyses, except near the model top, where spurious correlations degrade performance. These results demonstrate that MLWP models can propagate covariance information in a realistic DA cycling system and provide a proof of concept for their integration into future operational ensemble systems.

## Best-fitting open grant: #9 — GOOS (€50 M, deadline 2027-02-16)

Of the two open grants on the Plastic pathways slate, **#9** is the stronger fit. Here's why:

| | #9 GOOS | #16 OTIC |
|---|---|---|
| **Amount** | €50,000,000 | Not stated |
| **Deadline** | 2027-02-16 | 2027-02-15 |
| **Core ask** | Strengthen & operationalise the global ocean observing system; close structural gaps; coordinate EOVs; biodiversity & climate outcomes | Instrumentation development with broad applicability to ocean science |
| **Fit to Plastic pathways** | The project's Lagrangian particle-tracking work (e.g. #20, #24) is exactly the kind of observation-grounded, data-driven pathway modelling that GOOS wants to scale. The grant explicitly calls for "data delivery that is fit-for-purpose" and "strengthened global ocean observing capacities" — your lab's satellite + data-assimilation + Lagrangian toolkit maps directly onto that. | OTIC is narrower: it funds the *instrument* itself. Your lab's strength is in the modelling and data pipeline, not in building new hardware. No lab member has a declared instrumentation-development profile. |

**Gaps to fill for #9:** The nightly ranking flags that no one in the lab currently covers *observing system experiments (OSEs)*, *OSSEs*, *network optimisation*, or *areas beyond national jurisdiction*. You'll want to address those in the proposal — either by bringing in a partner who does, or by framing the Plastic pathways work as a concrete use-case that motivates those components.

---

## Who in the lab should lead

The ranking names two people with a declared-profile match to #9:

1. **Priya Raman (#4)** — declared: satellite oceanography, coastal water quality. Her satellite remote-sensing work is the closest single match to the grant's emphasis on "strengthened global ocean observing capacities and data coordination." She's also a member of the Plastic pathways project.
2. **You (Mara Ellison, #2)** — declared: data assimilation with ML, ocean extremes. Your data-assimilation + ML pipeline is the other pillar the ranking highlights.

**Recommendation:** **Priya should lead the application**, with you as co-lead. Her satellite-observation profile is the most direct match to the grant's core ask, and she's already on the project. You bring the data-assimilation and ML angle that ties the observing system to actionable forecasts. **Jonah (#3)** — declared: marine litter, Lagrangian analysis — is the natural third member; his Lagrangian work is the methodological backbone of the Plastic pathways project and the most concrete "use case" the grant will want to see.

**Tomás (#6)** and **Sun-hee (#5)** are not on the Plastic pathways project and their declared profiles (circulation/turbulence, physics-informed ML; ocean data tools) are less directly aligned with #9's observing-system focus. They could contribute as supporting partners if the proposal grows, but the core team should be Priya, you, and Jonah.

---

## External partners to consider

The grant explicitly asks for collaboration with "marine research infrastructures, European SMEs and technology providers, maritime industries, and service operators." Here are researchers outside your lab whose work overlaps with Plastic pathways and who could strengthen the proposal:

| Researcher | Why they fit | Source |
|---|---|---|
| **Erik van Sebille** (Netherlands) | Co-author of #24 (drifter groundings in the Wadden Sea). His group is a leader in Lagrangian transport of floating macroplastic and has the field-campaign + modelling combination the grant wants. | #24 |
| **Eugenia Pasanisi / Giovanni Coppini** (Italy, Mediterranean) | Co-authors of #20 (observation-based Lagrangian particle tracking in the Mediterranean, using Copernicus Marine Service data). Directly relevant to the grant's Copernicus and EOV themes. | #20 |
| **Philippe Cecchi / Pierrick Penven** (France, Ifremer) | Co-authors of #19 (Lagrangian + CROCO modelling of plastic dispersal in Côte d'Ivoire). They work in a data-scarce, beyond-national-jurisdiction-adjacent setting — exactly the kind of "structural gap" the grant wants to close. | #19 |
| **Z. Duan / B. Maurer** (US, Delaware) | Co-authors of #22 (coupled watershed–estuary microplastic transport). They bring the land-to-sea source-inventory angle, which the grant's "interconnected physical, biogeochemical and biological components" language calls for. | #22 |

**Practical note:** The grant is a Horizon Europe call, so you'll want at least three EU-based partners from different member states. The Italian (#20) and French (#19) groups are the most natural EU partners. Erik van Sebille (Netherlands) is also EU-based. The US group (#22) would be a valuable non-EU associate partner.

---

**TL;DR:** Apply to **#9 (GOOS, €50 M, due 16 Feb 2027)**. Lead with **Priya**, co-lead with **you**, and bring in **Jonah** for the Lagrangian core. Reach out to **Pasanini/Coppini (Italy)**, **Cecchi/Penven (France)**, and **van Sebille (Netherlands)** as external partners to close the observing-system and beyond-national-jurisdiction gaps.

#19 [paper] Modeling dispersal and beaching of urban plastic waste along the coastline of Côte d'Ivoire.
Authors: Amemou, Hilaire, Cecchi, Philippe, Koné, Vamara, Penven, Pierrick, Lett, Christophe
Venue: Marine pollution bulletin
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42735662/
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The processes governing the fate, dispersal, and coastal retention of urban plastic debris along the coastline of Côte d'Ivoire, which is vulnerable due to dense coastal populations and significant plastic inputs.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A Lagrangian particle-tracking model (Ichthyop) forced by surface currents from a high-resolution ocean circulation model (CROCO) to simulate the dispersal and beaching of plastic particles.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): The coastline of Côte d'Ivoire, specifically focusing on the region around Abidjan and the broader Ivorian coast.
Abstract:
Plastic pollution is a growing concern in West Africa's marine environment, yet the processes governing its fate remain poorly understood. The coastline of Côte d'Ivoire is particularly vulnerable due to dense coastal populations and significant plastic inputs from rivers and lagoons. This study investigates the dispersal and coastal retention of urban plastic debris using a Lagrangian particle-tracking model (Ichthyop) forced by surface currents from a high-resolution ocean circulation model (CROCO). We provide the first regional-scale assessment of seasonal beaching dynamics along the Ivorian coast using a high-resolution coupled hydrodynamic-Lagrangian framework. Simulations show that while a large fraction of particles is transported offshore (~52%), a substantial proportion (~48%) remains nearshore and beaches at least once. Persistent accumulation hotspots are identified around Abidjan, regardless of the release location. Seasonal variability strongly controls debris pathways. During the minor upwelling season (January-April), beaching occurs predominantly west of Abidjan, associated with weaker currents and enhanced coastal retention. In contrast, during the major upwelling season (June-September), intensified currents and mesoscale activity promote wider dispersal and shift beaching eastward. From October to December, beaching intensifies along the eastern coastline. These results highlight the dominant role of regional hydrodynamics in shaping marine debris distribution and demonstrate the value of high-resolution Lagrangian modeling for identifying pollution hotspots and supporting mitigation strategies in data-scarce coastal regions.

#20 [paper] Marine litter in the Mediterranean: observation-based Lagrangian particle tracking
Authors: Santiago Bravo, Eugenia Pasanisi, Svitlana Liubartseva, Giovanni Coppini, Alice Madonia, Igor Atake, Marta Azzolin, Lara Carosso
Venue: Frontiers in Marine Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2026.1936698
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The lack of spatially explicit, observation-grounded predictions for the transport and coastal deposition of floating marine macro-litter (FMML) in the Mediterranean.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A data-driven stochastic Lagrangian framework using Parcels, initialized with monthly gridded FMML observations from shipboard surveys and forced by Copernicus Marine Service Mediterranean reanalysis currents and ERA5 wind fields with a 1% windage coefficient and a 2D random-walk turbulent diffusio…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Mediterranean Sea, specifically areas surveyed via the LIFE Conceptu Maris Project using ferries from August 2023 to December 2024.
Abstract:
Introduction The Mediterranean is a major hotspot for floating marine macro-litter (FMML) accumulation, yet spatially explicit, observation-grounded predictions of its transport and coastal deposition remain scarce. We present a data-driven stochastic Lagrangian framework that uses monthly gridded FMML observations from systematic shipboard surveys as simulation initial conditions complementing existing source-based modelling approaches. Methods Observations were collected from August 2023 to December 2024 within the LIFE Conceptu Maris Project using ferries as monitoring platforms under a standardised protocol. A total of 158 surveys detected 4,801 FMML items across approximately 6,200 km² of surveyed sea surface, of which more than 62% were artificial polymers. Observed monthly FMML item counts at 5 × 5 km resolution initialised ensemble Lagrangian simulations (18 members per target month; 17.2–32.5 million virtual particles per seeding window, 5,000 particles per observed item) using Parcels, forced by Copernicus Marine Service Mediterranean reanalysis currents and ERA5 wind fields with a 1% windage coefficient and a 2D random-walk turbulent diffusion scheme. Monthly frequency-of-occurrence maps were computed at the sea surface and on coastlines. Results The Southern Tyrrhenian and Northern Ligurian seas, including the Pelagos Sanctuary, exhibited in 2024 near-persistent high sea surface FMML occurrence, peaking in late summer–autumn and reaching a seasonal minimum in winter–early spring. The Balearic Sea showed elevated occurrence from late spring through summer (May–September), declining through autumn. The Adriatic displayed intense sub-basin-scale spreading from January to June and again in December, with summer leakage into the Northern Ionian Sea. Coastal deposition frequencies were highest on Corsica, western Sardinia and northern Tunisia, then the south-eastern Tyrrhenian and Ligurian–Tuscan margins, with Valencia–Barcelona largely confined to summer. Integration with loggerhead turtle nesting records illustrates how coastal frequency-of-occurrence maps can support conservation applications. Discussion A web-based Particle Analysis Dashboard translates these outputs into an interactive tool with Marine Protected and Conserved Area overlays for scientists and decision-makers. The framework provides a scalable, observation-anchored foundation for MSFD Descriptor 10 monitoring, transferable to other semi-enclosed sea basins. Priority future work includes complementary validation against independent beach-litter monitoring data, integration of land-based source inventories, and linkage with species distribution models.

#22 [paper] Coupled watershed and estuary modeling of microplastic transport and retention in the Delaware river basin
Authors: Z. Duan, Y. Huang, M. Wigmosta, Z. Li, N. Sun, T. Wang, Z. Yang, B. Maurer
Venue: Scientific Reports
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-57910-7
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The need for accurate simulation of microplastic (MP) transport from terrestrial sources to estuarine systems and the estimation of MP export to the ocean.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A coupled watershed–estuary modeling framework that enhances the Distributed Hydrology Soil Vegetation Model (DHSVM) to represent point and nonpoint MP sources and couples it with the Finite Volume Community Ocean Model (FVCOM).
Setting (Mycelium's reading): The Delaware River Basin, including wastewater treatment plant (WWTP) discharges and airborne deposition.
Abstract:
Abstract Microplastics (MPs) are an emerging environmental concern owing to their widespread presence and ecological impacts. We develop a coupled watershed–estuary modeling framework to simulate MP transport from terrestrial sources to estuarine systems. The Distributed Hydrology Soil Vegetation Model (DHSVM) is enhanced to represent point and nonpoint MP sources and is coupled with the Finite Volume Community Ocean Model (FVCOM) to capture estuarine transport. Applied to the Delaware River Basin, the framework simulates MP build-up and wash-off, including airborne deposition and wastewater treatment plant (WWTP) discharges. Coupling the estuary model enables a more accurate estimation of MP discharge to the ocean, highlighting retention within Delaware Bay from salinity-induced circulation. MP retention on land is strongly influenced by watershed topography, urban distribution, and source configuration, with the “Lower Delaware” subwatershed exhibiting minimal residence time. These results demonstrate the importance of watershed–estuary coupling for accurate MP export estimates and provide a framework for evaluating MP fate in aquatic environments.

#24 [paper] Groundings of drifters in the Wadden Sea inform the transport of floating macroplastic
Authors: Marc Schneiter, Rolf Hut, Erik van Sebille
Venue: Ocean science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/os-22-3595-2026
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Understanding the transport and coastal interaction dynamics of floating macroplastic in intertidal regions, specifically through the analysis of drifter groundings.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Field campaign involving the release and tracking of 24 shallow surface drifters in the Dutch Wadden Sea; manual and statistical automatic detection of drifter groundings; characterization of groundings relative to wind conditions, tides, and duration.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Dutch Wadden Sea, an intertidal region driven by semi-diurnal tides and wind.
Abstract:
Abstract. We study floating marine macro plastic pollution with a dedicated campaign where we released and tracked 24 shallow surface drifters in the Dutch Wadden Sea, an intertidal region where water dynamics are driven by semi-diurnal tides and wind. The campaign captured water surface transport patterns, and around 150 observations of the drifters interacting with the coast and mudflats, where groundings of varying durations occurred. We identify these transitions in the recorded trajectories from both manual inspection and by formulating and evaluating a statistical approach for automatic detection. We then characterize the transitions by relating them to the coinciding wind conditions and tides, and with the duration of the groundings. The results of this analysis generally agree with the intuitions that wind towards the coast increases the frequency of interactions and that the drifters are rarely re-floated during falling tides. Furthermore, we find that groundings tend to be shorter duration when they occur shorter before the next high tide. We present multiple visualizations that characterize the groundings in more detail. The results provide a statistical characterization of coastal interactions that can be integrated in models and used for the planning of beach-cleanups. They may be improved by considering the specific environmental conditions of the campaign, and by analyzing the influence of the weight and size of the drifters, which are both larger than typical floating macroplastic.

Here's the picture for **Plastic pathways** (#2):

## Where the project stands
The project is a lab-level effort with three members: Jonah Whitcombe, Priya Raman, and you. I can only see the title and membership, though — no confirmed goals, method, stage, milestones, or blockers are on file, and there's no record of when the state was last confirmed. If the team has been working on it, it may be worth confirming the project's state in the app so Mylo can track it properly.

Its current slate has 15 items, most of which entered on 2026-11-10; four are new this week (entered 2026-11-13): #5, #9, #13, #16, #17.

## Three most relevant new papers
1. **#7** — *A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter* (Lim & Hong, 2026). The closest match to the project: a three-phase beaching kernel plus six particle kernels for OceanParcels, validated against field records from Uido, Korea, with full code and aggregated results. Directly usable for modelling where plastic ends up on shore.
2. **#12** — *A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery* (Rong et al., 2026). Not about plastic, but a strong methodological template: a YOLO11-based detector/segmenter for low-contrast, curved ocean features in MODIS imagery, applied to a decade of satellite data. The same approach could be adapted to detect and track debris plumes from space.
3. **#6** — *Daily Analyses of the Pacific Regional Ocean Forecast System model* (Zhang, 2026). A Zenodo deposit of daily analyses of a regional ocean forecast system — relevant as a source of the kind of daily, high-resolution flow fields that particle-tracking studies of plastic pathways depend on.

## One funding opportunity
**#10 — Ocean Technology and Interdisciplinary Coordination (NSF OTIC)**, still open, deadline **2027-02-15**. It funds instrumentation development and technology that enhances observational, experimental, or analytical capabilities for the ocean science community. A natural fit: a proposal to develop or adapt particle-tracking and beaching-kernel tooling (in the spirit of #7) for tracking marine debris pathways, with broad applicability to the ocean research community.

A second option worth noting: **#17** (Horizon, €3–8M, deadline 2027-09-22) on integrating remote sensing with in-situ observations — a fit if the project leans toward satellite-based debris detection, though its focus is biodiversity data integration, so it's a looser match than OTIC.

**Suggested next steps:** confirm the project's goals and blockers in the app so the slate can be tied to what's actually blocking you; and if OTIC looks right, start scoping the proposal around the beaching-kernel tooling — the deadline is about three months out.

#12 [paper] A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery over the Northern South China Sea
Authors: Guocai Rong, Huanhe Dong, Yuan Kong, Ze Liu, Yong Hui Fang
Venue: Remote Sensing
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18213843
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Automated extraction of internal solitary waves (ISWs) from satellite imagery is challenging due to their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast.
Method (Mycelium's reading): YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, incorporating Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) for curved structures and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for low-contrast features.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea; the framework was also applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020.
Abstract:
Internal solitary waves (ISWs) play an important role in ocean energy transport and mixing, yet their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast make automated extraction from satellite imagery challenging. To address these challenges, this study proposes YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint ISW detection and pixel-level segmentation. Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea was constructed for model training and evaluation. YOLO11-ISW achieved detection Precision, Recall, and F1-score values of 92.01%, 80.73%, and 86.00%, respectively, and segmentation values of 93.14%, 82.60%, and 87.55%, respectively. The model achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the evaluated methods. The segmentation results were further georeferenced to extract ISW crest-line locations, and the framework was applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020 to investigate satellite-observed ISW spatiotemporal variability. These results demonstrate the potential of YOLO11-ISW for automated, long-term, and large-scale monitoring of ISWs using satellite remote sensing imagery.

The paper that matters most for the Marine heatwave early warning project is **#4 — "Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish"** (Stuart-Smith et al., 2026, Conservation Science and Practice).

Here's why it stands out:

**It's the only paper in the slate that shows a marine heatwave forecast actually triggering a real-world action.** In the 2023/24 El Niño, forecasts flagged a high risk of extreme heatwaves in Australia. An expert workshop used those forecasts to trigger a pre-emptive rescue of 25 critically endangered red handfish — Australia's first of its kind. The fish were held in captivity for three months while in-situ temperatures exceeded records (80 days more than 2°C above the long-term mean), then released with confirmed post-release survival.

**Why this matters for your project specifically:**
- It demonstrates the full loop your project is building toward: *forecast → risk assessment → decision → action → outcome verification*. That's the "early warning" part of early warning.
- It gives you a concrete, published example of how forecast uncertainty and expert judgment can be combined to justify intervention — useful both as a methodological template and as a citation when you make the case to managers or funders.
- It's recent (2026) and from a high-visibility conservation venue, so it's a strong anchor for the "so what" of your work.

The other strong candidate is **#5** (ML-based 1–14-day MHW forecasts in the Bay of Bengal), which is directly relevant to the forecasting methodology side, but it's a thesis dataset release with a thin abstract — less to work with right now. **#3** (seasonal Northeast Pacific ocean forecasts) is also relevant to the forecasting infrastructure, but it's a comment on a preprint and focuses on seasonal rather than event-scale prediction.

If you want, I can pull the full text of #4 to dig into how they structured the forecast-to-decision workflow.

#4 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.
