#3 [paper] Comment on egusphere-2026-5844
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2026-5844-rc2
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Providing seasonal ocean forecasts for the Northeast Pacific to support marine resource management and ecosystem variability assessment.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A seasonal ocean forecasting system based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model, forced by GFDL-SPEAR global climate forecasts, with a ~10 km horizontal re…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Northeast Pacific region extending from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea; evaluation uses a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months, assessed against ocean reanalyses and in situ observations.
Abstract:
Abstract. Seasonal ocean forecasts offer critical insights for marine resource management, particularly in regions like the Northeast Pacific where ecosystem variability can have profound impacts on marine life, fisheries, and coastal communities. Under NOAA’s Changing Ecosystems and Fisheries Initiative, we developed a seasonal ocean forecasting system for the Northeast Pacific based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) ocean model coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) sea ice model and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model. The model domain extends from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea with ~10 km horizontal resolution. To evaluate forecast skill, we produced a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months. Forcing for the forecasts was derived from the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory's Seamless System for Prediction and Earth System Research (GFDL-SPEAR) global climate forecast system. Forecasts were assessed using ocean reanalyses and in situ observations, focusing on three ecologically- and societally-relevant variables: sea surface temperature, bottom temperature, and bottom oxygen concentration. Forecast skill varies by region, variable, and season, but generally remains high (anomaly correlation coefficient; ACC>0.5) for lead times of at least several months across all variables and regions. The downscaled forecasts reduce errors relative to the SPEAR global forecasts and in some cases increase ACC, while also enabling predictions of biogeochemical variables. These new forecasts compare favorably to previous downscaled ocean forecasts off the U.S. west coast, with increased ACC and small forecast errors that may be reduced further by future methodological changes. Routine real-time forecasts, available starting in October 2026, will support proactive decision making by managers, industry, and coastal communities.

The clear standout for Plastic pathways is **#4** — "Code and aggregated results for 'A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter: development and application to field records from Uido, Republic of Korea'" (Lim & Hong, 2026, Zenodo).

Why it matters most:

- **It's the only item on the slate squarely about marine litter.** The rest of the feed is phytoplankton production (#3, #9), ocean forecast model diagnostics (#5), internal waves (#7), turtle telemetry (#12), and so on — interesting, but adjacent at best. #4 is about tracking where plastic ends up on shore.
- **It's a method you can actually reuse.** It ships a three-phase beaching kernel plus six other particle kernels for OceanParcels 3.1.4, with the experiment scripts and aggregated results behind it. If your project involves particle-tracking plastic pathways, this is a ready-made, validated component rather than a paper to read and file.
- **It's validated against field records.** The kernel was developed and tested against real beaching observations from Uido, Korea, using ROMS flow fields — so it's not just a theoretical construct.
- **It's fresh and open.** It entered the slate on 2026-11-10 and is still current, so the code and results are available to pull right now.

One caveat: the project's confirmed state (goals, method, blockers) isn't visible to me in this conversation, so I'm judging fit from the project's name and the lab's declared interests (debris pathways, observing from space). If the team's current focus is, say, oceanic transport rather than final beaching, the fit might be narrower — but for a project called Plastic pathways, a tide-resolving beaching kernel is about as on-target as it gets.

Worth considering: have Jonah or Priya pull the kernel code and check whether it drops into your existing OceanParcels setup. If the project's state in Mycelium is stale, it's also worth updating it in the app so the feed ranking has better signal to work with.

final_text:
Here's the comparison, grounded in what each grant actually asks for and what the Marine heatwave early warning project is about.

## The two grants at a glance

| | #1 GOOS (OceanEye) | #2 Antarctica / Southern Ocean |
|---|---|---|
| **Amount** | €50,000,000 | €5,000,000–€11,000,000 |
| **Deadline** | 2027-02-16 | 2027-09-23 |
| **Core ask** | Strengthen and operationalise the *global ocean observing system* — deploy equipment, run observing-system experiments, optimise networks, co-create tech roadmaps with industry | Resolve uncertainties and improve *projections* for the Antarctic/Southern Ocean — ocean–ice–atmosphere interactions, tipping points, ecosystem vulnerability, monitoring indicators |
| **Setting** | Global, with emphasis on areas beyond national jurisdiction, polar regions, deep sea | Specifically the Antarctic and Southern Ocean, continental shelves, bottom-water formation regions |

## Which fits the Marine heatwave early warning project better

**#2 (Antarctica / Southern Ocean) is the closer fit**, for two reasons:

1. **It explicitly calls for extreme events.** The scope says proposals should "better understand the distribution, underlying mechanisms and impacts of changes in the Southern Ocean and sea ice to reduce uncertainties in projected future changes … This should include **extreme events** and mid-latitude weather" (#2, Scope). Marine heatwaves are exactly the kind of extreme event this language reaches for, and the project's whole purpose is forecasting them.

2. **It is about improving projections and monitoring indicators** — which is what an early-warning project does. The expected outcomes ask for "improved multidisciplinary scientific understanding … in the near term (∼2030), mid-term (2050–2060) and long-term" and for "key ocean, cryosphere, climate and biodiversity monitoring indicators" (#2, Expected Outcome). An early-warning system is a monitoring/forecasting instrument, so it slots naturally into that framing.

**#1 (GOOS) is a weaker fit** for this project. It is fundamentally about the *observing infrastructure itself* — deploying equipment, network optimisation, procurement readiness, EU strategic autonomy in observation (#1, Expected Outcome & Scope). The Marine heatwave early warning project is a *forecasting/prediction* effort, not an observing-network-building effort. The overlap is only indirect: better observations feed better forecasts, but the grant's centre of gravity is the observing system, not the prediction product.

## One honest caveat

The fit is **regional, not thematic**. #2 is locked to the Antarctic and Southern Ocean. If the Marine heatwave early warning project's work is centred on a different region (e.g. the Bay of Bengal, as in #8, or the Pacific, as in #13), then #2's geographic scope would be a real constraint and the "fit" becomes thinner. #1, by contrast, is global and region-agnostic, so it would accommodate any study area — but it asks for observing-system work rather than forecasting.

So: **if the project's focus region is the Southern Ocean, #2 is the better match.** If the project works elsewhere, neither is a clean fit, and #1's global scope is the more flexible of the two — though still aimed at observation infrastructure rather than early-warning forecasting.

Want me to check whether the project's current slate has any items that pin down its study region, so I can firm up which of the two actually applies?

## Best-fitting open grant: #3

**Advancing understanding, modelling and prediction of extreme events in a changing climate** (#3) is the strongest fit, and it's still open (deadline 2027-03-04, €3M–€15M).

Why it fits the Marine heatwave early warning project (#1):
- The call is explicitly about **prediction, projection and attribution of extreme events** and "improved early warning systems for single and multi-hazard events" (#3, Expected Outcomes) — which is exactly what a marine heatwave early-warning project is.
- It welcomes **AI-based approaches** and a hierarchy of models including **digital twins** and high-resolution Earth system models (#3, Scope) — matching the project's ML + data-assimilation method.
- It asks for **seamless prediction from short-term weather to sub-seasonal and multi-decadal scales** (#3, Scope), which is the core of heatwave forecasting.

The one big doubt: #3 is a broad, large, multi-hazard, Europe-and-global call that expects a full consortium and integration with Copernicus / Destination Earth. A single-lab marine-heatwave project is a *component* of that, not the whole thing — so it's best approached as part of a larger consortium rather than a standalone bid.

The next-best on the project's slate is #6 (Global Ocean Observing System, €50M, deadline 2027-02-16), but it's about *observation infrastructure and GOOS governance*, not prediction — a weaker match for an early-warning/prediction project.

## Who in the lab should lead

The nightly ranking names two people for #3:
- **Tomás Ferreira-Lind (#18)** — the ranking's top pick. He covers the "Earth system models" slot (declared: regional ocean models), and his **physics-informed ML surrogates for ocean models** map directly onto the call's "seamless prediction and projection modelling" requirement.
- **Jonah Whitcombe (#15)** — the ranking's second pick, on the strength of the lab's marine-heatwave forecasting focus.

My read: **Tomás should lead the technical/prediction core** of the application, since his physics-informed ML is the closest thing in the lab to the call's modelling-and-projection ask. As PI you'd anchor the overall proposal and the early-warning framing.

Gaps no one in the lab covers (from the call's requirement slots): **extreme events in a changing climate** as a named expertise, **digital twins**, **Copernicus**, and **Destination Earth**. These are the slots a partner has to fill.

## Who outside the lab could partner

I can't name specific external people here — collaborator search is turned off on this instance, so Mylo has no consented external profiles to draw on. What I can say is what the partnership *needs to supply*, based on the gaps:

- A **digital-twins / high-resolution Earth-system-model** group (fills the digital-twins and Earth-system-model slots).
- A **Copernicus / Destination Earth** integration partner — the call encourages interoperability with both, and possibly the EC's Joint Research Centre (JRC) for the Copernicus Emergency Management Service (#3, Scope).
- A **disaster-risk-reduction / climate-adaptation** actor (EU or national/regional) to carry the "extreme events in a changing climate" and resilience framing.
- Given the call's encouragement of international cooperation, a **low- to middle-income country** partner for capacity-building is a plus, not a requirement.

If you'd like, I can draft the consortium structure around those four partner roles, or pull the full text of #3 to check the exact eligibility and budget rules before you commit to leading.

results.name: read_skill
results.content:
# Judging a call's fit

1. Read the call with `corpus_item` (deadlines, eligibility, amount, whether it is
   still open). If it is closed, say so first.
2. Read who it is for: `projects_get` for a project, `org_lab` for a lab,
   `me_profile` / `me_interests` for the person.
3. Compare concretely: the call's aims against the project's problem and
   method; its eligibility rules (career stage, citizenship, institution type)
   against what you know; its deadline against the project's milestones.
4. Say what fits, what does not, and what you could not check (eligibility you
   cannot see, a budget you do not know). Never guess eligibility.
5. If the question is who should apply, read the `who-should-apply` skill.

Honesty rules, as in Mylo's reports: no scores or percentages, no hype, no
"perfect fit". One plain sentence on the strongest reason and one on the
biggest doubt. Cite the call and the project by #n.

results.name: read_skill
results.content:
# Who should apply

1. Read the call (`corpus_item`). Then `knowledge_people_for_call`, which
   returns, per person, the requirement slots they cover and the evidence tier
   of each: **declared** (they said so in their profile), **demonstrated**
   (their own papers), **confirmed in conversation** (they told Mylo and said
   yes when asked).
2. Present people by the slots they cover, strongest evidence first. Say the
   tier in plain words for each claim ("from her papers", "she told Mylo in
   October").
3. Name gaps: slots no one covers. Outside-the-lab suggestions only appear when
   collaborator search is on and people consented; never speculate beyond them.
4. Do not rank people with numbers, and do not judge anyone's eligibility you
   cannot see.

#3 [grant] Advancing understanding, modelling and prediction of extreme events in a changing climate
Amount: €3,000,000–€15,000,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-CL5-2027-01-D1-07
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-03-04
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Understanding, modelling, and predicting extreme events (isolated, compound, or cascading) in a changing climate, including their interaction, likelihood, and impact on resilience.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Utilizing a hierarchy of models (including high-resolution Earth system models and digital twins), data from past and recent climate, AI-based approaches, quantitative intercomparisons, retrospective analyses, and case studies to improve prediction, projection, and attribution capabilities across s…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Europe and globally, encompassing large-scale continental to local-scale phenomena, with specific focus on EU and national/regional actors, low- to middle-income countries, and integration with initiatives like Copernicus and Destination Earth.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- Improved understanding of past and present extreme events in the context of climate change in Europe and globally, as well as the interaction between different hazards, their cumulative and/or cascading effects.

- Enhanced seamless prediction and projection modelling and attribution capabilities for extreme events and their likelihood to support preparedness, response and resilience to climate change by EU and national and regional actors. The EU Union Preparedness Strategy, the EU Adaptation Strategy and the European Climate Adaptation Plan can act as a guidance in these efforts.

- Up-to-date contributions towards latest climate science, risk assessments, adaptation strategies and policies and improved early warning systems for single and multi-hazard events.

Scope:

Climate change is intensifying the frequency and severity of extreme events. Understanding and predicting extreme events and the interaction between different types of hazards is critical for building resilience and safeguarding communities.

Actions are expected to draw upon multiple lines of evidence from a hierarchy of models (including high resolution Earth system models and digital twins) and data of past and recent climate to further our understanding of processes, pre-conditioning and causality driving extreme events under climate change conditions, including anthropogenic factors and internal variability. Other innovative and efficient modelling and analysis methods, including AI-based approaches, to better predict, emulate and reveal climate change related extreme and unprecedented high impact events, and to capture their likelihood are particularly welcome.

Extreme events should be addressed in their broadest sense and types, encompassing isolated, compound or cascading events affecting lives, livelihoods, ecosystems, socio-economic sectors and infrastructures, from large-scale continental to local-scale phenomena.

Actions should encompass quantitative intercomparisons, retrospective analyses, lessons learned and case studies of recent emblematic and diverse extreme events, and demonstrate the corresponding progress offered by the project in terms of improved understanding, comprehensive integration of multiple lines of evidence, and seamless (e.g. from short-term weather to sub-seasonal and multi-decadal scales) prediction and projection capabilities and skills.

The work is expected to support the future European Climate Risk Assessment (EUCRA)[1], for example through storylines on extremes or other approaches. Project outcomes should demonstrate clear benefits for the prediction and attribution of extreme events and contribute to the activities of the EU Mission on Adaptation to Climate Change.

Cooperation with global, EU, national and regional actors in the field of Disaster Risk Reduction and climate adaptation, including through integration into or interoperability with Copernicus, Destination Earth and other relevant initiatives is encouraged. In addition, international cooperation with low- to middle-income countries automatically eligible for Horizon Europe funding[2] is encouraged in support of climate resilience efforts, especially for capacity building.

Selected proposals may consider the involvement of the European Commission's Joint Research Centre (JRC) whose contribution could consist of scientific advice and technical support in the context of the Copernicus Emergency Management Service and transfer of relevant research outcomes to operations.

This topic is part of a coordination initiative between ESA and the European Commission on Earth System Science (ESSI) under the new Extreme-Events Flagship Cluster. Successful consortia will be asked to coordinate with projects to be selected under ESA's FutureEO programme to facilitate access to and uptake of satellite data products and related tools or methodologies. Amount: €50,000,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-NATURE-2027-04-01
Still open/current: yes

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The global ocean observing system faces risks to continuity, openness, and resilience due to evolving geopolitical dynamics, reduced engagement by key international partners, and structural gaps in under-observed regions like the deep sea and polar regions, which threatens scientific sovereignty an…
Method (Mycelium's reading): Strengthening the Global Ocean Observing System (GOOS) through the deployment of observation equipment, performing observing system experiments (OSEs) and observing system simulation experiments (OSSEs), applying network optimization approaches, co-creating technology roadmaps with industry, and in…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Global ocean observing frameworks, specifically the Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission’s Global Ocean Observing System (GOOS), areas beyond national jurisdiction, and the Copernicus Marine Service.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Proposals are expected to contribute to all the following expected outcomes, in full alignment with the OceanEye initiative:

- scientists, public authorities and businesses benefit from strengthened and resilient global ocean observing capacities, coordinated under the Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission’s Global Ocean Observing System (GOOS),[1] through the deployment of ocean observation equipment, in particular for the provision of critical observations for marine biodiversity and ecosystem knowledge;

- public authorities prioritise investments on infrastructures and capacity building to advance ocean research, protect and restore ocean health and biodiversity and provide critical services through a global ocean observing system and data delivery that is fit-for purpose, cost efficient and designed across all its components;

- increased EU leadership and strategic autonomy in global ocean observation capabilities, in support of EU climate and biodiversity goals, strengthening the EU’s contribution to and influence within GOOS, and reducing the risk of critical dependencies, notably for key services (i.e. Copernicus Services);

- enhanced collaboration between observation communities, marine research infrastructures, European SMEs and technology providers, maritime industries, and service operators, actionably contributing to the validation, procurement readiness, uptake and large-scale deployment of innovative ocean observing technologies and approaches, in particular for biodiversity observations, while reinforcing the long-term sustainability of the global ocean observing system.

Scope:

The EU has committed to global leadership in climate action, biodiversity protection and ocean governance, notably through the EU Ocean Pact, the EU Ocean Observation Initiative “OceanEye”, the EU Biodiversity Strategy for 2030, the EU Mission Restore our Ocean and Waters, the EU Climate Law, and international commitments such as the Global Biodiversity Framework and Agreement on Marine Biological Diversity of Areas beyond National Jurisdiction (BBNJ). Achieving these objectives requires sustained, global, interoperable and open ocean observations, as well as the knowledge and the capacity to use these observations.

IOC-GOOS, constituting the internationally recognised framework for in situ ocean observations worldwide, provides the global backbone for the development and monitoring of Essential Ocean Variables (EOVs),[2] and underpins European capacities such as Copernicus Marine Service and EU-funded research and innovation activities under Horizon Europe. Sustained and resilient ocean observation is crucial for marine biodiversity conservation and restoration under a changing climate, meaning that maintaining an optimised global ocean observing system is very important to achieve biodiversity goals.

Evolving geopolitical dynamics and reduced engagement by key international partners pose significant risks to the continuity, openness and resilience of global ocean observing systems, in particular in areas beyond national jurisdictions, highlighting the need for reinforced European action to safeguard scientific sovereignty and long-term, reliable observations and predictions. final_text:
I have everything I need. Here's my read.

## 1. Best-fitting open grant

The strongest fit is **#24 — "A stronger Global Ocean Observing System to enhance Europe's strategic autonomy, climate resilience and biodiversity conservation"** (€50M, deadline 2027-02-16, still open). It's the only open grant on the Plastic pathways slate that is squarely about *how we observe and track what's in the ocean*, which is exactly what the project is built on.

- **What fits:** The project's core method — Lagrangian particle tracking, satellite remote sensing, and data assimilation feeding forecasts — is precisely the kind of "strengthen and operationalise the observing system" work #24 asks for. The lab's stated mission (combine ocean models, satellite observations and ML to forecast where floating debris ends up) maps directly onto the call's goal of fit-for-purpose, cost-efficient ocean observation and data delivery.
- **The biggest doubt:** #24 is a *system-level* call — it wants observing-system experiments (OSEs/OSSEs), network optimisation, and a focus on areas beyond national jurisdiction. The project's current work is more about *modelling and forecasting* debris pathways than about designing the observing network itself. So the fit is real but you'd be pitching the project's methods as a contribution to a broader observing-system agenda, not a one-to-one match.

The other open grant on the slate, **#31 (NSF Ocean Technology and Interdisciplinary Coordination)**, is a weaker fit: it's about *instrumentation development* with broad applicability to ocean science, not about plastic pathways specifically. And the plastic-specific grants I found (#1 recycling biotech, #4 microplastics health-effects coordination, #7 zero-carbon-fuel spills) are all about materials, health, or fuel pollution — not the transport-and-forecasting angle this project lives in.

## 2. Who in the lab should lead

For #24, the slot analysis comes back with two people who cover the core "strengthen and operationalise the observing system" requirement, both on **declared** evidence (their profiles):

- **You (Mara Ellison)** — ocean data assimilation. The ranking notes your data-assimilation-with-ML for ocean forecasting strengthens the observing system's outputs. As PI you're the natural lead.
- **Priya Raman (#21)** — satellite ocean remote sensing. Her satellite ocean-colour work for water quality is the clearest single contribution to "strengthened global ocean observing capacities and data coordination."

I'd frame it as **you leading, with Priya as the observing-systems co-lead** — she carries the strongest single declared match to the call's core ask, and the two of you cover the data-assimilation + remote-sensing spine.

**Gaps no one in the lab covers:** observing-system experiments (OSEs), observing-system simulation experiments (OSSEs), network optimisation, and areas beyond national jurisdiction. The call also asks for an **industry** role that no profile matches. These are the slots you'd need to fill with partners (below) or by scoping the proposal to lean on what you *do* have.

Note: Jonah (#20) is the lab's declared marine-litter/Lagrarian specialist and is on the project, but his declared profile doesn't map onto #24's *observing-system* slots — his strength is the debris-tracking method, which is the project's content rather than the call's specific ask.

## 3. Who outside the lab to partner with

Collaborator search is turned off on this instance, so I can't pull a consented list of people to approach. What I *can* do is point at the research groups whose recent work overlaps the gaps, so you have a concrete shortlist to reach out to yourself:

- **Santiago Bravo, Eugenia Pasanisi, Svitlana Liubartseva, Giovanni Coppini et al. (#47)** — "Marine litter in the Mediterranean: observation-based Lagrangian particle tracking." This is the closest methodological match to the project (Parcels-based, observation-initialised, Copernicus-forced, with a decision-maker dashboard). They also explicitly flag validation against beach-litter monitoring and land-based source inventories as open work — a natural hook.
- **Ross Vennell, Laurin Steidle, Malcolm Smeaton, Romain Chaput, Ben Knight (#56)** — the OceanTracker team. They build the fast, adaptable Lagrangian particle-tracking tooling; a strong technical partner for the particle-tracking and network-scaling side.
- **MD Millen Singh (#51)** — "Implementing AI in Ocean Waste Tracking and Management." Covers the AI/detection-and-forecasting angle and the government–industry–academic partnership framing #24 wants.

The #47 group is the best first call: same method, same data sources, and an explicit stated need for the kind of validation and source-inventory work that would let you fill the OSE/OSSE and beyond-national-jurisdiction gaps.

**What I couldn't check:** #24's full eligibility rules (EU/associated-country institution requirements, consortium size, industry-participation minimums) and the exact budget split — the abstract was truncated before those details. I'd confirm those in the call text before committing. And since I can't see anyone's full CV, I've only gone on declared profiles and published papers — worth confirming with Jonah, Priya, and the external groups directly.

Want me to pull the full text of #24 to check the eligibility and industry-participation rules, or draft the one-paragraph pitch framing the project's methods as a contribution to the GOOS agenda?

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The decarbonization of waterborne transport using renewable low and zero-carbon fuels introduces new, unexplored risks to marine and aquatic ecosystems, including pollution from normal operations and accidental spills, threatening the achievement of Good Environmental and Ecological Status in Europ…
Method (Mycelium's reading): The project aims to evaluate and forecast environmental impacts, model pollution sources, and develop, demonstrate, and test innovative prevention, abatement, and mitigation systems and strategies (targeting TRL 5) for managing spills and reducing harmful impacts of zero-emission fuels.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): European marine waters, inland waterways, and port areas, focusing on waterborne transport operations using renewable low and zero-carbon fuels.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes.

- Improved water resilience and good environmental and good ecological status in European waters and contribute to the achievement of the European Union's environmental targets, including the European Water Resilience Strategy and the European Ocean Pact.

- A comprehensive understanding of the future environmental impacts of waterborne transport on marine and other aquatic ecosystems, addressing in particular pollution sources from: i) navigation on renewable low and zero-carbon fuels; and ii) accidental spills of renewable low and zero-carbon fuels for marine waters, inland waters and ports (water and air quality).

- Innovative prevention, abatement and mitigation systems and strategies for reducing and eliminating the harmful impacts of waterborne transport on waters.

- Enhanced pollution prevention and mitigation in marine waters, inland waterways and port areas, reducing the likelihood and impact of accidents involving renewable low and zero-carbon fuels.

Scope:

The European Union aims to protect and conserve its marine and freshwater environments by achieving Good Environmental and Good Ecological Status[1]. The European Water Resilience Strategy and the European Ocean Pact further emphasize the need to enhance the resilience of European waters to human-induced pressures. Projects like the Horizon Europe EMERGE have researched the impacts of shipping on marine ecosystems. The introduction of technologies to decarbonize the sector may enable, to a certain extent, to phase-out relevant current sources of water and air pollution. However, renewable low and zero-carbon fuels and procedures pose new risks to marine and other aquatic ecosystems like rivers and lakes yet to be explored and addressed, both from the normal function of waterborne transport[2] and from accidental spills of renewable low and zero-carbon fuels. In addition, other pollution sources can be addressed today[3]. This topic aims to evaluate, forecast, control and mitigate the impact of waterborne transport on marine and other aquatic ecosystems, with a focus on developing and demonstrating innovative abatement and mitigation systems and strategies to mitigate and eliminate, where possible, the harmful impact of waterborne transport in the ocean and inland waters. New technologies and solutions addressing the decarbonization of waterborne transport will be considered, as well as the potential risks and challenges associated with these.

Actions should address all of the following aspects:

- Evaluate and forecast the environmental impacts of waterborne transport operations on marine, rivers and other aquatic ecosystems, in particular regarding the effects of renewable low and zero-carbon fuels (with particular attention to accidental spills) and related technologies. The proposal may include testing and experimental work in relation with spills.

- Develop and demonstrate effective response scenarios, including the associated abatement technologies and any potential new innovative equipment, for managing uncontrolled releases of renewable low and zero-carbon fuels in marine and inland waters or in port areas, including dedicated specific procedures and operational guidelines.

- Modelling scenarios on water and air pollution sources from each ship types and services running on renewable low and zero carbon fuels.

- Develop and demonstrate innovative and cost-effective abatement and mitigation systems and strategies to prevent, eliminate and reduce the harmful impacts of the use of renewable low and zero carbon fuels. Relevant TRL5 demonstration of such systems should be done.

- Identifying training needs and skills requirements to deploy developed solutions, as well as in relation to the management and use of renewable low carbon fuels in ports and on vessels in marine and inland waters, including relevant emergency response preparedness.

results.content:
#47 [paper] Marine litter in the Mediterranean: observation-based Lagrangian particle tracking
Authors: Santiago Bravo, Eugenia Pasanisi, Svitlana Liubartseva, Giovanni Coppini, Alice Madonia, Igor Atake, Marta Azzolin, Lara Carosso
Venue: Frontiers in Marine Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2026.1936698
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The lack of spatially explicit, observation-grounded predictions for the transport and coastal deposition of floating marine macro-litter (FMML) in the Mediterranean.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A data-driven stochastic Lagrangian framework using Parcels, initialized with monthly gridded FMML observations from shipboard surveys and forced by Copernicus Marine Service Mediterranean reanalysis currents and ERA5 wind fields with a 1% windage coefficient and a 2D random-walk turbulent diffusio…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Mediterranean Sea, specifically areas surveyed via the LIFE Conceptu Maris Project using ferries from August 2023 to December 2024.
Abstract:
Introduction The Mediterranean is a major hotspot for floating marine macro-litter (FMML) accumulation, yet spatially explicit, observation-grounded predictions of its transport and coastal deposition remain scarce. We present a data-driven stochastic Lagrangian framework that uses monthly gridded FMML observations from systematic shipboard surveys as simulation initial conditions complementing existing source-based modelling approaches. Methods Observations were collected from August 2023 to December 2024 within the LIFE Conceptu Maris Project using ferries as monitoring platforms under a standardised protocol. A total of 158 surveys detected 4,801 FMML items across approximately 6,200 km² of surveyed sea surface, of which more than 62% were artificial polymers. Observed monthly FMML item counts at 5 × 5 km resolution initialised ensemble Lagrangian simulations (18 members per target month; 17.2–32.5 million virtual particles per seeding window, 5,000 particles per observed item) using Parcels, forced by Copernicus Marine Service Mediterranean reanalysis currents and ERA5 wind fields with a 1% windage coefficient and a 2D random-walk turbulent diffusion scheme. Monthly frequency-of-occurrence maps were computed at the sea surface and on coastlines. Results The Southern Tyrrhenian and Northern Ligurian seas, including the Pelagos Sanctuary, exhibited in 2024 near-persistent high sea surface FMML occurrence, peaking in late summer–autumn and reaching a seasonal minimum in winter–early spring. The Balearic Sea showed elevated occurrence from late spring through summer (May–September), declining through autumn. The Adriatic displayed intense sub-basin-scale spreading from January to June and again in December, with summer leakage into the Northern Ionian Sea. Coastal deposition frequencies were highest on Corsica, western Sardinia and northern Tunisia, then the south-eastern Tyrrhenian and Ligurian–Tuscan margins, with Valencia–Barcelona largely confined to summer. Integration with loggerhead turtle nesting records illustrates how coastal frequency-of-occurrence maps can support conservation applications. Discussion A web-based Particle Analysis Dashboard translates these outputs into an interactive tool with Marine Protected and Conserved Area overlays for scientists and decision-makers. The framework provides a scalable, observation-anchored foundation for MSFD Descriptor 10 monitoring, transferable to other semi-enclosed sea basins. Priority future work includes complementary validation against independent beach-litter monitoring data, integration of land-based source inventories, and linkage with species distribution models.

#56 [paper] OceanTracker 0.5: fast adaptable Lagrangian particle tracking in structured and unstructured grids
Authors: Ross Vennell, Laurin Steidle, Malcolm Smeaton, Romain Chaput, Ben Knight
Venue: Geoscientific model development
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/gmd-19-10223-2026
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Modelling millions of particles in hydrodynamic ocean models is computationally challenging and time-consuming, particularly regarding trajectory recording and post-processing.
Method (Mycelium's reading): OceanTracker is a modular, adaptable Lagrangian particle tracking tool that assembles a computational pipeline from user-provided parameters. It supports both structured and unstructured grids and calculates multiple particle statistics during the computational run to eliminate post-processing time.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Hydrodynamic model outputs for unstructured grids (SCHISM, FVCOM, DELFT3D-FM) and structured grids (ROMS, NEMO/GLORYS).
Abstract:
Particle tracking is frequently used to compute particle movements within hydrodynamic ocean models; however, modelling millions of particles is computationally challenging. OceanTracker is designed to minimise the time required to obtain results from particle tracking. Firstly, by being computationally fast, it enables users to scale to large numbers of particles, thus obtaining better statistics or exploring a wider range of cases within acceptable run times. Secondly, OceanTracker can calculate multiple particle statistics during the computational run, eliminating the time needed to post-process large volumes of recorded particle trajectories. The adaptability of OceanTracker's modular computational pipeline allows users to add and modify components which govern particle physics, behaviour, and statistics. The computational pipeline is entirely assembled from user-provided parameters, supplied as a text file or built using helper methods. Coders can easily modify existing components through code inheritance. Currently, OceanTracker supports hydrodynamic model output for unstructured grids (SCHISM, FVCOM, DELFT3D-FM) and structured grids (ROMS, NEMO/GLORYS). Computing the trajectories for more than a million particles with OceanTracker on a single computer core is 35 times faster than the OpenDrift code and twice as fast as the Ocean Parcels code, despite treating structured grids as unstructured. As a result, on a basic laptop computers it can model one million particles for one month in less than one hour, or many more particles on better hardware. OceanTrackers design allows multiple variations of particle tracking to be configured to run in parallel.

Marine pollution has emerged as a significant environmental challenge, with millions of tons of waste flowing intooceans each year, causing disruptions in marine ecosystems. Traditional methods for monitoring and addressing thispollution are inadequate in dealing with its ineffable complexity. Researchers are thoroughly investigating the potentialof artificial intelligence (AI) as a revolutionary tool for tracking and reducing ocean pollution. This literature reviewexplores the application of cutting-edge technology in tracking and mitigating marine pollution, such as plastic waste,oil spills, and wastewater contamination. A comprehensive review of recent research was performed, concentrating ontechniques that employ advanced technology for the detection, forecasting, and elimination of marine debris. Researchshows that advanced computer vision and machine learning techniques significantly boost the efficiency and precisionof pollution detection, such as recognizing plastic waste through satellite images, and improving clean-up strategies bydirecting collection vessels for maximum effectiveness. Efforts are underway to form partnerships among governmententities, industry players, and academic scholars to advance these data-centric solutions. However, obstacles persist;AI systems typically demand significant amounts of data and are subject to time limitations, and it is essential toconsider the environmental impacts of AI deployment, including energy use and electronic waste. This paper bringstogether current applications, assesses their effectiveness and limitations, and highlights gaps in the existing research.The ability of AI to transform ocean waste management is substantial; however, achieving its complete potentialnecessitates collaboration across disciplines, strict data governance, and thoughtful attention to sustainability in AIresearch.

Here's where **Plastic pathways** (#2) stands, plus what's new on its slate and a funding angle.

## Where the project stands

I have to be upfront: Mylo holds very little confirmed state for this project. What I can see is:

- **Members:** Jonah Whitcombe, Priya Raman, and you
- **Scope:** lab-level project
- **Confirmed state:** none on file — no goals, method, blockers, milestones, or stage have been recorded, and there's no timestamp for a last confirmation

So I can't tell you how the work itself is progressing. If the team has been working on it, that context isn't in Mylo yet. You can add goals, blockers and milestones in the app, and I can then track them properly.

## Three most relevant new papers

All three entered the slate this week (since 2026-11-10):

1. **#6 — "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter" (Lim & Hong, 2026, Zenodo)** — The most directly on-point item: a three-phase beaching kernel plus six particle kernels for OceanParcels 3.1.4, validated against field records from Uido, Korea, using ROMS flow fields. If your project involves particle tracking or beaching modelling, this is a ready-made method and codebase to build on.

2. **#10 — "A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery" (Rong et al., 2026, Remote Sensing)** — A YOLO11-based detector/segmenter for low-contrast, curved ocean features in MODIS imagery, applied to a decade of data. Relevant as a template for satellite-based detection of plastic-related features (e.g. surface accumulations) at scale.

3. **#11 — "Basin-scale changes in net primary production from the biogeochemical-Argo array" (2026)** — Less directly about plastic, but useful context for the biogeochemical environment that plastic pathways interact with, and a reminder of what basin-scale Argo-based analysis can deliver.

## One funding opportunity to consider

**#3 — "A stronger Global Ocean Observing System to enhance Europe's strategic autonomy, climate resilience and biodiversity conservation"** (Horizon Europe, €50M, deadline 2027-02-16).

Why it fits: the call explicitly asks for proposals that strengthen observing networks and data delivery for marine biodiversity and ecosystem knowledge, with attention to structural gaps in under-observed regions. A plastic-pathways project that combines in-situ observations, particle tracking, and satellite data could position itself as a biodiversity/ecosystem-health observing use case within GOOS. The deadline is about three months out, so there's time to shape a proposal.

A second option worth a look: **#12 — "Integrating Remote Sensing and in-situ observations of Biodiversity"** (Horizon, €3–8M, deadline 2027-09-22) — more focused on data integration and FAIR frameworks, which could suit the analytical side of the project.

**Suggested next step:** if you'd like, confirm the project's goals and current blockers in the app, and I can re-run this review with the slate tied to specific gaps.

#10 [paper] A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery over the Northern South China Sea
Authors: Guocai Rong, Huanhe Dong, Yuan Kong, Ze Liu, Yong Hui Fang
Venue: Remote Sensing
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18213843
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Automated extraction of internal solitary waves (ISWs) from satellite imagery is challenging due to their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast.
Method (Mycelium's reading): YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, incorporating Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) for curved structures and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for low-contrast features.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea; the framework was also applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020.
Abstract:
Internal solitary waves (ISWs) play an important role in ocean energy transport and mixing, yet their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast make automated extraction from satellite imagery challenging. To address these challenges, this study proposes YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint ISW detection and pixel-level segmentation. Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea was constructed for model training and evaluation. YOLO11-ISW achieved detection Precision, Recall, and F1-score values of 92.01%, 80.73%, and 86.00%, respectively, and segmentation values of 93.14%, 82.60%, and 87.55%, respectively. The model achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the evaluated methods. The segmentation results were further georeferenced to extract ISW crest-line locations, and the framework was applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020 to investigate satellite-observed ISW spatiotemporal variability. The detected ISWs exhibited pronounced spatial clustering, strong spring–summer seasonality, and clear lunar-cycle modulation, consistent with previous observations in the northern South China Sea. These results demonstrate the potential of YOLO11-ISW for automated, long-term, and large-scale monitoring of ISWs using satellite remote sensing imagery.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Existing in-situ biodiversity data collections (genomic, ground, drone) lack the structure, interface, and metadata required for integration with satellite remote sensing and advanced AI analytics, hindering the assessment of ecosystem condition and biodiversity trends.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Develop and validate fit-for-purpose multisensory biodiversity data integration systems to harmonize omics-based and in-situ data with remote sensing, socio-ecological, and climatic data; design data integration approaches for predictive analytics and AI; and deliver FAIR data, harmonisation workfl…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Terrestrial, freshwater, and marine ecosystems in EU Member States and Associated Countries, specifically focusing on ecosystems under pressure or restoration priorities within the EU ecosystem typology.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- advancing robust, policy-relevant ecosystem assessment, nature protection and restoration planning activities, and biodiversity trend prediction based on fit for purpose data, thus supporting EU biodiversity and climate objectives;

- strengthened capacity of researchers, practitioners and decision-makers to improve biodiversity monitoring practices and address knowledge gaps via the integration of data and observations across sensors and platforms, ranging from omics-based data (genomic, transcriptomic, metabolomic), various in-situ to satellite-based Earth observation data;

- enhanced usability of in-situ datasets as training and validation resources for statistical, machine learning and advanced AI-based approaches, in support of applications such as habitat classification, ecosystem mapping and biodiversity trend prediction.

Scope:

Achieving the goals of the EU biodiversity strategy for 2030, the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, and assessing progress towards their defined targets, requires coherent, integrated and long-term monitoring approaches, underpinned by FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Re-usable) data systems. Many existing in-situ data collections (i.e. genomic assessments, ground sampling, drone and airborne observations) were not designed with Satellite Remote Sensing integration in mind (i.e. for validation and calibration, integrated data products, or statistical scaling of information) and lack the structure, interface and metadata required to support advanced analytics, including AI. FAIR data on species and ecosystems will also help to ensure that biodiversity preservation is a mainstream feature of other sectors, such as agriculture, transport, energy or the bioeconomy. There is a need for systemic, harmonised or standardised biodiversity data at Earth’s surface in order to support AI applications ranging from genome to space and to build up our knowledge on the status and trends of habitats, species, ecosystems, and on the drivers of decline.

To address these challenges, proposals should:

- develop and validate fit-for-purpose multisensory biodiversity data integration systems, to enable omics-based and in-situ data harmonization and integration with remote sensing data from space or sub-orbital platforms, as well as socio-ecological and climatic data for enhancing assessment of ecosystem condition and degradation, and the predictive modelling of biodiversity trends at international, regional and European scales;

- develop concrete technical capabilities able to answer to diverse use cases, across terrestrial, freshwater and marine ecosystems in Member States and Associated Countries. To this end, proposals should identify and prioritise critical biodiversity knowledge gaps and their data needs, with a focus on predictive analytics and the use of AI, and address them by designing data integration approaches that support scientific and policy needs, including biodiversity protection, restoration, and sustainable use goals and targets, as well as other related policy objectives;

- develop demonstration and verification cases focusing on specific ecosystems under the EU ecosystem typology[1] and habitats, including ecotones[2], identified as those under pressure or as restoration priorities. Proposals should take into account socio-economic pressures and activities impacting ecosystems, including land and sea use and emissions of pollutants (e.g. agriculture, aquaculture, urbanization, resource exploitation and management practices). Demonstration cases should be relevant to EO applications, such as AI-assisted ecosystem and habitat mapping, ensuring interoperability with European and global frameworks such as the Global Ecosystem Typology as well as EUNIS, and aligned with reporting requirements under the Habitats Directive, Birds Directive, Marine Strategy Framewor

"perfect fit". One plain sentence on the strongest reason and one on the

Here's the comparison.

## The two grants at a glance

| | #1 — Stronger GOOS | #2 — Antarctica & Southern Ocean |
|---|---|---|
| **Amount** | €50,000,000 | €5,000,000–€11,000,000 |
| **Deadline** | 2027-02-16 | 2027-09-23 |
| **Core focus** | Strengthening the *global* ocean observing system — deploying equipment, observing-system experiments, network optimisation, technology roadmaps with industry, closing structural gaps (deep sea, polar regions) | Resolving uncertainties and improving *projections* for the Antarctic and Southern Ocean — ocean–atmosphere–sea-ice–ice dynamics, tipping points, ecosystem vulnerability, monitoring indicators |
| **Setting** | Global, with emphasis on areas beyond national jurisdiction, GOOS/IOC framework, Copernicus Marine Service | Antarctic continental shelves, bottom-water formation regions, Southern Ocean and sea ice |

## Which fits the Marine heatwave early warning project better?

**#1 (Stronger GOOS) is the better fit**, for a few reasons:

1. **Observation infrastructure is the backbone of early warning.** The Marine heatwave early warning project (#3) is about detecting and forecasting marine heatwaves. That depends on a dense, reliable, continuous observing network — exactly what #1 funds: deploying observation equipment, running observing-system experiments (OSEs/OSSEs), network optimisation, and technology roadmaps. The project's data-assimilation and SST-forecasting work sits directly on top of the kind of infrastructure #1 is building.

2. **Geographic scope.** #1 is global and explicitly calls out closing structural gaps in under-observed regions. Marine heatwaves are a global, multi-basin phenomenon, and an early-warning system needs broad coverage, not a single region. #2 is tightly scoped to Antarctica and the Southern Ocean, which is a narrower slice of what a marine-heatwave early-warning project would need.

3. **Method alignment.** #1's method — OSEs/OSSEs, network optimisation, co-creating technology roadmaps with industry, operationalising observations — maps closely onto the data-assimilation and forecasting methods your lab uses. #2's method is more about long-term climate projections, ice dynamics, and distinguishing human-induced from natural change — valuable, but further from the operational early-warning question.

**Where #2 could still matter:** if the project has a specific interest in Southern Ocean or polar marine heatwaves, or in how Antarctic/Southern Ocean changes feed into global SST extremes, #2's emphasis on extreme events, tipping points, and long-term monitoring indicators is relevant. But as a primary fit, #1 is the stronger match.

One practical note: #1 is a €50M call with a February 2027 deadline, so it's likely a large consortium call — worth checking whether your project would be a core partner or a sub-component. #2 is smaller (€5–11M) and has a later deadline (September 2027), which gives more runway if you want to shape a proposal around it.

- **#9 A stronger Global Ocean Observing System** (Horizon Europe, €50M) — deadline 2027-02-16

**#9 is the stronger fit for the Marine heatwave early warning project (#1).** The project's core is turning ocean observations into marine heatwave forecasts — data assimilation, sea surface temperature, subseasonal forecasting. #9 is about stabilising and operationalising the global ocean observing system and the data that flows from it, which is exactly the upstream of what your project does. The strongest reason: your data-assimilation-with-ML forecasting work is a direct consumer of the observing capacities #9 wants to strengthen, so the project plugs straight into its expected outcomes.

The biggest doubt: #9 is a large, governance- and infrastructure-heavy call (€50M, GOOS frameworks, areas beyond national jurisdiction, industry partners). It is not a pure forecasting grant, so your project would need to be framed as one component of a broader observing-system effort rather than the whole thing.

**#4 is a weaker fit.** It funds instrumentation development with broad applicability to ocean science. Your project is about forecasting from existing data, not building new instruments — and no one in the lab has a declared profile that covers instrumentation development. I'd only go after #4 if you had a concrete new instrument or sensor in mind.

One thing I could not check: neither grant's full eligibility rules (institution type, career stage, EU vs. US applicant requirements) are visible to me here, so confirm those before committing.

- **Priya Raman (#16)** — satellite ocean remote sensing. A strong co-lead or co-PI, since satellite observation is a key observing-system component.

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes.

Scope:

The European Union aims to protect and conserve its marine and freshwater environments by achieving Good Environmental and Good Ecological Status[1]. The European Water Resilience Strategy and the European Ocean Pact further emphasize the need to enhance the resilience of European waters to human-induced pressures. Projects like the Horizon Europe EMERGE have researched the impacts of shipping on marine ecosystems. The introduction of technologies to decarbonize the sector may enable, to a certain extent, to phase-out relevant current sources of water and air pollution. However, renewable low and zero-carbon fuels and procedures pose new risks to marine and other aquatic ecosystems like rivers and lakes yet to be explored and addressed, both from the normal function of waterborne transport[2] and from accidental spills of renewable low and zero-carbon fuels. In addition, other pollution sources can be addressed today[3]. This topic aims to evaluate, forecast, control and mitigate the impact of waterborne transport on marine and other aquatic ecosystems, with a focus on developing and demonstrating innovative abatement and mitigation systems and strategies to mitigate and eliminate, where possible, the harmful impact of waterborne transport in the ocean and inland waters. New technologies and solutions addressing the decarbonization of waterborne transport will be considered, as well as the potential risks and challenges associated with these.

Project results are expected to contribute to some of the following expected outcomes:

Scope:

Understanding the mechanisms and drivers of land (including inland waters) and ocean carbon sinks and sources is crucial for accurate climate models and scenarios and informing climate mitigation strategies. However, significant gaps and uncertainties remain in quantifying these complex processes and their components. It is essential to better understand the roles of anthropogenic and natural drivers of carbon fluxes, in particular the surface-to-air flux. This is necessary for reconciling conceptual discrepancies among estimates and assessing the implications for future trends and mitigation potential, taking into account that mitigation actions need to be additional to natural processes and business-as-usual and that the remaining carbon budget depends, inter alia, on assumptions on sinks.

Successful consortia will be asked to coordinate with projects that will be selected under ESA’s FutureEO programme to facilitate access to and uptake of satellite data products and related tools or methodologies. International cooperation is generally encouraged, in particular with low and lower/upper-middle-income countries[1].

The ocean’s capacity to act as a carbon sink is determined by a variety of factors, including changes in climate, atmospheric composition (in particular CO2 concentration) and chemical, physical and biological processes of the ocean, all influenced by human activities. final_text:
Here's where **Plastic pathways** (#2) stands, plus what's new on its slate and one funding lead.

## Where the project stands
The project is a lab-scoped effort with three members: Jonah Whitcombe, Priya Raman, and you. Its purpose is clear from the lab's own statement (#13): tracking where floating debris ends up, combining ocean models, satellite observations and machine learning, and handing the results to coastal managers.

One honest caveat: the project record I can see holds only the name, scope and membership — no confirmed problem statement, method, milestones or open blockers are stored for it yet. If the team has confirmed state in the app, it isn't visible to me here, so this summary leans on the lab profile and the slate.

## Three most relevant new papers
All three entered the slate this week (since 2026-11-10):

1. **#6 — "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter" (Lim & Hong, 2026, Zenodo).** The closest match to the project's core question. It develops a three-phase beaching kernel plus six other particle kernels for OceanParcels 3.1.4, validated against field records from Uido, South Korea, using ROMS flow fields and particle trajectories. Directly usable as a method and codebase for modelling where litter washes ashore.
2. **#10 — "A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery" (Rong et al., 2026, Remote Sensing).** Not about litter itself, but a strong methodological template: a YOLO11-based detector (with Dynamic Snake Convolution and CBAM) that achieved detection F1 of 86.00% and segmentation F1 of 87.55% on low-contrast, curved ocean features in MODIS imagery, and was applied to imagery from 2011 to 2020. The same detection-and-segmentation pattern is exactly what you'd apply to spotting floating debris in satellite imagery.
3. **#5 — "Daily Analyses of the Pacific Regional Ocean Forecast System model" (2026).** Relevant as the operational forecasting side: daily analyses of a regional ocean forecast system, i.e. the kind of model output and assimilation workflow that would drive particle-tracking of debris pathways in a real-time setting.

The other new slate items (#4, #7, #9, #11) are about phytoplankton, a comment piece, multi-object tracking of generic objects, and biogeochemical Argo — none of which touch debris pathways.

## One funding opportunity
**#8 — NSF Ocean Technology and Interdisciplinary Coordination (OTIC) program** (NSF PD-98-1680), still open, with an application deadline of **2027-02-15**.

- **Why it fits:** OTIC accepts unsolicited proposals for instrumentation and technology development with broad applicability to ocean science that enhance observational, experimental or analytical capability. A project that builds a satellite-detection pipeline for floating debris (in the spirit of #10) plus a tide-resolving beaching model (#6) is squarely "technology that enhances analytical capability for the ocean science community" — and it has broad applicability beyond your own lab, which is what OTIC looks for.
- **The biggest doubt:** OTIC favours tools and instrumentation with wide community use; the proposal would need to be framed as a reusable capability (a debris-detection + tracking toolkit) rather than a single study of one region. Also, I can't see the full eligibility rules (US institution/citizenship requirements are typical for NSF) — worth checking against your institution before committing.

A second option worth keeping in view: **#12 — Horizon "Integrating Remote Sensing and in-situ observations of Biodiversity"** (€3–8M, deadline 2027-09-22). It's a bigger, more competitive call focused on biodiversity data integration, so the debris angle would need to be framed as pollutant pressure on marine ecosystems; it's a longer runway but a harder fit than OTIC.

**Suggested next step:** if OTIC looks right, the team could draft the proposal around "a reusable satellite-to-shore debris pathway toolkit" — detection (#10-style), particle tracking (#6-style), and daily model assimilation (#5-style) — and confirm NSF eligibility in the app. I can't edit the project or save anything myself; the project record and saves are yours to update there.

results.content:
#10 [paper] A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery over the Northern South China Sea
Authors: Guocai Rong, Huanhe Dong, Yuan Kong, Ze Liu, Yong Hui Fang
Venue: Remote Sensing
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18213843
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Automated extraction of internal solitary waves (ISWs) from satellite imagery is challenging due to their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast.
Method (Mycelium's reading): YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, incorporating Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) for curved structures and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for low-contrast features.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea; the framework was also applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020.
Abstract:
Internal solitary waves (ISWs) play an important role in ocean energy transport and mixing, yet their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast make automated extraction from satellite imagery challenging. To address these challenges, this study proposes YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint ISW detection and pixel-level segmentation. Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea was constructed for model training and evaluation. YOLO11-ISW achieved detection Precision, Recall, and F1-score values of 92.01%, 80.73%, and 86.00%, respectively, and segmentation values of 93.14%, 82.60%, and 87.55%, respectively. The model achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the evaluated methods. The segmentation results were further georeferenced to extract ISW crest-line locations, and the framework was applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020 to investigate satellite-observed ISW spatiotemporal variability. The detected ISWs exhibited pronounced spatial clustering, strong spring–summer seasonality, and clear lunar-cycle modulation, consistent with previous observations in the northern South China Sea. These results demonstrate the potential of YOLO11-ISW for automated, long-term, and large-scale monitoring of ISWs using satellite remote sensing imagery.

Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- advancing robust, policy-relevant ecosystem assessment, nature protection and restoration planning activities, and biodiversity trend prediction based on fit for purpose data, thus supporting EU biodiversity and climate objectives;

- strengthened capacity of researchers, practitioners and decision-makers to improve biodiversity monitoring practices and address knowledge gaps via the integration of data and observations across sensors and platforms, ranging from omics-based data (genomic, transcriptomic, metabolomic), various in-situ to satellite-based Earth observation data;

- enhanced usability of in-situ datasets as training and validation resources for statistical, machine learning and advanced AI-based approaches, in support of applications such as habitat classification, ecosystem mapping and biodiversity trend prediction.

Scope:

Achieving the goals of the EU biodiversity strategy for 2030, the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, and assessing progress towards their defined targets, requires coherent, integrated and long-term monitoring approaches, underpinned by FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Re-usable) data systems. Many existing in-situ data collections (i.e. genomic assessments, ground sampling, drone and airborne observations) were not designed with Satellite Remote Sensing integration in mind (i.e. for validation and calibration, integrated data products, or statistical scaling of information) and lack the structure, interface and metadata required to support advanced analytics, including AI. FAIR data on species and ecosystems will also help to ensure that biodiversity preservation is a mainstream feature of other sectors, such as agriculture, transport, energy or the bioeconomy. There is a need for systemic, harmonised or standardised biodiversity data at Earth’s surface in order to support AI applications ranging from genome to space and to build up our knowledge on the status and trends of habitats, species, ecosystems, and on the drivers of decline.

To address these challenges, proposals should:

- develop and validate fit-for-purpose multisensory biodiversity data integration systems, to enable omics-based and in-situ data harmonization and integration with remote sensing data from space or sub-orbital platforms, as well as socio-ecological and climatic data for enhancing assessment of ecosystem condition and degradation, and the predictive modelling of biodiversity trends at international, regional and European scales;

- develop concrete technical capabilities able to answer to diverse use cases, across terrestrial, freshwater and marine ecosystems in Member States and Associated Countries. To this end, proposals should identify and prioritise critical biodiversity knowledge gaps and their data needs, with a focus on predictive analytics and the use of AI, and address them by designing data integration approaches that support scientific and policy needs, including biodiversity protection, restoration, and sustainable use goals and targets, as well as other related policy objectives;

- develop demonstration and verification cases focusing on specific ecosystems under the EU ecosystem typology[1] and habitats, including ecotones[2], identified as those under pressure or as restoration priorities. Proposals should take into account socio-economic pressures and activities impacting ecosystems, including land and sea use and emissions of pollutants (e.g. agriculture, aquaculture, urbanization, resource exploitation and management practices). Demonstration cases should be relevant to EO applications, such as AI-assisted ecosystem and habitat mapping, ensuring interoperability with European and global frameworks such as the Global Ecosystem Typology as well as EUNIS, and aligned with reporting requirements under the Habitats Directive, Birds Directive, Marine Strategy Framewor

# Judging a call's fit

1. Read the call with `corpus_item` (deadlines, eligibility, amount, whether it is
   still open). If it is closed, say so first.
2. Read who it is for: `projects_get` for a project, `org_lab` for a lab,
   `me_profile` / `me_interests` for the person.
3. Compare concretely: the call's aims against the project's problem and
   method; its eligibility rules (career stage, citizenship, institution type)
   against what you know; its deadline against the project's milestones.
4. Say what fits, what does not, and what you could not check (eligibility you

#10 [paper] A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery over the Northern South China Sea
Authors: Guocai Rong, Huanhe Dong, Yuan Kong, Ze Liu, Yong Hui Fang
Venue: Remote Sensing
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18213843
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Automated extraction of internal solitary waves (ISWs) from satellite imagery is challenging due to their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast.
Method (Mycelium's reading): YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, incorporating Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) for curved structures and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for low-contrast features.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea; the framework was also applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020.
Abstract:
Internal solitary waves (ISWs) play an important role in ocean energy transport and mixing, yet their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast make automated extraction from satellite imagery challenging. To address these challenges, this study proposes YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint ISW detection and pixel-level segmentation. Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea was constructed for model training and evaluation. YOLO11-ISW achieved detection Precision, Recall, and F1-score values of 92.01%, 80.73%, and 86.00%, respectively, and segmentation values of 93.14%, 82.60%, and 87.55%, respectively. The model achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the evaluated methods. The segmentation results were further georeferenced to extract ISW crest-line locations, and the framework was applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020 to investigate satellite-observed ISW spatiotemporal variability. The detected ISWs exhibited pronounced spatial clustering, strong spring–summer seasonality, and clear lunar-cycle modulation, consistent with previous observations in the northern South China Sea. These results demonstrate the potential of YOLO11-ISW for automated, long-term, and large-scale monitoring of ISWs using satellite remote sensing imagery.

That's seven days from today. It sits on the Marine heatwave early warning slate (#1).

On the Plastic pathways slate (#2). The next call after that is the WHOI GFD fellowship (#12, 2027-02-05), so IGARSS is the second-most-urgent across both projects.

**ICGDA (#13) — geoinformatics and data analysis**
- **Sun-hee Park (#22)** — declared interest in ocean data tools; the natural lead for a data-analysis methods paper.
- **Mara Ellison (#19)** — data assimilation with ML; a strong co-author if the paper leans on ML forecasting or assimilation.

**IGARSS (#4) — geoscience and remote sensing**
- **Priya Raman (#21)** — satellite oceanography; the clearest fit for a remote-sensing paper.
- **Mara Ellison (#19)** — can co-author if the paper uses satellite SST for heatwave detection.
- **Jonah Whitcombe (#20)** — marine litter / Lagrangian analysis; fits if the paper is about debris pathways observed from space.

**For ICGDA (#13):** #11 — *Evaluation of 1-14-Day Machine-Learning Forecasts of Marine Heatwaves in the Northern Bay of Bengal Against Persistence Benchmarks* (Mojumder, 2026). **For IGARSS (#4):** #10 — *A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter: development and application to field records from Uido, Republic of Korea* (Lim & Hong, 2026). It's a particle-tracking / debris-pathways result with field validation, which anchors the Plastic pathways project and gives Priya a concrete methods story to build a remote-sensing angle on.

**Why it stands out:**

- **It's a real-world proof of concept for exactly what your project is building.** The paper documents Australia's first pre-emptive rescue of a protected marine species, triggered *by a marine heatwave forecast* ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño. An expert workshop assessed the forecasted extremes (>20°C or +~3°C) as a severe threat, and that assessment triggered the emergency intervention. That's the forecast-to-action loop your project is trying to close.

- **It shows the operational value of early warning, not just forecast skill.** The fish were captured in January 2024, held for three months, and released after the heatwave subsided — with post-release survival confirmed. #5 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.
