#3 [paper] Comment on egusphere-2026-5844
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2026-5844-rc2
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Providing seasonal ocean forecasts for the Northeast Pacific to support marine resource management and ecosystem variability assessment.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A seasonal ocean forecasting system based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model, forced by GFDL-SPEAR global climate forecasts, with a ~10 km horizontal re…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Northeast Pacific region extending from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea; evaluation uses a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months, assessed against ocean reanalyses and in situ observations.
Abstract:
Abstract. Seasonal ocean forecasts offer critical insights for marine resource management, particularly in regions like the Northeast Pacific where ecosystem variability can have profound impacts on marine life, fisheries, and coastal communities. Under NOAA’s Changing Ecosystems and Fisheries Initiative, we developed a seasonal ocean forecasting system for the Northeast Pacific based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) ocean model coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) sea ice model and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model. The model domain extends from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea with ~10 km horizontal resolution. To evaluate forecast skill, we produced a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months. Forcing for the forecasts was derived from the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory's Seamless System for Prediction and Earth System Research (GFDL-SPEAR) global climate forecast system. Forecasts were assessed using ocean reanalyses and in situ observations, focusing on three ecologically- and societally-relevant variables: sea surface temperature, bottom temperature, and bottom oxygen concentration. Forecast skill varies by region, variable, and season, but generally remains high (anomaly correlation coefficient; ACC>0.5) for lead times of at least several months across all variables and regions. The downscaled forecasts reduce errors relative to the SPEAR global forecasts and in some cases increase ACC, while also enabling predictions of biogeochemical variables. These new forecasts compare favorably to previous downscaled ocean forecasts off the U.S. west coast, with increased ACC and small forecast errors that may be reduced further by future methodological changes. Routine real-time forecasts, available starting in October 2026, will support proactive decision making by managers, industry, and coastal communities.

It's the top-ranked grant on the Plastic pathways slate, and the fit is real: the call asks for work that strengthens and operationalises the global observing network, and the project's core — tracking where marine litter moves and where it ends up — is exactly the kind of data-driven, observation-informed work that feeds into that. The biggest doubt: the call is heavily weighted toward *deploying* observation equipment and governance frameworks, so the proposal would need to frame the plastic-pathways modelling as a consumer of the observing system's data, not just a standalone modelling effort.

The other open grant on the slate, #16 (NSF OTIC), is about instrumentation development with broad applicability — a weaker match for a pathways/modelling project.

Here's the corrected summary.

## Where the project stands

I can see the project has three members — Jonah Whitcombe, Priya Raman, and you — but its confirmed state (goals, method, blockers, milestones) isn't visible to me right now. If the team hasn't confirmed the state in the app recently, it may be out of date; you can update it there.

## Three most relevant new papers

All three entered the project's slate this week:

1. **#6 — "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter"** (Lim & Hong, 2026, Zenodo). The closest match to the project: a three-phase beaching kernel for OceanParcels 3.1.4, validated against field records from Uido, Korea, using ROMS flow fields and particle trajectories. If Plastic pathways involves particle tracking of debris, this is the one to read first — it's a ready-made method plus code.

2. **#10 — "A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery"** (Rong et al., 2026, Remote Sensing). A YOLO11-based framework (with Dynamic Snake Convolution and CBAM) that detects and segments low-contrast, curved ocean features in MODIS imagery. It achieved detection Precision, Recall, and F1 of 92.01%, 80.73%, and 86.00%, and segmentation values of 93.14%, 82.60%, and 87.55%, the highest F1-scores among the evaluated methods. Relevant as a template for ML-based detection of debris or plumes in satellite imagery.

3. **#7 — "Comment on egusphere-2026-5844"** (2026). A seasonal ocean forecasting system for the Northeast Pacific (MOM6 + SIS2 + COBALT, ~10 km resolution, 32-year retrospective evaluation, routine forecasts from October 2026). Relevant to the transport side of the project: seasonal current and temperature forecasts are the kind of forcing field you'd drive a debris-tracking model with.

(The other new slate items — #4 on Arctic phytoplankton, #5 on a Pacific forecast system, #9 on multi-object tracking, #11 on biogeochemical-Argo — are further afield from plastic pathways.)

## One funding opportunity to apply to

**#8 — Ocean Technology and Interdisciplinary Coordination (OTIC), NSF** — deadline **15 February 2027**. It supports unsolicited proposals for instrumentation and technology development with broad applicability to ocean science. A natural angle for Plastic pathways: a novel observation or tracking capability for marine debris (e.g., a new sensor, a low-cost drift-tracker, or a detection pipeline) that the wider ocean science community could adopt. The project's method work on particle tracking and beaching kernels (#6) would give you a strong technical foundation for the proposal.

A second option worth keeping in view: **#12 — Integrating Remote Sensing and in-situ observations of Biodiversity** (Horizon Europe, €3–8M, deadline 22 September 2027), if the project can frame debris as a pollutant pressure on marine ecosystems and pair satellite detection with in-situ validation.

Suggested next steps: have the team confirm the project's state in the app so blockers and milestones are current, and read #6 in full to see how its beaching kernel maps onto your own tracking setup.

results.content:
#10 [paper] A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery over the Northern South China Sea
Authors: Guocai Rong, Huanhe Dong, Yuan Kong, Ze Liu, Yong Hui Fang
Venue: Remote Sensing
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18213843
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Automated extraction of internal solitary waves (ISWs) from satellite imagery is challenging due to their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast.
Method (Mycelium's reading): YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, incorporating Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) for curved structures and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for low-contrast features.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea; the framework was also applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020.
Abstract:
Internal solitary waves (ISWs) play an important role in ocean energy transport and mixing, yet their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast make automated extraction from satellite imagery challenging. To address these challenges, this study proposes YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint ISW detection and pixel-level segmentation. Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea was constructed for model training and evaluation. YOLO11-ISW achieved detection Precision, Recall, and F1-score values of 92.01%, 80.73%, and 86.00%, respectively, and segmentation values of 93.14%, 82.60%, and 87.55%, respectively. The model achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the evaluated methods. The segmentation results were further georeferenced to extract ISW crest-line locations, and the framework was applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020 to investigate satellite-observed ISW spatiotemporal variability. The detected ISWs exhibited pronounced spatial clustering, strong spring–summer seasonality, and clear lunar-cycle modulation, consistent with previous observations in the northern South China Sea. These results demonstrate the potential of YOLO11-ISW for automated, long-term, and large-scale monitoring of ISWs using satellite remote sensing imagery.

Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- advancing robust, policy-relevant ecosystem assessment, nature protection and restoration planning activities, and biodiversity trend prediction based on fit for purpose data, thus supporting EU biodiversity and climate objectives;

- strengthened capacity of researchers, practitioners and decision-makers to improve biodiversity monitoring practices and address knowledge gaps via the integration of data and observations across sensors and platforms, ranging from omics-based data (genomic, transcriptomic, metabolomic), various in-situ to satellite-based Earth observation data;

- enhanced usability of in-situ datasets as training and validation resources for statistical, machine learning and advanced AI-based approaches, in support of applications such as habitat classification, ecosystem mapping and biodiversity trend prediction.

Scope:

Achieving the goals of the EU biodiversity strategy for 2030, the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, and assessing progress towards their defined targets, requires coherent, integrated and long-term monitoring approaches, underpinned by FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Re-usable) data systems. Many existing in-situ data collections (i.e. genomic assessments, ground sampling, drone and airborne observations) were not designed with Satellite Remote Sensing integration in mind (i.e. for validation and calibration, integrated data products, or statistical scaling of information) and lack the structure, interface and metadata required to support advanced analytics, including AI. FAIR data on species and ecosystems will also help to ensure that biodiversity preservation is a mainstream feature of other sectors, such as agriculture, transport, energy or the bioeconomy. There is a need for systemic, harmonised or standardised biodiversity data at Earth’s surface in order to support AI applications ranging from genome to space and to build up our knowledge on the status and trends of habitats, species, ecosystems, and on the drivers of decline.

To address these challenges, proposals should:

- develop and validate fit-for-purpose multisensory biodiversity data integration systems, to enable omics-based and in-situ data harmonization and integration with remote sensing data from space or sub-orbital platforms, as well as socio-ecological and climatic data for enhancing assessment of ecosystem condition and degradation, and the predictive modelling of biodiversity trends at international, regional and European scales;

- develop concrete technical capabilities able to answer to diverse use cases, across terrestrial, freshwater and marine ecosystems in Member States and Associated Countries. - develop demonstration and verification cases focusing on specific ecosystems under the EU ecosystem typology[1] and habitats, including ecotones[2], identified as those under pressure or as restoration priorities. #7 [paper] Comment on egusphere-2026-5844
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2026-5844-rc2

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Providing seasonal ocean forecasts for the Northeast Pacific to support marine resource management and ecosystem variability assessment.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A seasonal ocean forecasting system based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model, forced by GFDL-SPEAR global climate forecasts, with a ~10 km horizontal re…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Northeast Pacific region extending from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea; evaluation uses a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months, assessed against ocean reanalyses and in situ observations.
Abstract:
Abstract. Seasonal ocean forecasts offer critical insights for marine resource management, particularly in regions like the Northeast Pacific where ecosystem variability can have profound impacts on marine life, fisheries, and coastal communities. Under NOAA’s Changing Ecosystems and Fisheries Initiative, we developed a seasonal ocean forecasting system for the Northeast Pacific based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) ocean model coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) sea ice model and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model. The model domain extends from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea with ~10 km horizontal resolution. To evaluate forecast skill, we produced a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months. Forcing for the forecasts was derived from the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory's Seamless System for Prediction and Earth System Research (GFDL-SPEAR) global climate forecast system. Forecasts were assessed using ocean reanalyses and in situ observations, focusing on three ecologically- and societally-relevant variables: sea surface temperature, bottom temperature, and bottom oxygen concentration. Forecast skill varies by region, variable, and season, but generally remains high (anomaly correlation coefficient; ACC>0.5) for lead times of at least several months across all variables and regions. The downscaled forecasts reduce errors relative to the SPEAR global forecasts and in some cases increase ACC, while also enabling predictions of biogeochemical variables. These new forecasts compare favorably to previous downscaled ocean forecasts off the U.S. west coast, with increased ACC and small forecast errors that may be reduced further by future methodological changes. Routine real-time forecasts, available starting in October 2026, will support proactive decision making by managers, industry, and coastal communities.

#10 [paper] A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery over the Northern South China Sea
Authors: Guocai Rong, Huanhe Dong, Yuan Kong, Ze Liu, Yong Hui Fang
Venue: Remote Sensing
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18213843
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Automated extraction of internal solitary waves (ISWs) from satellite imagery is challenging due to their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast.
Method (Mycelium's reading): YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, incorporating Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) for curved structures and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for low-contrast features.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea; the framework was also applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020.
Abstract:
Internal solitary waves (ISWs) play an important role in ocean energy transport and mixing, yet their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast make automated extraction from satellite imagery challenging. To address these challenges, this study proposes YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint ISW detection and pixel-level segmentation. Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea was constructed for model training and evaluation. YOLO11-ISW achieved detection Precision, Recall, and F1-score values of 92.01%, 80.73%, and 86.00%, respectively, and segmentation values of 93.14%, 82.60%, and 87.55%, respectively. The model achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the evaluated methods. The segmentation results were further georeferenced to extract ISW crest-line locations, and the framework was applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020 to investigate satellite-observed ISW spatiotemporal variability. The detected ISWs exhibited pronounced spatial clustering, strong spring–summer seasonality, and clear lunar-cycle modulation, consistent with previous observations in the northern South China Sea. These results demonstrate the potential of YOLO11-ISW for automated, long-term, and large-scale monitoring of ISWs using satellite remote sensing imagery.

The paper that matters most for the Marine heatwave early warning project is **#4 — "Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish"** (Stuart-Smith et al., 2026, Conservation Science and Practice).

Here's why it stands out:

**It's a real-world demonstration of your project's core idea working end-to-end.** The paper documents Australia's first pre-emptive rescue of a protected marine species, triggered specifically by a marine heatwave forecast. Ahead of the 2023/24 El Niño, forecasts indicated a high risk of MHWs. An expert workshop assessed the forecasted extremes (>20°C or +~3°C) as a severe threat, and that assessment triggered the emergency intervention. 25 red handfish were captured in January 2024 and held for 3 months while in-situ temperatures exceeded records — including 80 days more than 2°C above the long-term mean summer temperature. After the heatwave subsided, 18 were released and post-release survival was confirmed.

**Why it matters for your project specifically:**

1. **It validates the "early warning → action" pipeline.** Your project is about building the early warning capability. This paper shows what happens when that capability actually exists and is trusted enough to trigger a real conservation response. It's a concrete example of the value chain your project is building toward.

2. **It highlights the operational gap your project addresses.** The rescue was triggered by a climate forecast and expert judgment, not by a dedicated, systematic MHW early warning system. That's exactly the gap your project is working to close — turning ad-hoc forecast interpretation into a reliable, repeatable early warning process.

3. **It's a strong reference for impact and urgency.** If you're writing up the project's motivation, seeking funding, or communicating with stakeholders, this is a compelling, recent, peer-reviewed example of what's at stake when MHWs hit without warning.

The next most relevant paper is **#5** (Mojumder, 2026), which evaluates 1–14-day ML forecasts of MHWs against persistence benchmarks in the Northern Bay of Bengal. It's directly relevant to the forecasting methodology side of your project, but it's a thesis data/code release with a thinner abstract, so it's more of a methodological reference than a strategic one. #4 is the one that tells the story of why your project matters.

#4 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

The one that matters most is **#7 — "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter: development and application to field records from Uido, Republic of Korea"** (Lim & Hong, 2026, Zenodo).

Why it stands out for Plastic pathways:

- **It is the only item in the slate that is directly about marine litter.** The others are about ocean observing systems, phytoplankton, ocean forecast models, or unrelated ML topics.
- **It is a methods paper with open code.** It provides a three-phase beaching kernel plus six other particle kernels for OceanParcels 3.1.4, along with the scripts and aggregated results behind the manuscript (#7). That is directly reusable for particle-tracking work on where plastic ends up on shore.
- **It is validated against field records** from Uido, Korea, using ROMS flow fields and particle trajectories (#7) — so it's not just a model exercise, it's been checked against real beaching observations.

The practical value for your project: if Plastic pathways involves tracking where debris goes and where it beaches, this paper gives you a working, reproducible kernel and a full experiment setup to build on or adapt.

The next most relevant items are #12 (deep learning for detecting internal solitary waves in satellite imagery) and #4 (IEEE GRSS conference) if your project also has a remote-sensing detection component, but #7 is the clear top match for the core "pathways" question.

Here's the comparison, grounded in what each call actually asks for and what the Marine heatwave early warning project (#3) is about.

## The two calls at a glance

| | #1 GOOS / OceanEye | #2 Antarctica & Southern Ocean |
|---|---|---|
| **What it funds** | Strengthening the *global observing system*: deploying equipment, observing-system experiments (OSEs/OSSEs), network optimization, technology roadmaps with industry | *Understanding and projecting* the Antarctic/Southern Ocean: ocean–atmosphere–sea-ice–ice dynamics, Earth System Models, monitoring indicators |
| **Core question** | How do we keep global ocean observation continuous, open and resilient, and operationalise it? | How do we resolve uncertainties and improve near/mid/long-term projections of the region? |
| **Setting** | Global, with attention to under-observed regions (polar, deep sea) and areas beyond national jurisdiction | Specifically the Antarctic continental shelves and Southern Ocean, incl. bottom-water formation |
| **Amount** | €50,000,000 | €5,000,000–€11,000,000 |
| **Deadline** | 2027-02-16 | 2027-09-23 |

## Which fits the Marine heatwave early warning project better

**#1 (GOOS / OceanEye) is the stronger fit**, for three reasons:

1. **It's about the data backbone, which is what an early-warning system runs on.** The project's whole point is producing reliable marine heatwave forecasts, and that depends on a continuous, well-placed observing network feeding the models. #1 explicitly funds deploying observation equipment, running OSEs/OSSEs, and network optimization — exactly the "make the observations fit-for-purpose so the forecasts work" layer. #2 is about *understanding and projecting* a specific region's future, not about building the observation-to-forecast pipeline.

2. **It's global and service-oriented, matching a forecasting project.** #1 is framed around operational services (Copernicus Marine Service), data delivery, and climate resilience — the same "turn observations into a usable service" logic as an early-warning system. #2 is a regional science call centred on Antarctica and the Southern Ocean; unless the project's heatwave focus is specifically in that region, it's a narrower and less direct match.

3. **The scale fits a multi-partner, infrastructure-heavy effort.** At €50M, #1 is built for a consortium that deploys hardware and coordinates across communities — a natural shape for a lab building an early-warning capability. #2's €5–11M is a more contained research project.

**Where #2 could still make sense:** if the project's heatwave work is specifically about the Southern Ocean / Antarctic shelves (e.g. heatwave impacts on bottom-water formation or sea-ice–ocean feedbacks), #2's explicit mention of "extreme events" and improving regional projections would be a genuine hook. But as a general marine-heatwave early-warning project, #1 aligns more directly.

One caveat: I could only see the project's name and members (#3), not its full confirmed state (problem, method, blockers), so this is grounded in the project's stated aim and the two calls' scopes rather than its detailed current plan. If you tell me whether the project's focus is global/coastal or specifically Southern Ocean, I can sharpen the call.

Here's what I found, in three parts.

---

## 1. Best-fitting open grant

**#2 — "Advancing understanding, modelling and prediction of extreme events in a changing climate"** (Horizon CL5-2027-01-D1-07) is the strongest match.

- **Why it fits:** The call explicitly asks for AI-based approaches, a hierarchy of models (including digital twins), seamless prediction from short-term to multi-decadal scales, and improved early warning systems for extreme events. Your project's core — ML-driven marine heatwave prediction and data assimilation for early warning — sits squarely in that scope. The deadline is **4 March 2027**, giving you about four months.
- **Biggest doubt:** The call is broad (all extreme events, continental to local scale), so a marine-heatwave-only proposal would need to be framed as a concrete case study within a wider extremes narrative. You'd want to show how your work contributes to the EU's climate risk assessment and early-warning strategy, not just a single hazard.

The other open grants on the project's slate are less aligned:
- #29 (NSF OTIC) is about instrumentation development, not prediction.
- #30 (GOOS) is about observing-system infrastructure and governance.
- #31 (carbon sources/sinks) is a different science question.
- #32 (Antarctica/Southern Ocean) is regionally specific.
- #9 (biodiversity data integration) is adjacent but not the core fit.

---

## 2. Who in the lab should lead

The nightly ranking and the requirement-slot check point to two people:

- **Tomás Ferreira-Lind (#18)** — the ranking names him first. His declared interest in **physics-informed ML** and his work on fast surrogates for ocean models maps directly onto the call's ask for "AI-based approaches" and "seamless prediction and projection modelling." He's the strongest technical lead for the modelling/prediction core of the proposal.

- **You (Mara Ellison, #14)** — the ranking names you second, on the strength of the lab's focus on marine heatwave forecasting with ML and data assimilation. As PI and the person who declared interests in **marine heatwave prediction**, **ocean data assimilation**, and **sea surface temperature forecasting**, you're the natural lead for the application as a whole — you can frame the project's problem, connect it to the call's expected outcomes, and anchor the early-warning narrative.

**Suggested split:** You lead the application (PI), with Tomás as the technical lead on the modelling/prediction work package. Sun-hee Park (#17) could contribute on the data-tools and operationalisation side, though her declared profile is more general ("ocean data tools") than the others.

**Gaps the call names that no one in the lab covers (from the slot check):**
- "Extreme events in a changing climate" as a declared expertise (the lab covers marine heatwaves specifically, but no one has declared the broader extremes framing)
- Digital twins
- Copernicus / Destination Earth integration

These are the slots you'd need to fill with external partners or by reframing existing work.

---

## 3. Who outside the lab could partner

This is where I have to be honest: **collaborator search is turned off on this instance**, so I could not run introduction-path lookups for external people. I tried several routes (by name, by paper reference, by username) and none returned a visible co-authorship chain. What I *can* say from the papers in the project's slate:

- **Alexia Karwat** (first author, #26, *Nature Communications* 2026) — multi-year MHW predictability in coral reef regions, using CESM2 and ocean-assimilated hindcasts. Her work on multi-year prediction skill and anthropogenic warming as a dominant source of forecast skill is directly complementary to your project's early-warning goal.
- **Young-Jin Kang** (first author, #28, *Frontiers in Marine Science* 2026) — operational multi-horizon MHW forecasting for South Korean aquaculture, with a graph–temporal deep-learning architecture and a demonstrated 38-hour advisory lead time. This is the closest published work to your project's operational early-warning aim.
- **Eurida Liyana** (first author, #19, 2026) — ROMS-based MHW detection with eddy diagnostics in the Adriatic, linking mesoscale dynamics to MHW precursors. Useful for the "understanding and attribution" side of the call.

These three are the most natural external partners based on the papers Mycelium has already surfaced for your project. I could not verify whether any of them are reachable through a co-authorship chain visible to you, so I'd suggest you check your own networks or reach out directly.

---

**What I could not check:**
- Eligibility rules for #2 (career stage, institution type, EU membership requirements) — the call text I read does not spell these out, and I have no visibility into your institution's eligibility.
- Whether the external authors above are in institutions eligible for Horizon Europe funding.
- Any introduction paths, because collaborator search is off.

If you'd like, I can dig into any of the other open grants in more detail, or pull the full text of any of the papers above to help you draft the partnership case.

results.content:
# Judging a call's fit

1. Read the call with `corpus_item` (deadlines, eligibility, amount, whether it is
   still open). If it is closed, say so first.
2. Read who it is for: `projects_get` for a project, `org_lab` for a lab,
   `me_profile` / `me_interests` for the person.
3. Compare concretely: the call's aims against the project's problem and
   method; its eligibility rules (career stage, citizenship, institution type)
   against what you know; its deadline against the project's milestones.
4. Say what fits, what does not, and what you could not check (eligibility you
   cannot see, a budget you do not know). Never guess eligibility.
5. If the question is who should apply, read the `who-should-apply` skill.

Honesty rules, as in Mylo's reports: no scores or percentages, no hype, no
"perfect fit". One plain sentence on the strongest reason and one on the
biggest doubt. Cite the call and the project by #n.

4. Do not rank people with numbers, and do not judge anyone's eligibility you
   cannot see.

#26 [paper] Marine heat waves in vulnerable coral reef regions are skillfully predictable on multi-year timescales
Authors: Alexia Karwat, June‐Yi Lee, Christian L. E. Franzke, Yong‐Yub Kim, Eun Young Kwon, Sun‐Seon Lee
Venue: Nature Communications
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-78279-1
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The limited understanding of the predictability of marine heat waves (MHWs) in coral reef regions beyond seasonal timescales.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Analysis of Community Earth System Model version 2 simulations, ocean-assimilated experiments, and five-year hindcasts initialized annually from 1981 to 2020 to assess MHW frequency, cumulative intensity, and duration.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): 12 vulnerable coral reef regions across various ocean basins, using historical data from 1981 to 2020.
Abstract:
Marine heat waves (MHWs) increasingly threaten coral reefs, but their predictability beyond seasonal timescales remains poorly understood. Here we assess the seasonal-to-multi-year predictability of MHW frequency, cumulative intensity, and duration across 12 coral reef regions. Using Community Earth System Model version 2 simulations, ocean-assimilated experiments and five-year hindcasts initialized annually from 1981 to 2020, we show that frequency and cumulative intensity are predictable for several months to multiple years across many ocean basins, with skill varying strongly by region and season. Anthropogenic warming is the dominant source of multi-year skill across most hotspots, while internal variability limits predictability in the equatorial Pacific. El Niño-Southern Oscillation and Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation further modulate regional forecasts through coupled ocean-atmosphere processes. These findings reveal strong regional contrasts in the sources and limits of forecast skill, identifying where advance warning can support timely, targeted regional preparedness, coral reef conservation and adaptation to escalating thermal stress. The study shows that marine heatwave frequency and cumulative intensity across vulnerable coral reef regions are skillfully predictable from months to years ahead, with long-term anthropogenic warming accounting for most multi-year forecast skill, while internal variability, particularly El Niño, limits predictability in the equatorial Pacific.

#28 [paper] Multi-horizon forecasting of coastal high water temperature events for operational marine-heatwave early warning in South Korean aquaculture: a walk-forward benchmark of eleven statistical and deep-le
Authors: Young-Jin Kang, Ki-Hwan Kim, Seok Chan Jeong
Venue: Frontiers in Marine Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2026.1887350
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Introduction High water temperature (HWT) marine-heatwave events along the southern coast of South Korea cause repeated mass mortalities in cage aquaculture of olive flounder (Paralichthys olivaceus), rock bream (Oplegnathus fasciatus), red sea bream (Pagrus major) and Korean rockfish (Sebastes schlegelii). Existing operational forecasts rely on coarse numerical ocean models that lack the temporal granularity and site specificity required by farm managers, while the recent wave of deep-learning sea surface temperature (SST) models has been tuned almost exclusively on smoother open-ocean grids. Methods We present the Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM, a 3.1 M-parameter graph–temporal architecture combining a weighted spatial GNN with a BiLSTM temporal core, reversible instance normalization (RevIN) and a persistence skip connection, and benchmark it against ten alternatives – three reference baselines (Persistence, Seasonal-naïve, Climatology), the ARIMAX statistical model, four lightweight or linear deep models (DLinear, PatchTST, N-HiTS, CNN-LSTM) and two attention-based models (Informer, Temporal Fusion Transformer) – on a five-year hourly insitu panel from 30 monitoring stations along the Tongyeong–Geoje–Yeosu coast (2020–2025) under a unified rolling-origin walk-forward protocol (720 h lookback, 168 h horizon, one forecast per station every 24 h across a 12-month validation window). Marine-heatwave detection is scored at tiered 26/28/30 °C operational thresholds. Results The Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM achieves the lowest 1 h RMSE (0.057 °C), 0.85 °C at h = 72 and 1.24 °C at h = 168, with the highest long-horizon residual skill of any deep model on this panel (SS_res = 0.71 at h = 72). CNNLSTM attains the lowest mean horizon root-mean-square error (RMSE = 0.636 °C) thanks to a nearly flat error curve, and PatchTST is competitive at short-to-medium horizons (0.694 °C mean). The Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM reaches F1 = 0.82 at 26 °C and F1 = 0.65 at 28 °C, and a probabilistic Gaussian negative-log-likelihood head supplies calibrated 90 % prediction intervals without post-hoc recalibration. Discussion A 38 h mean advisory lead time was demonstrated in the 2024 NIFS regional HWT alert period, indicating that a site-specific graph–temporal model can deliver operationally actionable early warning for coastal aquaculture.

#19 [paper] Model-Based Marine Heatwave Detection with Eddy Diagnostics in the Adriatic Sea: Regional Insights with Global Relevance
Authors: Eurida Liyana, Francesco Memmola, Pierpaolo Falco
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.22541/essoar.15010054/v1
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The intensification, increasing frequency, and duration of marine heatwave (MHW) events, particularly in vulnerable semi-enclosed coastal basins like the Adriatic Sea.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Integration of a high-resolution Regional Ocean Modeling System (ROMS) with an eddy detection and tracking algorithm and analysis of long-term observational temperature data.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): The Adriatic Sea (AS).
Abstract:
Marine heatwave (MHW) events are intensifying globally, doubling in frequency and increasing in duration and spatial distribution over recent decades. Semi-enclosed coastal basins are particularly vulnerable, and the Adriatic Sea (AS) exemplifies a fast-reacting system, making it a natural laboratory for studying climate-driven ocean variability and impacts on ecosystems, fisheries, and aquaculture. In this study, we assess the capability of a high-resolution Regional Ocean Modeling System (ROMS) to detect and simulate MHW events in the AS. We integrate this modeling framework with an eddy detection and tracking algorithm, alongside comprehensive analysis of long-term observational temperature data, to investigate the role of mesoscale eddies in modulating surface and subsurface MHW evolution. Results demonstrate that ROMS effectively reproduces the timing and spatial patterns of historical MHWs in the AS, showing strong agreement between modeled and observed MHWs, with eddy structures frequently coinciding with subsurface thermal anomalies preceding MHWs. These findings highlight the value of coupling regional ocean models with mesoscale eddy diagnostics to advance understanding of MHW occurrences and drivers, and to strengthen early-warning capabilities. Enhanced understanding of MHW precursors and eddy interactions in the AS provides a pathway for anticipating hazards, informing adaptive measures for coastal stakeholders, and improving regional climate resilience. Beyond the Adriatic, this framework offers a transferable approach to other semi-enclosed and shelf seas, where reliable detection of MHW drivers is essential. By linking detection with predictive understanding, this work contributes to broader efforts to improve preparedness for marine extremes and safeguard ecosystems and dependent economies in a warming ocean.

#25 [paper] Rethinking Marine Heatwaves: Towards a Probabilistic Marine Heat Stress
Authors: Natalija Dunić, Krešimir Ruić, Ivica Vilibić
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.22541/essoar.15011394/v1
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Standard marine heatwave (MHW) definitions rely on statistical temperature anomalies relative to a climatological baseline, which does not directly account for the thermal exposure experienced by marine organisms or its biological consequences.
Method (Mycelium's reading): The Probabilistic Marine Heat Stress Wave (PMHSW) framework, which integrates temperature exceedance above a biological threshold across time and depth to estimate cumulative thermal exposure and relates this exposure to the probability of a defined biological response.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Synthetic examples used to demonstrate the estimation of response functions from biological observations and the derivation of binary event definitions.
Abstract:
Marine heatwaves (MHWs) are commonly defined as statistically extreme temperature events relative to a climatological baseline. While this approach provides a consistent description of ocean temperature extremes, it does not directly account for the thermal exposure experienced by marine organisms or its biological consequences. Here, we propose the Probabilistic Marine Heat Stress Wave (PMHSW) framework, which shifts the focus from temperature anomalies toward biologically relevant thermal exposure. The framework integrates temperature exceedance above a biological threshold across time and depth to estimate cumulative thermal exposure and relates this exposure to the probability of a defined biological response. The probabilistic formulation allows differences among organisms, habitats and thermal tolerances to be represented while retaining a continuous description of biological heat stress. Using synthetic examples, we demonstrate how the response function can be estimated from biological observations and how a binary event definition can be obtained when needed. The PMHSW framework is intended as a complementary approach to existing MHW definitions, particularly when the objective is to assess the potential biological consequences of marine thermal extremes under present and future climate conditions.

The paper that matters most for the Marine heatwave early warning project is **#4 — "Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish"** (Stuart-Smith et al., 2026, Conservation Science and Practice).

Here's why it stands out from the rest of the slate:

**It's the only paper that closes the loop from forecast to action.** The others are about building or evaluating forecasts; #4 shows what happens *after* a forecast — a concrete, pre-emptive rescue of a Critically Endangered species triggered by a marine heatwave forecast ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño. For an early warning project, the value of a forecast is only as good as the response it enables, and #4 is a worked example of exactly that chain.

**It gives you a template for your own early warning pipeline.** The paper describes the whole decision sequence: climate forecast → expert workshop risk assessment → threshold definition (>20°C or +~3°C) → approval → intervention → post-release monitoring. That's essentially the operating model your project is building, documented with real numbers (25 fish captured, 80 days >2°C above the long-term mean, 18 released, survival confirmed after 2 months).

**It's recent and directly on-topic.** The other slate items touch adjacent areas — #5 is an ML forecast evaluation in the Bay of Bengal, #3 is a seasonal ocean forecasting system for the Northeast Pacific, #8 is a regional forecast system analysis — but none of them connect a heatwave forecast to a management or conservation response the way #4 does.

If I had to pick a second, it would be **#5** (the 1–14-day ML forecast evaluation against persistence benchmarks), since it speaks to the forecasting skill question your project depends on. But #4 is the one that shows the project's end goal in practice.

One caveat: I couldn't see the project's confirmed state or open blockers in this conversation, so I'm ranking by topical fit to the project's stated goal. If the team has a specific blocker — say, defining alert thresholds or a response protocol — #4 speaks to that directly.

#4 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

Method (Mycelium's reading): A seasonal ocean forecasting system based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model, forced by GFDL-SPEAR global climate forecasts, with a ~10 km horizontal re…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Northeast Pacific region extending from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea; evaluation uses a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months, assessed against ocean reanalyses and in situ observations.
Abstract:
Abstract. Seasonal ocean forecasts offer critical insights for marine resource management, particularly in regions like the Northeast Pacific where ecosystem variability can have profound impacts on marine life, fisheries, and coastal communities. Under NOAA’s Changing Ecosystems and Fisheries Initiative, we developed a seasonal ocean forecasting system for the Northeast Pacific based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) ocean model coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) sea ice model and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model. The model domain extends from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea with ~10 km horizontal resolution. To evaluate forecast skill, we produced a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months. Forcing for the forecasts was derived from the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory's Seamless System for Prediction and Earth System Research (GFDL-SPEAR) global climate forecast system. Forecasts were assessed using ocean reanalyses and in situ observations, focusing on three ecologically- and societally-relevant variables: sea surface temperature, bottom temperature, and bottom oxygen concentration. Forecast skill varies by region, variable, and season, but generally remains high (anomaly correlation coefficient; ACC>0.5) for lead times of at least several months across all variables and regions. The downscaled forecasts reduce errors relative to the SPEAR global forecasts and in some cases increase ACC, while also enabling predictions of biogeochemical variables. These new forecasts compare favorably to previous downscaled ocean forecasts off the U.S. west coast, with increased ACC and small forecast errors that may be reduced further by future methodological changes. Routine real-time forecasts, available starting in October 2026, will support proactive decision making by managers, industry, and coastal communities.

The clear stand-out is **#7 — "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter: development and application to field records from Uido, Republic of Korea"** (Lim & Hong, 2026).

**Why it matters most for Plastic pathways:**

- **It is the only item on the slate that is about marine litter itself.** The others are about ocean observing systems (#3), remote sensing symposia (#4), phytoplankton (#5), ocean forecast systems (#6, #9), or computer-vision tracking (#11, #12). #7 is squarely in the project's domain.
- **It is a methods paper with open code.** It ships a three-phase beaching kernel plus six other particle kernels for OceanParcels 3.1.4, the experiment scripts, and the aggregated result files behind every number in the manuscript (#7). That means Jonah, Priya and you could lift the kernel directly into your own particle-tracking setup rather than rebuilding a beaching scheme from scratch.
- **It is validated against field records.** The kernel was developed and tested against actual beaching records from Uido, Korea, using ROMS flow fields and particle trajectories (#7) — a useful template for how to validate your own pathway models against ground truth.
- **It is recent and current** (2026, still open) and entered the slate on 2026-11-10, so it is fresh.

**Honorable mention:** #9 (the seasonal ocean forecasting system for the Northeast Pacific) is the second most relevant — its ~10 km MOM6-based forecasts of SST, bottom temperature and oxygen could feed the transport models that drive plastic pathway predictions — but it is a forecasting-systems paper, not a litter paper.

One caveat: I could not see the project's confirmed state or open blockers for Plastic pathways in this conversation, so this ranking is based on topical fit with the project's subject matter. If the team has a specific open blocker (e.g., "need a validated beaching scheme" or "need flow fields for a region"), #7 is the item that speaks to it most directly.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Automated extraction of internal solitary waves (ISWs) from satellite imagery is challenging due to their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast.
Method (Mycelium's reading): YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, incorporating Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) for curved structures and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for low-contrast features.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea; the framework was also applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020.
Abstract:
Internal solitary waves (ISWs) play an important role in ocean energy transport and mixing, yet their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast make automated extraction from satellite imagery challenging. To address these challenges, this study proposes YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint ISW detection and pixel-level segmentation. Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea was constructed for model training and evaluation. YOLO11-ISW achieved detection Precision, Recall, and F1-score values of 92.01%, 80.73%, and 86.00%, respectively, and segmentation values of 93.14%, 82.60%, and 87.55%, respectively. The model achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the evaluated methods. The segmentation results were further georeferenced to extract ISW crest-line locations, and the framework was applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020 to investigate satellite-observed ISW spatiotemporal variability. The detected ISWs exhibited pronounced spatial clustering, strong spring–summer seasonality, and clear lunar-cycle modulation, consistent with previous observations in the northern South China Sea. These results demonstrate the potential of YOLO11-ISW for automated, long-term, and large-scale monitoring of ISWs using satellite remote sensing imagery.

Authors: Zhenhua Zhang, Peng Chen, Siqi Zhang, Delu Pan
Venue: Science Advances
Year: 2026

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Arctic marine productivity is traditionally considered concentrated in the sunlit season, yet low-light winter-shoulder periods remain poorly constrained because passive ocean color observations require sufficient solar illumination.
Method (Mycelium's reading): The authors used 2.39 million spaceborne LiDAR profiles from CALIOP (2006–2023) to reconstruct Arctic net primary production (NPP). A bio-optical retrieval model was trained using MODIS-constrained observations under illuminated conditions, and low-light estimates were generated as physically const…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Arctic region, specifically marginal seas and seasonal ice-edge regions, using spaceborne LiDAR data from 2006 to 2023.
Abstract:
Arctic marine productivity is traditionally considered concentrated in the sunlit season, yet low-light winter-shoulder periods remain poorly constrained because passive ocean color observations require sufficient solar illumination. Here, we use 2.39 million spaceborne LiDAR profiles from CALIOP (2006–2023) to reconstruct Arctic net primary production (NPP) and evaluate how active-sensor observations reduce this seasonal blind spot. The bio-optical retrieval model was trained using MODIS-constrained observations under illuminated conditions; accordingly, low-light estimates represent physically constrained extrapolations beyond the primary MODIS-observable training domain rather than direct NPP measurements. Within this framework, LiDAR increases winter half-year observational coverage from ∼20 to 30% to ∼70 to 75% and reveals widespread low-light winter-shoulder production across marginal seas and seasonal ice-edge regions. Pan-Arctic NPP integrated over this period increased at an estimated rate of 0.75 Tg C year −1 during 2007–2023, whereas the corresponding passive-sensor signal was negligible. Accounting for this component raises annual Arctic NPP estimates by ∼13.3% indicating that passive sensor-based assessments may underrepresent the magnitude and seasonal structure of Arctic productivity. Associations with declining sea ice and surface warming suggest this underrepresented production is consistent with ongoing seasonal reorganization of Arctic carbon fixation. Uncertainties from model parameterization, low-light extrapolation, and limited in situ validation are largest in the lowest-light and highest-latitude regimes. These findings do not imply photosynthesis during absolute polar night, but show that active LiDAR observations with explicit light constraints and transparent extrapolation limits can test how unresolved low-light winter-shoulder production may alter Arctic NPP seasonality under continuing sea-ice loss.

Method (Mycelium's reading): A seasonal ocean forecasting system based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model, forced by GFDL-SPEAR global climate forecasts, with a ~10 km horizontal re…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Northeast Pacific region extending from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea; evaluation uses a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months, assessed against ocean reanalyses and in situ observations.
Abstract:
Abstract. Seasonal ocean forecasts offer critical insights for marine resource management, particularly in regions like the Northeast Pacific where ecosystem variability can have profound impacts on marine life, fisheries, and coastal communities. Under NOAA’s Changing Ecosystems and Fisheries Initiative, we developed a seasonal ocean forecasting system for the Northeast Pacific based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) ocean model coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) sea ice model and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model. The model domain extends from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea with ~10 km horizontal resolution. To evaluate forecast skill, we produced a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months. Forcing for the forecasts was derived from the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory's Seamless System for Prediction and Earth System Research (GFDL-SPEAR) global climate forecast system. Forecasts were assessed using ocean reanalyses and in situ observations, focusing on three ecologically- and societally-relevant variables: sea surface temperature, bottom temperature, and bottom oxygen concentration. Forecast skill varies by region, variable, and season, but generally remains high (anomaly correlation coefficient; ACC>0.5) for lead times of at least several months across all variables and regions. The downscaled forecasts reduce errors relative to the SPEAR global forecasts and in some cases increase ACC, while also enabling predictions of biogeochemical variables. These new forecasts compare favorably to previous downscaled ocean forecasts off the U.S. west coast, with increased ACC and small forecast errors that may be reduced further by future methodological changes. Routine real-time forecasts, available starting in October 2026, will support proactive decision making by managers, industry, and coastal communities.

Here's the comparison.

**#1 — A stronger Global Ocean Observing System** (€50M, deadline 2027-02-16)
This call is about building and sustaining the *infrastructure* of ocean observation — deploying equipment, running observing-system experiments, network optimisation, and technology roadmaps with industry, all under the GOOS/Copernicus framework. The expected outcomes are about resilient observing capacity, EU strategic autonomy, and biodiversity data delivery.

**#2 — Unlocking a safe operating space for Antarctica and the Southern Ocean** (€5–11M, deadline 2027-09-23)
This call is about *understanding and projecting* the future of the Southern Ocean and Antarctic cryosphere: resolving uncertainties in near/mid/long-term change, improving Earth System and regional coupled models, distinguishing human from natural change, and — explicitly — studying **extreme events** and abrupt/irreversible changes in ocean circulation.

**Which fits the Marine heatwave early warning project (#3) better?**

#2 is the stronger fit. The project's core is *predicting* marine heatwaves — a forecasting/projection problem — and #2's scope directly names extreme events, improving regional coupled models, and reducing uncertainty in projected ocean changes. That is the same kind of work the project does. #1, by contrast, is an infrastructure and governance call: it wants deployed sensors, observing-system experiments, and technology roadmaps. A heatwave early-warning project could *use* the data #1 produces, but it is not itself an observing-systems project, so it would be a stretch to frame it under #1.

**Biggest doubt / what I could not check:**
- I could not open the project's full state (its confirmed problem, method, milestones, or blockers) — the detail view was not available to me in this conversation — so I'm comparing the grants against what the project's name and your declared interests (marine heatwave prediction, SST forecasting) tell me. If the project has a strong *observing* component (e.g. it is building a new sensor network or data-assimilation pipeline for heatwave detection), #1 becomes more competitive.
- I could not see either call's full eligibility rules (consortium size, country/citizenship requirements, SME participation), so I can't confirm your lab is eligible for either.

**Practical note:** #1 has a much earlier deadline (2027-02-16) and a much larger budget (€50M vs €5–11M). If you want to pursue #1, you'd need to reframe the project around an observing-systems contribution. If the project is primarily a forecasting/modelling effort, #2 is the natural home and you have until 2027-09-23.

# Judging a call's fit

1. Read the call with `corpus_item` (deadlines, eligibility, amount, whether it is

Here's what I found:

---

## Best-fitting open grant: #15 — A stronger Global Ocean Observing System (€50M, deadline 2027-02-16)

**Why it fits the Marine heatwave early warning project (#7):**

The project's core method is combining ocean data assimilation with machine learning to produce marine heatwave forecasts and hand them to coastal managers. Grant #15 asks for proposals that "stabilise, further strengthen and operationalise the global ocean observing system" — which is exactly what a heatwave early-warning system does: it turns observations (satellite, in-situ) into actionable forecasts. The grant explicitly values data delivery "fit-for purpose, cost efficient and designed across all its components," and the project's dashboard-to-manager pipeline maps directly onto that.

**The biggest doubt:** #15 is a €50M Horizon Europe call focused on *global* observing infrastructure, areas beyond national jurisdiction, and EU strategic autonomy. The project is a lab-scale, regional early-warning effort. The scale gap is real — you'd need to frame the project as a component of a larger consortium, not as the whole proposal.

**By comparison, #10 (NSF OTIC, deadline 2027-02-15)** is about *instrumentation development* with broad applicability. The project's method is data assimilation and ML forecasting, not building new instruments. No one in the lab has a declared profile covering instrumentation development, so the fit is weaker.

---

## Who in the lab should lead

For #15, the nightly ranking and declared profiles point to two people:

- **You (Mara Ellison, #2)** — declared: ocean data assimilation, ocean extremes. You cover the "strengthen and operationalise the observing system" slot from your declared profile. You're also the PI and the project's lead, so you're the natural applicant.
- **Priya Raman (#4)** — declared: satellite oceanography, coastal water quality. She covers the same slot from her satellite remote sensing expertise, which is a strong complement to your data-assimilation angle.

**Suggested lead:** You, as PI and project owner, with Priya as co-PI or senior co-applicant to bring the satellite-observation pillar. Tomás (#6) is a project member with physics-informed ML, which supports the forecasting method, but his declared profile (circulation and turbulence) is less directly tied to the observing-system framing that #15 asks for.

**Gaps no one in the lab covers:** observing system experiments (OSEs), observing system simulation experiments (OSSEs), network optimisation approaches, and areas beyond national jurisdiction. These are the slots you'd need to fill with external partners.

---

## Who outside the lab could partner

Collaborator search is turned off on this instance, so I can't pull a list of specific external people. But based on the gaps and the grant's requirements, here's what to look for:

1. **An OSE/OSSE specialist** — someone who runs observing system experiments or simulation experiments. This is a core method #15 asks for and no one in the lab declares it. Look for oceanographers who run data-assimilation experiments with satellite or in-situ networks.
2. **A network-optimisation person** — someone who designs or optimises observing networks (e.g., Argo, glider arrays, satellite constellations). This is another gap.
3. **An ABNJ (areas beyond national jurisdiction) expert** — the grant explicitly asks for focus on areas beyond national jurisdiction. A physical oceanographer or marine policy person with that focus would strengthen the proposal.
4. **An industry or technology-provider partner** — #15 lists "industry" as a role it asks for but never matches to a profile. A marine-technology SME or a Copernicus service operator would cover this.

**Practical next step:** Since collaborator search is off, you'd need to identify these partners manually — through your department, the GOOS community, or existing co-author networks. If you turn on collaborator search in the app, Mylo can match people to the gaps above.

#11 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

#16 [paper] Data‐Driven Parameterization of Arctic Ocean Turbulent Mixing
Authors: Rafael Sebastian Reiss, Lisanne Blok, Nicholas Leonard, Kate Oglethorpe, Alberto C. Naveira Garabato, Colm-cille P. Caulfield, Ali Mashayek
Venue: Geophysical Research Letters
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1029/2026gl123721
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Arctic Ocean turbulent mixing is poorly characterized due to sparse observations, limitations of conventional parameterizations, and incomplete understanding, despite its importance for regional dynamics and global overturning.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Training gradient-boosted decision trees on global microstructure turbulence data to predict turbulent dissipation from hydrographic variables, using spatial block cross-validation for evaluation.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Global microstructure turbulence data (>5,000 profiles) for training; pan-Arctic hydrographic observations and high-resolution model output for application.
Abstract:
Abstract Turbulent mixing may become increasingly important in a changing Arctic Ocean, influencing regional dynamics and global overturning. Arctic turbulence remains poorly characterized due to sparse observations, limitations of conventional parameterizations, and incomplete understanding. We train gradient‐boosted decision trees on global microstructure turbulence data (>5,000 profiles; ∼ data points) to predict turbulent dissipation from more widely available hydrography. Global training is essential for skill across non‐Arctic and Arctic regions (, 75% within a factor of 2 of observations; = 0.47–0.55 under spatial block cross‐validation). Applied to pan‐Arctic hydrographic observations, predictions show enhanced dissipation along margins and shelves and weaker values in basin interiors, consistent with current understanding. Applied to high‐resolution model output, predictions reveal diffusivities and a basin‐integrated irreversible buoyancy flux consistent with observations, yet markedly different from the common K‐Profile Parameterization—with implications for simulated tracer transport. Our parameterization can help assess climate‐mixing feedbacks in projections while physics‐based parameterizations mature.

#17 [paper] Rescene-ESM: an Earth system model built around a frozen AI weather model
Authors: Minjong Cheon, Kaoru Kakinuma
Year: 2026
Link: https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/e1c22d8441861158dd7f9e6021cb718096d3f29f
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The high computational cost of Earth system models limits the exploration of scenarios and ensemble members, while existing machine-learning weather models coupled to oceans have produced weak El Niño variability or relied on climate-model output, and none effectively routes climate impacts through…
Method (Mycelium's reading): Rescene-ESM, an Earth system model using a coupler named YAHO that links a frozen 20.8-million-parameter AI weather model to physically formulated ocean, sea-ice, land, river, carbon, and energy components constrained by observations; the model uses an interactive mixed layer, an equatorial wave oc…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Simulations of approximately 1,000 years on one graphics processing unit; evaluation against observed climate data from 1979-2022; routing of runoff to 212 river gauges; and future projections for SSP1 and SSP3 scenarios for the period 2081-2100.
Abstract:
Earth system models underpin climate projections, but their cost limits how many scenarios, ensemble members and impact pathways can be explored. Machine-learning weather models forecast as skillfully as physics-based models at a fraction of the cost, yet coupled to an ocean they have produced weak El Nino variability or have learned it from climate-model output, and none carries the climate through rivers to the people exposed to it. Here we present Rescene-ESM, an Earth system model whose coupler, YAHO, yokes a frozen 20.8-million-parameter AI weather model to physically formulated ocean, sea-ice, land, river, carbon and energy components constrained by observations. Adding the couplings one at a time shows what each contributes: over a climatological ocean the AI atmosphere varies from year to year by a third of the observed amount over the oceans, and an interactive mixed layer, an equatorial wave ocean, the residual of the observed sea surface temperature (SST) equation as stochastic forcing and the land's moisture flux raise this step by step and bring El Nino and its teleconnections, leaving the mean climate almost unchanged. The full model simulates about 1,000 years per day on one graphics processing unit, holds the observed climate for a thousand years without drift, reproduces the observed 1979-2022 global warming, carries forced change with a physically based structure around the frozen network (transient climate response 1.60 K), routes runoff to 212 river gauges with a median seasonal-cycle correlation of 0.79 and, driven by emissions, separates the heatwave exposure of an SSP1 and an SSP3 world by a factor of 4.7 in 2081-2100, three-quarters of it through the warmer climate.
